subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUSPENSION OF REGULATIONS MADE UNDER ACT OF 1950
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that an order in council has been passed, effective tomorrow, suspending all the regulations made under the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act.
This act was passed by parliament in September, 1950, and the first regulations under the act came into force in November of that
year. The regulations were considerably stiffened in March, 1951, and generally speaking required down payments of one-half of the selling price in the case of motorcars and motorcycles, and one-third for all other commodities, with the balance to be paid within the succeeding twelve months. Last January the regulations were relaxed by permitting payments of the balance to be spread over a maximum period of eighteen months.
The situation with respect to consumer credit is now such that I believe we can safely suspend the operation of these regulations. However, if conditions made it necessary, I would have no hesitation in recommending the reintroduction of consumer credit controls, and in view of existing uncertainties I believe the present legislative basis for such control should be maintained. For this reason the government will invite both houses of parliament to present addresses to the governor general praying that the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act be continued for a further period. Hon. members will recall that this act is purely an enabling act authorizing the governor in council to make regulations respecting the control of consumer credit, and that under its own terms it will expire on July 31 next, unless the action I have suggested is taken.

subtopic: BREAK IN P.F.R.A. DAM ON FRENCHMAN RIVER
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the federal government been asked for financial assistance to restore damaged property, including that in Eastend, Saskatchewan, resulting from the break in the P.F.R.A. dam on the Frenchman river? Will such assistance be granted?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BREAK IN P.F.R.A. DAM ON FRENCHMAN RIVER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman sent me notice of his intention to ask this question. On April 29 the premier of Saskatchewan telegraphed me about floods in southwestern Saskatchewan, and stated that Hon. J. H. Sturdy, minister of social welfare, was then in Ottawa, and asked if he could not see me, or some other member of the government, in that connection. I replied at once as follows:
Re your telegram concerning floods in Saskatchewan. All the information that we have comes to us through the P.F.R.A., and because the P.F.R.A. reports to the Minister of Agriculture, arrangements are being made for Mr. Sturdy to see Mr. Gardiner.
I understand that Mr. Sturdy and the deputy minister of his department, together with the mayor of Swift Current and the mayor of Eastend, did see the Minister of [Mr. Speaker.)

Agriculture, and perhaps it would be more convenient if the Minister of Agriculture informed the house as to what took place during their meeting.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: BREAK IN P.F.R.A. DAM ON FRENCHMAN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister has stated, I was interviewed by Mr. Sturdy, the minister of social welfare in the Saskatchewan government, and the mayor of Eastend, together with the mayor of Swift Current, and as well the deputy minister of the department of social welfare in Saskatchewan. They presented the case for assistance both to Swift Current and to Eastend. I discussed the question with them and indicated that I did not think it came under the class of national calamities, and therefore suggested that the matter be dealt with in some other manner.
The procedure that has been followed by provinces generally., and always has been, at least since the days of the calamity in Nova Scotia and the cyclone in Regina, is for the provincial governments to make representations to the effect that the damage done is so great that they themselves are not in a financial position to deal with it, and that the federal government give some assistance. I said I doubted very much whether either of these cases of damage would come even within that class; and then we went on to discuss the matter further. I intimated to them that there had been some damage as a result of irrigation operations in certain areas, and that the matter should be dealt with as between Dr. Thomson, our man at Regina, and the deputy minister, who was along with Mr. Sturdy and the mayor of Eastend. The matter was left there; and from that time to this I have not had any further representations; but I expect there will be representations made.

subtopic: BREAK IN P.F.R.A. DAM ON FRENCHMAN RIVER
speechtext:
I should like to ask this supplementary question:	Does not this damage
result from the collapse of a federal works project, namely a dam under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and therefore come into the category for which the federal government is responsible, as defined by the Prime Minister to the House of Commons on April 7?

subtopic: BREAK IN P.F.R.A. DAM ON FRENCHMAN RIVER
speechtext: In the opinion of our officials it is not damage that results from the breaking of the dam; some others, however, may think it is. That is a question which will have to be dealt with and determined as between the two parties.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 2, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and *the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned on Friday evening I had begun to make a few remarks concerning the business now before the house. At that time I dealt with the question whether second sessions were necessary on the two occasions on which they were held, and whether the remuneration
The Budget-Mr. Gillis for members of parliament was adequate or otherwise. I made my position clear, and I am not going to pursue the subject further.
There is another matter about which I want to say a few words at this time. The press and members of the house have commented on a speech made in the house by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). I make my observations now because I know that when the next election rolls around there will be a united front of Liberals, Progressive Conservatives, and any others who may be opposing us, supported by a copy of that little bible, Hansard, in their hands, trying to prove to the people of Canada that the C.C.F. generally is opposed to social security.
I want to make this clear, that the member for Moose Jaw as a citizen of Canada has a right to say what he likes; but when the member for Moose Jaw accepts the responsibility of running on a ticket and supporting a program that has certain basic principles, he is expected to conform as closely as he can to those basic principles.
There is all kinds of room for quarrelling on many matters-and I think I am a pretty good example of it myself, because I have stood in the house on many occasions and discussed matters concerning which other members of the group did not see eye to eye with me. But those matters did not have to do with the basic principles of the movement.
I do not expect the hon. member for Moose Jaw to think as I do, and I do not expect to think as the hon. member for Moose Jaw does. We are all more or less creatures of our environment; we are conditioned by it. There is considerable difference between my background and early environment and that of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. And when we see two people thinking exactly alike we know that there is only one of those people thinking, anyway. So this kind of controversy does not do any harm.
I am not concerned about what the hon. member said; he has a right to say it. But when a member gets up in the house and makes a speech such as that made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, setting forth certain proposals that presuppose a reduction in expenditures, and so on, then that speech is at least subject to analysis by other members. It is the analysis he made, and the economies it was supposed to bring about, with which I am now concerned.
On Friday night I dealt with his proposal that no second session was necessary. While the hon. member did not give many reasons why there should not be a second session, on
1860	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gillis Friday evening I gave many reasons why I thought a second session could hardly be avoided.
His second proposal to save money is one with which I completely disagree. For example, he said in no uncertain terms that broadcasts to points behind the iron curtain should be discontinued, and in that way we would save a couple of millions of dollars. In my opinion the broadcasts being sent to points behind the iron curtain are one of the most important parts of our national defence setup. In my view of Europe today, Russia is in much the same position as Hitler was in when we invaded Europe. It has expanded to a point where I am pretty sure it will find it difficult to police the whole territory while continuing to maintain its machinery of production. I believe Stalin is in the position of the fly that has captured the fly paper: he is there, but he is stuck with it.
The only assurance millions of people behind the iron curtain have is that which is conveyed to them in these broadcasts, indicating that there are people on the outside of the curtain who have an interest in them.
Some day, either by means of negotiation or otherwise, there will be deliverance for them. I think it would be one of the most disastrous things that could happen if these broadcasts to points behind the iron curtain should be discontinued.
The hon. member made some other miscellaneous recommendations which did not amount to very much. I am just going to deal with the major ones where he thought that some money could be saved. He said that post offices, wharves and drydocks should be cut to the extent of some $20 million. I can understand the hon. member making that recommendation because there are not many docks or wharves on the prairies. I am sure we have all heard the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) stressing the necessity for improvement, expansions and extensions of the facilities at Saint John, and I have no doubt Halifax is in the same position as well as other eastern Canadian ports. The renovation and improvement of post offices right across the country is badly needed at the present time. I do not think the hon. member thought the matter through very much when he chose those particular items as offering a saving of $20 million.
Then he proposed that the civil service should be cut by five per cent. I suppose anyone could get up here and say that there are too many civil servants and therefore they should be cut by ten, fifteen or twenty per cent, but the hon. member did not present any valid reason why any reduction should 

be made. To cut the civil service by five per cent would mean a reduction of about 10,000 right across the country, but the major reductions would be made here in Ottawa. Those reductions would not be made at the top levels; we would find junior clerks, filing clerks and perhaps some stenographers being relegated to the streets. What would happen to them? They would have to go on unemployment insurance. I certainly would not recommend the cutting down of any service which would mean the throwing into unemployment of those who are barely making the means of livelihood, barely making enough to pay their rent, buy some clothes and get a bite to eat. I am certainly not prepared to accept the recommendation that a particular classification in the civil service should be reduced unless I can be presented with facts and figures to show what money will be saved and what is going to be done with the money saved. I am opposed to that recommendation.
The hon. member also suggested that transport be cut by five per cent. We have the board of transport commissioners, and in addition we find that this department handles aids to navigation, telegraph lines, telephone lines, airports, and many other things. I cannot see how the personnel of that department could be cut. In my own end of the country I would think that the different branches of this department need more employees. I cannot understand why the hon. member for Moose Jaw picked on that particular department.
The hon. member proposed that there be set up a commission similar to the Hoover commission for the purpose of pruning government expenses, and all that kind of thing. Anyone who remembers the Hoover commission will recall that in summing up their recommendations they merely said that they were opposed to certain things because they added up to nothing more or less than liberal recommendations and liberal policies. I am sure that the hon. member for Moose Jaw does not want that kind of commission set up here for the purpose of pruning the civil service of this country and cutting expenditures. That is a job for the members of the House of Commons, and I for one am not prepared to hand it over to any commission.
Then the hon. member referred to old age security. We have had many statements to the effect that old age security should not be paid to people in the higher income brackets. However, I think the present arrangement is the best one. It would need a great number of additional personnel to cull out month by month those who were ineligible because of income; you would practically

have to duplicate the present number of employees in the department. The present set-up is the simplest one you could have. Much of this money comes back in taxes, in some cases more than is paid out.
The payment of $40 a month in many cases puts the recipients in a higher income bracket and when they are taxed on that basis you will perhaps get more than the $40 back. The present arrangement cuts down on the needed personnel and avoids many mistakes that would be made in checking and rechecking. I am completely opposed to that device for saving money, because I do not think any money would be saved. I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw was ill advised in picking on that particular thing. Exactly the same argument could be advanced in connection with his suggestion for reducing family allowances. If you placed the payment of those allowances on a "look and hunt" basis, as suggested by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, it would mean increased costs of administration.
That is all I want to say on that, but I thought it was necessary to say it. Practically every newspaper from one end of the country to the other has played up this theme during the last couple of weeks. We have Conservative members to our right, with Liberals to their right as well as in front of us, and they would all offer a united front at the next election in trying to prove that the C.C.F. did not believe in old age security, family allowances, and so forth. If I did not say something about it the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) would say, "You were in the house and you did not say anything; silence gives consent. Why did you not express your opinion then?" I am not expressing my opinion for the purpose of injuring the hon. member for Moose Jaw-he will learn as he goes along-but I did think it was necessary to make the points I have in connection with the recommendations he placed before the house.
In the time remaining at my disposal I want to say a few words with regard to a statement made by Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, to a committee which was set up a few days ago and which has finished its work. Its formal report will be presented to the house within the next day or so.
The coal industry of Nova Scotia has been having a pretty tough struggle over the years. The government set up a coal board to supervise and assist the industry. Money has been lent for the purpose of mechanizing the industry in the Atlantic provinces. With all these things one would have naturally
The Budget-Mr. Gillis assumed that there was a future for the coal industry. Then Mr. Gordon came before the committee a few days ago and when I asked him some questions with regard to the use of diesel engines on the main lines east of Montreal he told us that they were going to use them one hundred per cent and that no steam locomotives were to be purchased.
The coal industry of the maritime provinces sells some 1,200,000 tons of coal annually to the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Gordon made it quite clear that that market for coal was going to shrink year by year. He said that at the present time they have a five-year program in effect, which began in 1951, and which will mean shrinkage of some 280,000 tons a year in that industry. I asked Mr. Gordon if that figure represented an annual reduction, and he said that was so, but the next day he amended his statement somewhat. However, to my mind he did not amend it in such a way as to alter his first statement. His last statement was rather ambiguous. It was not very clear, and I am still sticking to the figure of 280,000 tons as the annual amount of shrinkage, beginning in 1951, in the market for maritime provinces' coal.
This situation has caused a lot of apprehension in those provinces. I have in my hand an article that appeared recently in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald containing a statement of Mr. L. A. Forsyth, president of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company, with respect to the year 1951. Mr. Forsyth says that there has been a steady decline in the production of coal, and that the coal industry is facing a crisis at the present time. On the other hand there is an encouraging feature about his report. He said that while the production of coal was going down, the production of steel was improving. He said that the steel position was much better from the standpoint of profits and production than it ever has been in the history of the corporation.
It would appear that there is going to be a swing in the base of the economy of Nova Scotia from coal to steel. In my opinion that is a good development, because the coal industry not only faces the loss to oil of the Canadian National Railways market for coal, but also faces the threat of natural gas from Alberta. Last year the house passed a bill giving a pipe line company the right to pipe natural gas from Alberta into Quebec city and greater Montreal. Natural gas can replace coal in the domestic field, and in the whole industrial field, with the exception of the production of basic steel. Therefore, in addition to the shrinkage in coal production because of the loss of the C.N.R. market to oil,

The Budget-Mr. Gillis in a few years' time we are going to be faced with the problem of meeting the competition of natural gas.
I said that I thought the swing in the economy from coal to steel was a good one. As the production of steel increases, it will create an additional demand for coal, because basic steel cannot be made without coal. I think the whole future of that industry in eastern Canada depends on the extent to which the government is prepared to assist the industry and encourage it in the creation of that new base for the use of Nova Scotia coal. In addition, a lot of consideration should be given to the establishment of subsidiary fabricating and steel plate industries. Such industries, as we lose markets to oil, as in the case of the Canadian National Railways, and to natural gas from Alberta, which will cover the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, would then be able to take up the slack of what we lose in these other fields.
I have no illusions about the period through which we are passing. Anyone who has watched the situation closely will realize that the world is in a transitional period of a new industrial revolution. I believe that ten years from now we shall be having similar discussions in the house about the threat of atomic energy to fuel oil, natural gas and other fuels. We are now in the transitional period of swinging from one basic fuel to several others that are more economical, and I think there are things that the government can do during that period to lessen the shock to the areas that will be affected by new technological advances. Do not make any mistake about it; I am not arguing against technological advances. They are inevitable, and I hope that as a result of them every miner who has to work underground in order to earn the means of livelihood will be able to come up to the surface and secure employment where he will be able to get some fresh air and sunshine and prolong his life for a good many years rather than have to work underground, whether in a rock or coal mine, where he is subject to health and accident hazards.
I am not arguing to keep the coal miners down in the mines, but I recognize the fact that these men now have a means of livelihood there, and that money is invested in these operations that are being displaced. There should be a transitional program when markets are being lost because of such advances, and people living in these areas should be given a chance to protect their investment. They should be given the opportunity to secure employment in order that they may live, eat, wear clothes, have homes and pay


taxes. The man in the street, who could contribute to the pool of wealth, is not much good to the country if he is just walking the street and drawing something from the pool without contributing to it.
Considerable encouragement is to be found in the research that is now being carried on. I noticed another article in the Chronicle-Herald with the heading, "Coal Research Program Reviewed by Experts, Progress is Reported." A search is being made for other uses for coal rather than just burning it and letting it go up the chimney in smoke. That is encouraging. One never knows what may come out of it. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald suggests, and I think rightly so, that in the transitional period it may be necessary for the coal board and the government to get together and decide whether more assistance is not necessary for the industry until such time as the picture is clearer. The subventions were fixed some ten years ago. They are statutory, and in the light of the new circumstances, the drop in production and the worsening of the position with respect to markets, it may be necessary to sit down with the coal operators, have a look at the subventions and see whether additional assistance is not necessary.
There is another encouraging feature, as pointed out by Mr. Gordon before the committee. I refer to the good future in Canada for gas turbines, as reported by a Vickers engineer. Research is going on, and it may be possible that the diesel will be displaced by the gas turbine engine which will burn coal. All these things are encouraging. I raise the question at this time because the government has a huge investment in the coal industry. For instance, the government has made a loan of $375,000 to the Avon Coal Company. The Dominion Coal Company has a program of mechanization under way at the present time which will cost $13 million when completed. To that end a loan of $7,500,000 has been advanced by the dominion government to this company. Four Star Collieries Limited has a loan of $100,000 from the dominion government.
If the industry is as shaky as indicated by Mr. Gordon and Mr. Forsyth when reporting to his board of directors, I find it hard to understand why the government would lend such a large amount of money to an industry whose future looks so bleak. I do not think it is as bleak as it looks, and if there is a proper approach to the problem by the government, the coal board, the operators and the miners themselves, the industry has a future in the production of steel. The logical place to expand the production of steel is in that part of the

country. The logical place to do some fabrication and to have some subsidiary industry built around steel is in that part of the country. All the ingredients necessary to make steel are there, with iron ore ninety miles away, coal within ten miles of the steel plant, and a huge establishment there with many trained personnel in the community, many of whom are unemployed at the present time. I hope the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) with his coal board will keep in touch with those responsible for the operation of the industry and with the miners themselves so that while this transition is taking place during this new industrial revolution the shock of displacement will be lessened as much as possible.
I am sorry I had to take this much time for the second time in this debate, but I did feel it necessary to deal with the two subjects on which I have spoken.

Mr. Speaker, I avail myself of the occasion offered by the debate on the budget to inform the government that I have received a large number of representations from my constituents, asking me to take steps with the proper department so that the sums paid out under the Family Allowances Act as well as the Old Age Security Act be increased to compensate for the high cost of living.
I do not hesitate to declare, Mr. Speaker, that family allowances and old age pensions should be raised in proportion to the cost of living-as was done for the whole salary scale-so that these social services, so well initiated by the present government, may be appreciated as fully by every Canadian mother as they have been in the past. Family allowances, after all, are given to mothers as a salary, to help them improve their children's food and shelter.
I sincerely believe, therefore, that family allowances should be increased, since it is food especially-milk and meat, for instance, which are essential for a proper diet-and the price of rents and heating that have gone up the most.
A single person can find a room close to where he or she works. The head of a family cannot. He has to find a house-children are no longer admitted in apartments-and he must pay heating and transportation, the cost of the latter having almost doubled these last few years. A single person can balance his or her budget, but the head of a family cannot, with prices being what they are. One
The Budget-Mr. Dube need only inquire at the banks and loan companies to know or to find out in what state of anxiety some householders are living today.
I also ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to give consideration to heads of families who send their children over 21 years of age to a university. I do hope the minister will take into consideration the remarks I am now making and that he will see to it that an exemption is granted to the heads of families who are doing their utmost to have their children educated and thus give Canada a pick of young people who will be a credit to our country. In the name of all my constituents, I therefore ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to remedy this situation which has been in existence for quite a time, in order to be fair to all without prejudice to anyone.

I do not intend to reply to facetious remarks. Regardless of the fact that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe emphasized that taxation is the power to destroy, I am sure no one would wish to return to the days of small budgets and no income taxation in this country. Just for a moment or two I want to review the history of income taxation as it has evolved in Great Britain, the United States and Canada over the last hundred years.
Great Britain has had some form of income taxation for over a hundred years. It was given effect to at the beginning of the nineteenth century. It was dropped. It was given effect to again, and again dropped. As a matter of fact there was no effective


form of income taxation in Great Britain until the concluding days of the nineteenth century.
What did we have when we had these small budgets, when budgets were supposed to provide only for the army, the navy, the police and the bare necessities of government? We had the industries of Manchester, with the Lancashire cotton mills making the largest percentage profits in history in relation to the total capital investment. At the same time we had poverty and slums. We had the coal mines in Lancashire and in Wales also making the largest profits in modem commercial history in relation to the investment, and at the same time we had child labour, hovels and squalor. At the same time we also had the great landowners in Great Britain, with their large returns, their elegance and their security, with farm labourers being paid a wage that provided a bare existence. The adoption of a measure of income tax in Great Britain in the latter days of the nineteenth century was also the beginning of the first form of social welfare legislation in that country.
If you read the records of the British parliament, of the American congress or our own Hansard you will find that large corporations and wealthy individuals fought the imposition of the income tax and described it as unethical and financially unsound. Repeatedly was heard the slogan that taxation is the power to destroy. You find that in the records of the British parliament. Another slogan was that the income tax was a method of soaking the rich. Those slogans have been in existence since the first liberal or reformthinking people conceived of an income tax as a fair form of redistributing the wealth.
When we come to the United States, what do we find? Income tax proposals were advanced in the congress of the United States in the latter days of the nineteenth century and they were fought vigorously. Prior to the bringing in of income tax legislation we had the meat packing industry and the steel industry, making enormous profits, slums in Chicago, slums in Pittsburgh, and poverty, fortunes in railroad building, fortunes in land speculation, fortunes in grain speculation while farmers were robbed of their fair share of the national income and left in a most insecure position.
As I read the record, in the United States congress in 1894 attempts were made to pass legislation providing for income tax in that country, and the same people who say that taxation is the power to destroy, when income tax is mentioned, were the people who termed that legislation as a "communistic socialist march". I am exceedingly glad that we have

gone a long way since that time. However, as a result of the efforts of the people who really saw that income tax provided an opportunity to redistribute wealth under capitalism, on July 12, 1909, a joint resolution was passed by both houses of congress recommending a law to levy an income tax. Yet we find even in the United States during the depression, former President Hoover still pleading with congress for a' small and balanced budget and for a paring of expenses to the bone in an effort to protect investments and to protect capital. At the same time the standards of living in the United States fell to a disastrous level.
What is our Canadian experience? I think the income tax was first given effect to in Canada during the first world war, owing to the necessity of raising an unusually large amount of revenue with which to prosecute the war. From that time on it has been more or less generally accepted, although the rates were fairly low until recent years. But what happened in Canada? The point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that a person's attitude towards taxation reflects one's attitude to life.
We can remember the depression budget of Lord Bennett in 1931, and what happened. Still in the belief that taxation is the power to destroy; still in the belief that one must reduce expenses, must pare them to the bone and must consider investments before human beings, in the budget of 1931 income tax was increased in the medium brackets but was reduced in the higher brackets, sales tax was increased from one per cent to four per cent, and there was an increase in postal charges in Canada.
What was the result of that taxation philosophy? We had thousands of single men unemployed in this country and receiving twenty cents a day in relief camps. Many farmers across Canada lost their farms to mortgage companies and many small businesses went into bankruptcy. All of that happened just because of that approach to the question of taxation and the desire to protect investments. That was done sincerely because those in control believed that investments were the bedrock of security in the country and therefore there was this policy to protect investments.
The Budget-Mr. Herridge depression. It was a world-wide depression and it affected our external markets and so on. But I think that a different taxation policy, with the use of the national credit, would have made it possible during the depression to employ people-at building houses and doing constructive things in Canada which would be useful, and which would be much appreciated at this time- rather than to pay men twenty cents a day in relief camps.
That is all I am going to say in that respect, Mr. Speaker, except that recently I was reading a book on taxation-and I thought it was a good one-entitled "Taxation for Prosperity", by Randolph E. Paul. I want to quote briefly from that book, because I think in one paragraph is to be found an excellent statement of a philosophy so far as the purposes of taxation are concerned. At page 207 of this book I read:

, .	.	. reciuirea is that we build a tax system
which is intelligently directed toward creating and maintaining the kind of world we want. The basic struggle hinges on our choice of worlds. The later and more technical, struggle is concerned with means to the desired end. that is, the specific taxes we select. The battleground of conflict will not always be sharply delineated. The critics of particular taxes frequently say one thing and mean another. The real objection to a tax may be that it tends to produce the kind of economic or social order which its opponent does not want But the critic does not always speak out in such ultimate and candid terms. He pleads that the tax will not produce revenue, or cannot be administered, or that taxes should not be used to promote social and economic results. Even while his objection is premised on fear that a particular tax will have unwanted social and economic consequences, he mav deprecate the notion that taxes can produce such effects. But we need not let our thinking be confused across levels. The fundamental question is always the kind of world we want; our choice of taxes is always a selection of means to that end.
That is why we in this group believe that income taxation provides an opportunity under capitalism for the redistribution of wealth. That is why we in the C.C.F. have pioneered the fight for universal old age security without a means test; and we will continue to do so because we believe it is still sound and practical. That is why we in this group have continued to support proposals for all the nation's children to receive family allowances without a means test, and will continue to support those proposals.

I remember this friend of mine, a fine gentleman, ordered 200 day-old chicks from a hatchery, and put them under setting hens. They gradually began to die, until half of them had died. I now intend to make some criticisms of the budget. Mr. Speaker, I have a few criticisms of the budget to make and they are mainly on the ground that something more could be done to equalize the burden more fairly on the Canadian people. We believe that the present income tax exemption should be raised from $1,000 to $1,500 for single persons and from $2,000 to $3,000 for married persons. Our leader dealt with this question on the occasion of his budget speech last year, and I want to re-emphasize his representations in that connection. We believe we are sound in this suggestion because business is allowed exemption for the cost of operation, repairs, depreciation and transportation expenses. Why not do the same things for human beings?
At this point I want to bring to the attention of the minister and of the parliamentary assistant a situation which exists in my constituency, and which I think must exist in many districts. I think this matter should receive some serious consideration by the minister. I am making direct reference to the employees of the Canadian Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. Many of them live up to 25 miles away from their work, because of better living conditions and the opportunity to live in the country, away from the plant itself, and away from the congested city conditions. They drive back and forth night and morning to their employment. In fact, if many of them did not live at this distance there would not be housing for all the employees of that company. This is a considerable expense to these employees. They have co-operative societies. They own buses. Their transportation is actually provided at cost, as the result of co-operation. Thousands of these men have to travel some distance every day. I have had talks with quite a number of the men. They have also written to me and they have suggested that it would only be fair if they were allowed that cost of transportation to

and from work daily. They say it should be allowed as an exemption from their income for computing income tax. I do ask the minister to give consideration to their suggestion. I think it is fair. It is a cost which the men cannot avoid. It is a daily cost, and in the period of a year it amounts to a considerable sum. Once again I do urge that the minister give some consideration to permitting the men to charge these costs as an exemption before the income tax is calculated. As I said before, we make all kinds of allowances for business. Why can we not make the same allowances for the human machine? That is why we in this group suggest that the exemption for single and married men could be raised.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore Mr. J. H. Blackmore (Lethbridge): Mr. Speaker, during the time at my disposal this afternoon I propose to discuss in a thoroughly friendly way United States foreign policy, either as a means to lasting peace or as a means of interference with the establishment of lasting peace. In this connection I wish to quote from a speech which, it is reported, Mr. Woodward, United States ambassador to Canada, is giving in southern Ontario towns. This quotation is from an American publication called Labour, in its issue of April 26, 1952. This is what it says:
Woodward, who is making a speaking tour in southern Ontario, emphasized that the U.S. is now striving "to promote conditions throughout the world which will make peace possible."
He added: "In simple terms we must set up an environment in which peace can flourish. We need to provide economic and social aid to both the war-devastated and the underdeveloped lands, so that their peoples can satisfy material, social and spiritual needs.	.
"We are not trying to establish an international dole. Self-help is the only way that people can grow. Our aid can only be a stimulus to the efforts of the peoples themselves. At the same time, we must extend the helping hand to those living at barest subsistence levels."
However, Woodward continued, implementation of this policy cannot be accomplished by unilateral action alone. "The safety of every nation," he declared, "is bound to that of others. Collectively we can so organize as to prevent the fall of any single nation. For this reason, the U.S. has consistently supported the United Nations."
Further on in the report he states:
"Yet, while we rearm, we remain determined not to neglect our own well-being or our program of preserving peace through economic aid to others. We know full well that our own security is intimately related to the economic strength of our friends."
He reaffirmed the position of the U.S. towards the concept of collective action. "We do not go the path alone, we are fully conscious of the importance of collective action," Woodward asserted. "We will continue to support the United Nations. We will continue to develop the North Atlantic Treaty Organization."
The whole tenor of that report is highly commendable. Anyone reading it, or anyone listening to Mr. Woodward's speech, undoubtedly would be impressed with the idea that the United States actually is pursuing policies conducive to lasting peace. Mr. Woodward is manifestly sincere; of that there can be no question. He is genuinely sincere in the belief that his country is really striving to promote throughout the world conditions which will make peace possible, and to set up an environment in which peace can flourish. Mr. Woodward is convinced, when he says:
"We know full well that our own security is intimately related to the economic strength of our friends."
"We do not go the path alone, we are fully conscious of the importance of collective action. We will continue to develop the North Atlantic Treaty Organization."
IMr. Herridge.]
Mr. Woodward is confident that his country will be working toward the laudable objectives he envisages when, and so long as, it will continue to support the United Nations and to develop the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
I wonder if Mr. Woodward has had time to study fully the meaning of the United Nations and the organization known as NATO. I propose now to devote a little time to the consideration of those two organizations.
This parliament in 1945 rushed into the acceptance of the United Nations, little realizing just what it was running into-just as it rushed into the acceptance of Bretton Woods, with hardly anyone, with the exception of the Social Crediters, dreaming of what that agreement involved. Most members are only now beginning to find out what kind of noose we put our heads into when we accepted those two commitments.
Now parliament has rushed into the NATO organization with very little real comprehension of what that organization stands for or involves; so far as I know it has never been explained to us in elucidating detail. Does Mr. Woodward know that if not specifically stated it is clearly implied, in the United Nations charter, that that charter is, in essence, a glorified embodiment of four most pernicious concepts? This will come as a surprise, not only to Mr. Woodward but I imagine to nearly all people in the United States and in Canada including members of this house.
Those concepts are: First, the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause designed to be expressed in, and enforced through the international trade agreement and the international trade organization.
Second, the unlimited pursuit of favourable trade balances with no practical assured provision whereby the victims of the process can possibly liquidate the international debts inevitably imposed and saddled upon them by the more favoured nations while those favoured nations are achieving favourable trade balances, the working out of this mischievous concept and its devastating effects being by its United States advocates called by the deceptive euphemism "expansionist policy".
Third, an internationalist world federation headed by, controlled by and ultimately dictated to by, the United States of America, and the United States of America alone.
Fourth, an international gold standard expressed in and enforced through the international monetary fund provided for in the Bretton Woods agreement.

If my time will permit I intend to develop adequately each of these four pernicious concepts and show the accuracy of what I have said concerning them. If not, I shall endeavour to cover briefly with some degree of adequacy these important aspects of the international situation as they confront us today, and point out, or at least imply, how hopeless it is for people who are pursuing policies such as are embodied in the United Nations charter to obtain a lasting peace.
What evidence can be adduced to establish my contention that the United Nations charter does embody principles based upon these four pernicious concepts? May we deal with each of these concepts in turn? I should like to quote from a book of great value called "The British Declaration of Independence," which is a recent work by Henry Drummond-Wolff, one of the most able students of	our times, and	critics	of	our
ways. On page 34 he said:
The structure of the United Nations is determined by the most-favoured-nation principle and expansionist policy. The organization forms the nucleus of international federation and is situated in the United States.
Mr. Drummond-Wolff is famous for his brevity and	conciseness; he	is famous	forthe amount	of information	which	he	can
crowd into a few words.
This quotation definitely conveys that the most-favoured-nation principle is designed to be the determining factor in shaping the policies of the United Nations. The international trade organization	is one	of	the
specialized agencies of the United Nations. All the proceedings of that organization up to the present time have indicated that the sole objective behind the authors and designers of the international trade organization was to destroy the principle of imperial preferences throughout the British empire and prevent that principle being applied by other nations.
Hon. members who did me the honour of listening to my remarks on April 9 or of reading my speech will remember that I pointed out that it was the determination by the United States to prevent Japan from using preferences in her dealings with China, and the equal determination by Japan that she would use preferences because she had to in order to live, that brought on the war between the United States and Japan in world war II. As I pointed out on that occasion, this is a desperate matter to everyone who is anxious to establish peace in this world of ours.
In the course of the endeavours to establish the international trade organization hon. members will recall that conferences were held at Geneva, Havana, Annecy and Torquay. The United States representatives at those
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore conferences seemed to be actuated by only one motive, to beat down imperial preferences. They wanted to beat down the tariff protection of other nations but at the same time maintain their own tariff protection at a level high enough to enable them to use that device in conjunction with the various other techniques which they employ to hinder imports from coming into the United States, to keep out goods from almost any nation in the world. All these conferences indicated with abundant clarity the type of thinking that actuated United States leaders. They were all for the elimination of preferential tariffs and bilateral agreements.
That ought to be sufficient to establish the first of my four points. If the international trade organization was to be one of the specialized agencies through which the United Nations was to work, and if the objective of that organization was to eliminate imperial preferences and the use of preferences throughout the world, then beyond all shadow of a doubt the objective of the international trade organization and everything pertaining to it was to jam down the world's throat the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause.
Those who are interested in this matter will find some profit I believe in reading my speech on April 2 in which I discussed the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause with the object of enabling people out in the country and on farms to get some idea as -to what this thing was -all about and how it would work.
The quotation which I have already read establishes the accuracy of my statement to the effect that the United Nations charter embodies the freedom for a nation adequately powerful to pursue unlimited favourable trade balances. This freedom to pursue unlimited favourable trade balances is what the United States calls an expansionist policy. The -ordinary individual reading about expansionist policies will surely say, "I believe in an expansionist policy; certainly I do." But what is -the use -of our believing in an expansionist policy when the only nation that can actually expand unlimitedly in accordance with that concept is -the United States? What the United States was -actually standing for was an expansionist policy primarily if not wholly for and in behalf of the United States.
As an illustration which will help us to think a bit concretely about this matter, in 1947 the United States exported between $11 billion and $12 billion of goods more than she imported. It must be obvious to anyone that it is utterly impossible for the people of the world to live in a community of nations in which the United States is free to go on doing that kind of thing indefinitely, with no

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore check, no balance, no restriction, no means to rectify the wrong which is being committed. There is no way whereby this $11 billion or $12 billion can be paid off.
I turn to the third principle. The quotation I gave a while ago establishes the soundness of my contention concerning a dictatorship under an internationalist federation ruled by the United States. The foundations of this mechanism were laid in the Dumbarton Oaks conference meeting in two sessions, first, between Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States from August 21 to September 28, 1944, and second, between China, the United Kingdom and the United States from September 29 to October 7, 1944. Those who wish to check on this point may refer to page 263 of the World Almanac for 1952.
Chapter 1, section 1, of the Dumbarton Oaks proposals for a joint international organization reads as follows:
The purposes of the organization should be to maintain international peace and security; and to that end to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace and the suppression of acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace.
This may be checked by reference to the United Nations conference on international organization, volume 3, page 2, to be found in our own library.
Could anyone imagine more convincing proof of dictatorship objective with the United States telling the world what to do, than we see developing in the NATO organization? There is only one authority in the world that is trying to tell the other nations what to do, and that is the United States. She is not only telling them what to do but is forcing them to do it by every economic means at her disposal, and she has an abundance thereof. We see the thing working out. We heard a member of the house talking in favour of it only the other day.
There remains my assertion that the United Nations charter embodies an international gold standard under the international monetary fund. Is that assertion based upon truth and sound logic? In order to establish what I want to say I must read an authority whom I think everyone will find beyond any question whatsoever.
First, however, let me recall for the house that the Bretton Woods agreement was one of the first specialized agencies established by the United Nations. In fact the Bretton Woods agreement was all settled and signed by a conference in July, 1944, before the San Francisco conference of 1945 took place. We in Canada merely rubberstamped, during the dying hours of the fall session of 1945, what

had been done at the Bretton Woods conference. Members of the house would not even listen to any kind of reasoning as to the recklessness of our behaviour in thus dashing into acceptance of this dangerous document, a document to be proved even more and more dangerous as the days went
by.
In support of what I have said concerning the Bretton Woods agreement and the gold standard I should like to read now from an article written by Paul Einzig, one of the most brilliant and authentic young economists in the world today. The article I am reading is taken from the April 7, 1945, issue of a periodical published in Toronto, Canada, in those days, under the name, The News. Here are the words:
It must be clear to those who understand the meaning of the report of the Bretton Woods international monetary conference, that the experts of forty-four nations have agreed on a return to the gold standard after the war. Unfortunately, very few laymen can possibly understand the report. If the public were to realize what it is being led into it would raise its voice in a powerful protest, instead of allowing the experts a free hand to do their worst, as they did in 1925.
That is, when England went back to the gold standard after world war I. I continue:
Some weeks ago Lord Bradbury, in a letter to the Times, complained that the previous joint statement of the allied experts on the post-war monetary system, which was published in April, so far from being plain English was hardly even English at all. Yet that document was clarity itself compared with the tangle of tricky technical clauses contained in the final draft of the experts' plan of the new gold standard. These clauses conceal from the British public the fact that, for the second time within the life of the present generation, sterling is going to be linked with gold, this time much more rigidly even than nineteen years ago.
In 1925 the gold standard was, at any rate, restored in the full light of publicity. The public knew what was happening. It had only itself to blame for having failed to heed the advice of the lone voices crying in the wilderness-that of the Daily Express prominently among them-warning the country against the consequences of the proposed step. In 1944, on the other hand, the public is only too well aware that a return to the gold standard would be unmitigated evil, spelling ruin and misery. It would now be politically impossible to reintroduce the gold standard openly. But it is being introduced just the same, this time in disguise, under another name. The public is lulled into a false feeling of security by being told again and again that the new system is not the gold standard.
And the text of the measures with the aid of which sterling is supposed to be wedded to gold has been made so obscure and complicated that even the expert, with the specialized study of a lifetime behind him, has to read it many times before fully grasping its true meaning. Yet, once the plan is translated into intelligible English and is denuded of all camouflage, every layman of normal intelligence is bound to realize that it is the gold standard, the full gold standard, and nothing but the gold standard.

Admittedly, it is a different gold standard from the one we abandoned in 1931, just as the gold standard adopted in 1925 was different from the one suspended in 1914. But the changes are, for the most part, considerably for the worse.
That is striking enough, is it not? I do not know whether or not members would be prepared to accept readily the words of Paul Einzig. There is no greater authority on monetary matters, national and international, than Paul Einzig, but in case they might desire a little more evidence on this matter of Bretton Woods I should like to quote the words of Mr. Rene Leon in his book, "Bretton Woods". The passage from his book is found in a very fine book called "The Awakening" by L. S. Amery, published in 1948. It reads as follows:
Under conditions of extreme readjustment, social, political and economic, can expansion of trade and also balance be achieved on the basis of fixed exchanges? My answer is, No ... To harness world economy to static exchanges at such a time and under such conditions is to stifle action and obstruct reaction, because it is by their very fluctuations that the exchanges create those correctives which make for balance in international trade relations.
. . . Fixed exchanges are the conduits through which economic ills will flow and spread across national boundaries. They will shackle the weak economies to the strong, and debilitate the strong without strengthening the weak. The sum of all economic activities will be a gravitation downwards towards a generally lower standard of life all round . . .
I leave that for hon. members to take at face value. It is perfectly clear that what Mr. Leon foresaw is occurring today. In spite of the fact that we are engaged in a cold war and preparation for war on a huge scale, we still see danger signs of the breakdown of the system we are trying to make operate.
I believe I should quote one more passage from Paul Einzig's work because it is of such value to all those who are really interested in trying to see their way through the difficulties of our times. Speaking of Britain he says:
But let the reader judge for himself from the following facts:
(1)	Under the old gold standard the value of sterling was legally fixed in terms of a given weight of gold. This will be precisely the same under the new gold standard.
(2)	Under the old gold standard our monetary authorities were under the obligation to buy and sell gold freely at a fixed buying and selling price. This will be the same under the new gold standard, with the difference that gold will not be available for internal hoarding.
But then even under the gold standard of 1925 the authorities had the right to call in hoarded gold in excess of 10,000, so that this difference is not very important.
Under the old gold standard sterling was allowed to fluctuate within a range of about 1 per cent. Under the new gold standard its range of fluctuations has been rigidly fixed at 1 per cent.
Under the old gold standard there was no limit for the fluctuation of the price of sterling for
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore future delivery. In this respect the new gold standard is much more rigid, for under it a limit will be set also to the fluctuations of "forward" sterling.
When, before 1931, Britsh export trade was handicapped by the unduly high exchange value of sterling, the cheapening of the price of "forward" sterling bought in advance by foreign importers to pay for British goods to be delivered later provided some relief. Under the new gold standard there can be no such relief.
I have several other quotations along this line with which I do not think I will burden the house; but those facts which Paul Einzig has given concerning the Bretton Woods agreement and its application in Britain must be evidence beyond question that as far as exchange is concerned things are far worse under the United Nations, with its Bretton Woods gold standard agreement, than they were before.
I am sure Mr. Woodward will read these remarks of mine, and I want him to know that I have the kindliest feelings toward him and his nation, but I do hope they will discover the error of their ways before it is too terribly late. I would like to ask Mr. Woodward, whether or not he thinks the four principles or four concepts I have indicated as being in operation in the world under the United Nations charter are conducive to world peace. I would ask him how in the world he believes they can be. I may say more about that.
He may doubt the prevalence and the ill-effects of the unconditional most-favourednation clause. I would invite him to recall with me certain facts about his country's history since the beginning of world war I. These facts taken together and appropriately related to each other will, I fancy, tend fully to convince him that ever since at least as far back as January 8, 1918, the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause has been a guiding consideration in drafting United States foreign policy pertaining to trade.
On January 8, 1918, President Wilson, in a speech before congress, made a statement of the war aims and peace terms of the United States, enunciating his famous fourteen points.
The third of those fourteen points was worded as follows:
The removal, so far as possible, of all economic barriers and the establishment of an equality of trade conditions among all the nations consenting to the peace and associating themselves for its maintenance.
That unquestionably is a call for the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause. Let me adduce in this connection some evidence that I believe deserves respect. I refer to "The Commonwealth" a relatively recent work written by the British economist, Henry Drummond-Wolff, to whom I have already referred, published recently by Hutchinson

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore and Company, London, New York, Melbourne, Sydney and Capetown. From page 9 I quote:
In 1922, the United States, having become the principal creditor, changed its traditional mostfavoured-nation policy from the conditional to the unconditional form.
And on the same page:
The effect of this change was described by the economic committee of the league of nations on September 12, 1936, in the following terms:
"The United States adopted the principle of the unconditional clause, but as they did not at the same time adopt a policy of tariff agreements the clause-for which they invariably pressed-enabled them to continue to impose duties, which were in some cases prohibitive, without fear of discrimination, while they had the benefit of all concessions made to one another by other countries.
And again from page 9:
In April, 1925, the chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Winston Churchill, restored the gold standard. Western Europe was exposed to dumping from the Soviet union and to imports of low cost surpluses from the United States. Tied to the gold standard and prevented by the most-favoured-nation clause from exchanging complementary trade among themselves, European countries were compelled to borrow heavily.
That does not speak very well for the principles underlying the new system that was set up through the United Nations charter, does it? Then from pages 22 and 23 I quote:
The principal creditor maintains its condition of monopoly through control of monetary gold, guaranteed markets, export of surplus production and unrestrained price competition. The insistence by corporations, on unconditional most-favourednation rights throughout the world, leads to the denial of export trade to nations that, possessing adverse balances, are deficient in monetary gold, foreign investments, exchange and credit.
And now from page 27:
Genuine equality of treatment and opportunity would demand equality of producing, consuming and purchasing power, which depend on access on equal terms to trade and to the raw materials of the world.
Access on equal terms is not provided by an equal, legal right to purchase in the open market. It becomes a reality only when nations receive equal access to effective reciprocity through bilateral and regional action. Promiscuous, multilateral commerce cannot afford effective reciprocity.
And again from the same page:
The most favoured nation thus enjoys favourable balances, and money returns from external sources. The less favoured nations suffer adverse balances and are compelled to increase their foreign debt in order to avoid default. They are subjected to exploitation and domination which they will, sooner or later, resist by force.
That is quite clear. Again I quote from page 28:
The gold standard-most favoured nation mechanism is the cause of booms and depressions. It prevents the free, regional co-operation of sovereign nations, through effective reciprocity.
IMr. Blackmore.1
Then from page 30, referring to expressions used in the Atlantic charter, Henry Drum-mond-Wolff has this to say:
"Access on equal terms" can be achieved only by the better or, if necessary, complete balancing of trade through bilateral or regional reciprocity. Such reciprocity can be effected only by preferences or priorities. It is not provided by "reciprocal" trade agreements that establish a general most favoured nation rate of tariff.
The Atlantic charter opened a new phase in the militant opposition of the United States to preferences and controlled economies.
Once more I would like to ask Mr. Woodward how, in the face of declarations like that, he can conceive that in supporting the United Nations charter the United States is working to establish conditions under which peace "can flourish".
It will be wondered whether or not evidence can be produced to show that the United States has actively used the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause to prevent nations from co-operating with each other. Once more I adduce evidence that cannot be lightly treated. From Henry Drummond-Wolff's "Commonwealth" I quote, this time from page 10:
An attempt by Belgium and Holland to Introduce a system of reciprocal tariffs at the Ouchy convention of 1932, was promptly vetoed as conflicting with the most favoured nation principle. Negotiations at Oslo in 1930 and 1937 among the Scandinavian countries were similarly circumscribed. Repeated attempts by the Balkan countries to establish preferences among themselves and with the central European countries were frustrated.
And on page 11:
In 1935, Germany's use of exchange control and clearing agreements in southeast Europe was countered by the withholding of most favoured nation rights from her . by the United States. This had the effect of imposing a penal rate of tariff against German imports into the American market.
And again from page 11:
The Anglo-American trade agreement was entered into on November 17, 1938, as a result of powerful pressure from the United States.
Some will wonder whether or not this man Henry Drummond-Wolff is an authority. There is no question that he is a great authority, and knows exactly what he is talking about. His words are weighty words. They contain solemn warnings for us.
Why has the United States inflicted upon the world this unconditional most-favourednation clause, and why has she been following the policy which I have indicated in my talk? There is a definite reason. At the close of world war I the United States was a creditor nation for the first time in her history. She was greatly industrialized and thus able to produce more than she could sell to her own people for the purchasing power they were able to obtain. In 1918 she produced $60 billion worth of goods but the

effective purchasing power in the hands of her people was only $45 billion distributed, and of that $5 billion went back out of circulation in payment for life insurance and in other kinds of investment which took the money out of consumer purchasing circulation. At that time the United States, realizing that she had more goods being produced than her people were being provided with money to buy, should have introduced social credit. By distributing purchasing power to her people, by the social credit technique, she could easily have kept her people employed, could have raised the standard of living of all of her people, and could have avoided making herself a nuisance in the markets of the world.
But she chose not to do this. Instead, she tried to force her goods into the markets of the world no matter how much injury was thereby done to other nations in the process. In other words, she continued to export her unemployment all over the earth, regardless of whom she hurt.
During the inter-war period the United States had accumulated from annual creditor balances on trade and income account between $13 billion and $14 billion. She had not increased her imports. She had not invested abroad. She had acquired between 85 per cent and 90 per cent of the nonmonetary gold stocks of the world. The New Deal had failed after $58 billion was fruitlessly expended upon it.
What was she going to do? In October, 1944, President Roosevelt made a statement that has a tremendously important bearing on this whole matter I am discussing. He said:
I intend to find jobs tor 60 million Americans by trebling our exports abroad.
Thus we find that all the acts, the agreements, the insistencies of the United States during those troublesome times from 1922 to 1933 and onward have been as a result of a selfish though understandable desire on her part to keep her people busy by exporting their goods into the markets of the world in spite of what that could possibly mean to the world.
If we are to find any solution to the troubles which confront the world, may I urge Mr. Woodward that he report to his president and his government that the only possible peaceful solution for the United States and for mankind is to introduce social credit into the United States, enabling her to sell her goods within her own country and thus to take care of that one-third of the United States people who, according to Roosevelt's declaration, are always the submerged third and whose income is so low as 55704-119
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore to constitute a scandal to the United States of America.
Next, the United States should accept imports that other nations offer her in payment for the goods they wish to buy from her; she should accept those imports, not necessarily to take them into her country to compete with the product of her own producers but to redistribute them to other nations needing such goods. Just think what she could do with regard to cheese for one instance if she accepted it from Canada and western Europe. Think how she could help the needy nations by accepting that cheese, not in order to let it compete with the output of her own producers but to help other needy nations, by sending it abroad to them. This cheese she could buy with debt-free money created by congress under authority granted to it by the constitution of the United States, money like the $450,000,000 of greenbacks, with which Lincoln freed the slaves.
Next the United States should adopt, and lead out in, a system of scientific world distribution based upon the principles of social credit, a system that would enable all the people who produce goods in the world to dispose of their goods profitably to people who need the goods, a system that would enable all the people in the world to derive the benefit they should have from the productive capacity of the other nations of the world.

I submit this to Mr. Woodward, with all kindliness and good feeling, as being the only possible solution under which "peace can flourish".

It has already been said in the house by others that in the province of Ontario there is a minimum need for some 450,000 housing units and that in the country as a whole there is a need for some 700,000 units. I think it would be interesting to place on record our achievement with respect to housing since 1946. It is as follows:

As a result of continuing high employment, a continuing high birth rate, a high rate of family formation and large scale immigration we find ourselves in about the same position with respect to housing as we were in 1945. Despite the achievement-and it was great- we have not made as much progress as we had originally anticipated. In the departmental annual report Mr. Mansur said that on the assumption that an average family cannot afford more than about 23 per cent of its income for shelter, the average prospective home owner in 1950 required a gross income of about $2,700 to purchase a new minimum house. By the end of 1951 family income of about $3,300 was required to meet the debt service on a similar house. The only conclusion that we can draw from that is that now we are rationing houses by purse. Persons with less than $3,000 income-and that is 70 per cent of our population-appear to bear an unfair share of the national sacrifices made necessary by the defence program. Of course the immediate need is for mortgage money to be made readily available, for easier down payments, a longer amortization period and more rental housing of perhaps the multiple type. I think the government should give consideration to further subsidization. When I say that I have in mind that, instead of dealing with the provinces on a basis of 75-25, for low rental housing we could make it more attractive if we put it on the basis of 80-20 or 85-15, in order to give the provinces some greater incentive to start building low rental housing under section 35.
Quoting Mr. Mansur further-he is president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-he said there was a decline of 24 per cent in dwelling starts, which were 72,000 in 1951. He said that situation arises for four reasons and those are-and I quote-(1) shortage of mortgage funds; (2) shortage of serviced lands; (3) large down payment requirements; and (4) increased level of debt service. By that he means increased level of municipal taxes.
Then he has this to say-I am still quoting Mr. Mansur:
The supply of mortgage funds from all sources under present arrangements constitutes a definite limitation on the value of house building.
If for social reasons an annual housing program equal to or greater than those accomplished in 1949 and 1950 is a requirement, it may prove necessary to find additional sources of credit to be made available for mortgage on new residential construction.	*
That is the challenge.
What I have to say is particularly directed to the shortage of mortgage funds. We have in the past always considered mortgage funds


as an exclusive field of private enterprise. We have often been asked by private enterprise: Why does the government enter the field of private enterprise? I think the government does it for two primary reasons. First, in the interest of national security. The government has Chalk River, which is the atomic energy plant, and Canadian Arsenals, which make munitions. It was felt that both should be a public endeavour. They also have Polymer, which made synthetic rubber during the war. I do not think anyone quarrels with these three endeavours in the interest of national security; but the government also enters the field of what is considered private enterprise for another reason, and a very good one indeed, and that is to meet a social need and to fill a vacuum in a field vacated by private enterprise.
Historically lending institutions have always made conventional house loans. But from time to time they have left the field open, with the result that the government has had to enter it. I will carry you back first to some 40 years ago when the government, out of a desire to provide a measure of security for the people of this country, passed the annuities act. At that time private enterprise was not interested in writing small annuities. They failed to meet a social need, and they failed to meet a requirement for personal security. Today it is an entirely different picture. Private enterprise is becoming very interested in the annuities field, and is attempting to regain its foothold to the extent that it is alleged that they are doing some lobbying against the government bill which was intended to raise the annuity level from $1,200 to $2,400. It is true and cannot be denied that, at the present time, the dominion government annuity is by far the best and the cheapest annuity on the market. We need to continue in that field in order to meet a need that exists there. We entered the field because private enterprise abdicated it. The government stepped in to meet a social need, which was found very essential by the people. I think it would be well to say here that once government steps into the social field it never vacates it.
Let me again bring to the attention of these lending institutions something that they may have forgotten. Back in 1929 farmers were unable to obtain loans from private institutions on their properties, on land, on livestock, equipment and improvements. It was necessary for the government of the day to pass an act to set up a farm loan board, because the private institutions had turned a cold shoulder to that particular field, and there was urgent need for it. The government is now making a considerable amount of

loans in that field. In 1951 they made 3,242 loans, and 94 per cent of the interest that was due was paid. The arrears amounted to less than 2 per cent. Since 1929 they have written 34,485 first mortgages, 17,000 of which have been paid in full. At the end of 1951 they had a profit of $131,705.21. That field was partially abdicated by private enterprise, and the government stepped in again to meet a very great social need.
The Veterans Land Act provides an opportunity for veterans to build their own homes and to own small holdings. I merely indicate that the government has invested some $250 million in 31,000 properties, and they have received in repayment of these loans 95-5 per cent. There again the government stepped in when private enterprise abdicated or refused to participate in that field.
On May 5, 1951, the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) made a statement of policy in this house, and a very interesting statement it was. It provided that a defence worker would be able to obtain a house under very easy conditions. A defence worker is a person certified by his employer to be engaged in the production of defence supplies in a plant designated in whole or in part by the Department of Defence Production as a defence plant. The only requirement was that the house must be owned and occupied by the defence worker. The defence worker can build a house under his own steam, or he can purchase it from a builder who would build it under supervision by the Central Mortgage, which would be the architect, the planner, the guarantor as to quality of building and the adequacy of the house. All he had to pay was 10 per cent down, and it is amortized over a period of some 25 years. The loan would be 90 per cent on the agreed contract price fixed by Central Mortgage, and the monthly payments would include principal, taxes and interest. All the employer had to do was to make monthly deductions to meet the payments while the employee was so employed at the plant. There was to be no liability on the employer at all. If at any time the employee terminated his employment the employer had no further responsibility toward the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the employee who had obtained a home as a defence worker could retain the home. He could sell the home to other than a defence worker during the five-year period immediately after completion by paying one-ninth of the original amount of the loan. After doing that he could sell it on his own terms. He could sell to another defence worker without having to pay the one-ninth of the original loan.

Up to the present time about 600 homes have been built in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, or are in the process of building. Homes cost from $8,650 on which there is a down payment of $870, and monthly payments of $59 which include principal, interest and taxes, to $10,700 upon which there is a down payment of $1,070 and monthly payments of $71 which include principal, interest and taxes.
It is a bit disheartening and disappointing to know that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have never had an application by a defence worker to build a house. They have never refused an application by a plant to be designated as a defence plant. Yet we find an opportunity there for housing of which no one seems to be aware; and my purpose in speaking today is to try to bring about some awareness of that situation.
Mark you this: the house that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is building for defence workers at a top price of $10,700 is selling privately today for about $14,000. The difference is the profit the builders are obtaining for this same house. Yet, for some reason or another, there are few takers. I cannot understand it.
