In the minister's statement of October 5 he had this to say:
To the extent that mortgage financing is not available from lending institutions for defence workers. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be prepared to make direct loans. The Minister of Defence Production will from time to time designate defence plants to which these special housing arrangements are applicable.
Here, again, was an invitation by the minister asking lending institutions to make money available to defence workers. Lending institutions defaulted again, and it was necessary for the government to step in and to make direct loans.
At the last session of the provincial legislature of Ontario an act was passed authorizing the lending of $10 million to young farmers to start into farming in Ontario. That surely could have been made available by lending institutions, if they had thought it was worth their trouble.
It has been pointed out to me that I have neglected to mention that the government is lending money to veterans, by way of business and professional loans, under plans very similar to those applying to housing. All this business could have been available to the lending institutions of this country if they had wanted to make those loans.
They say they are short of money. The other argument they use is that the bond market gives them a good return. They say

The Budget-Mr. Croll that they can obtain 4 per cent or something slightly in excess of that on bonds, and that they receive a better net return on a 4 per cent bond than on a 5-J per cent mortgage. As a matter of fact the bond I have in mind is that of the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission, which was put on the market recently.
That is not the whole story. Last year we amended the Insurance Act, which gave the lending institutions powers far wider than they formerly had, with the result that they can now invest in real estate, in debentures and in common stock, which they were unable to do some years ago. What is happening is this, that these same lending institutions are using their money to buy up large chunks of valuable real estate. I know in my own city of Toronto they are buying office buildings, they may be first class investments-they would know best about that. But, more than that, they are buying up Dominion store, Wool worth store and Loblaw store leases, and holding them as an investment. That is where their money is, with the result that they do not have it available for those people in Canada who need to build homes.
It is true that what they are doing may be more profitable and easier; but on the other hand it seems to me that they have a social responsibility and that, from their point of view, it ought to be more desirable to help build up this country, rather than keep the profit motive entirely before them.
From time to time all of us have seen institutional advertising by mortgage, trust and insurance companies. We see page-size ads in newspapers and magazines showing a picture of two old people, a man and his wife, talking to one another and saying, "We have provided security for ourselves." Then there is some talk about a paid-up pension plan or an annuity. We see at the bottom the name of an insurance company, with information as to its assets, how much insurance it has written, and so on. These are first class ads, and they serve a purpose. It does seem to me that these lending companies have missed a great opportunity.
Why should they not run one of these ads showing a picture of a subdivision of perhaps a hundred houses, with the caption, "We did this with your money. We helped build this subdivision. We financed the building of these houses because we believe it is a good investment. This is what we think you would want us to do with your money."
I had occasion to go out on Sunday to look through some of the subdivisions already completed. It is a pleasure to see them. One sees thousands of small homes with combined living and dining-rooms, small breakfast

nooks, modern kitchens, good basements and satisfactory heating units. True, these houses are small-almost like dolls' houses. These subdivisions are filled with children-little ones, some of whom are still creeping, others walking and still others running about. The subdivisions are full of life.
We want these lending institutions to be helpful in building up our country. In those subdivisions we see fathers digging their gardens, building fences, painting and weeding; and unless we make mortgage money available for these kind of people we are not likely to have much more building in this country-unless, of course, we do something about it. And I am about to propose that we do.
I am sure the house will agree with me when I say that the homes built through national housing loans are a complete and absolute answer to communism, nazism, collectivism and totalitarianism. It should be our main objective to make homes for all the Canadian way of life.
If these lending institutions are more concerned with using their gold-plated scissors to clip coupons or to collect rents from downtown office buildings than they are in meeting social needs at a profit, then they are also vacating a field which, traditionally, has been their own. We now have on the statute books the authority to make direct loans for homes. If they are not forthcoming from private enterprise, then there is no alternative for us but to enter the field.
Once we are in the field we will never vacate it. Neither this nor any other parliament will permit us to vacate it. Private enterprise as represented by these various institutions has only itself to blame. They have not discharged a public trust or shown any social consciousness. That field is historically theirs, and I think all of us in this house would want them to continue in it, but if they abdicate and abandon the field, even in a slight degree, then this government must enter that field and improve it in every conceivable way possible. More than that, once we are in the field we will be able to lend money more cheaply and be able to make sure that the people benefit to a greater extent than they are benefiting now.
For the moment we have section 35 of the housing act and we have the defence workers' scheme. We have our hands full in making subsidies available for low rental housing to the people. I appeal to the minister and I submit to the house that this problem must be faced. Complaints have been made from members of the opposition-just the other day we had one from the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland)-that mortgage money

is not being made available to all communities. It is claimed that it is partially available only in the larger cities and not in the small municipalities. We ought to make certain that the same facilities are available to them as are available to those who live in the large cities. It is the responsibility of the government to see that that is done. I bring this matter to the attention of the house, of the minister and of the lending institutions now. I suggest to the latter that if they do not fully re-occupy that field on the double the government must enter it at this particular time in order to meet the great need that exists.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to take part in the budget debate this year. Rising at this time I am faced with the question of what I can say that has not been said already. For my part I do not intend to be associated with all the remarks of those who have spoken in this debate, particularly those who do not see any merit in this year's budget, who seem to have lost all sense of direction and who apparently do not realize that civilization is at stake. Their voices sound like voices crying in the wilderness with no one to lead them out of their Gethsemane. Surely this is a great nation in which we are privileged to live. It was not built on wailings and lamentations; it was built by the hard work, the industry and the integrity of the men and women who came to Canada's shores. So today I prefer to take my stand with the government of today who with equal integrity, with equal industry and with equal hard work is placing first things first for Canada and its people, and sees in the future a great destiny for our country.
I realize that it is not wealth and riches that brings greatness to a nation. Rather it is the men who travel in its service. So at this time I want to join my voice with those who have already paid a tribute in this chamber to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and members of the government of today, who are pursuing the wise course they have followed on behalf of the people of our country. It has been said:
Give me men to match my mountains,
Give me men to match my plains;
Men of courage, men of action,
Men with Canada in their brains.
It seems to me that that is typical of the St. Laurent government. So I repeat that while there may be nothing new that I can say in this debate, on the other hand it seems to me that there is a need for a repetition and reiteration of those fundamentals and principles upon which our nation was built and likewise upon which this year's budget has been founded.
The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray
Assembled as we are here today we represent constituencies, we represent homes, we represent business, we represent agriculture, we represent professional life; we are all wrapped up in this bundle of life. We all have our problems, but I say that whatever those problems are they are not very different from the problems of the men and women living behind the iron curtain or at or near the 38th parallel. After all, it is a way of life-a way of living. We feel that our way of life is the best way, and I for one know that it is. However, in saying that I realize also that there may be a great number of people living within our nation today who apparently have no sense of direction.
It seems that over the years we have developed a sense of speed to the maximum but in co-distinction to that sense of speed we may be co-equally losing our sense of direction. I think it is immeasurably more important to retain a sense of direction, to retain a sound fiscal policy for our nation, to retain a sound budget than it is to retain a sense of speed.
Sometimes I think it is good for all of us to be reminded of the great country in which we are privileged to live. I recall that after last year's budget I took time out to kodak, to develop and to print the finest flower in the garden, the first-prize chrysanthemum-the constituency of Oxford, which I have the honour to represent.
Today I should like to preface my remarks in this budget debate by indicating how privileged we are to live in this land of Canada, one of the finest nations in the world today. I think Dr. John Fisher has done and is doing a great deal to educate Canadians, not only as to the geography of their country but as to its potential wealth and resources. Dr. Fisher has described our country as being a tri-oceanic country, bounded by the Atlantic and the Pacific with a coastline of five thousand miles and the Arctic with a coastline of twenty-six thousand miles.
I wonder if at times we appreciate that this country in which we live is as high as it is wide, that from Pelee island in Ontario to Ellesmere at the top of the roof of the world, and still in Canada, is practically the same distance as from British Columbia to Nova Scotia.
I like the metaphor used by Dr. Fisher in describing our country when he referred to it as being a house of many rooms. First of all we have the veranda. We call it the American veranda and we are glad to have United States tourists come to our country and spend their dollars. Then we have the ground room in this house. At the

The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray moment I think of the cities as being on the ground floor. I think of my home city of Woodstock, Ontario, and the surrounding towns of Ingersoll, noted for its cheese, about which I shall say something later on, and the town of Tillsonburg, noted for its prowess in the field of sport. Then I think of other cities like Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and Vancouver. I think of the great contributions they have made to the industrial growth of our nation. Then, sir, above this ground floor we have another room. We call it the mezzanine floor. I am thinking at this time of the cities on that mezzanine floor that are so well represented by different members in the House of Commons, cities such as Sudbury, Kirkland Lake-whose member we think of at this time-and other places such as Noranda, Haileybury and Val d'Or. I think of the great contributions in minerals they have made to Canada.
Back and beyond the mezzanine floor there is a bedroom. There are not many tenants living in that bedroom today. About the only time we hear from them is when Churchill on Hudson bay speaks out during the white sheets of winter or when the ships go sailing in there for two or three months of the year. Last week we heard the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) speak about that region, and I would recommend his excellent speech to every member of the house. I predict, as did the hon. member for Churchill, that some day many thousands of people will live in that far northern bedroom of Canada. If you do not think so just remember this. You will be amazed, as I was, to learn that Stockholm in Sweden is as large and beautiful a city as Toronto, yet Stockholm is on the same latitude as the Yellowknife area hundreds of miles north of here. Therefore I say that some day there will be many people living in that great far northern bedroom of Canada.
At this time I should like to compliment the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) for the part he is playing in endeavouring to populate that area. I recall that some little'time ago I heard Dr. Pleva of the University of Western Ontario make the prediction that the population of Canada will double itself within the next thirty years. Therefore I foresee, as was emphasized by the hon. member for Churchill the other day, a great future for that northern bedroom of Canada.
Some time ago I remember reading an article in the Financial Post to the effect that members of parliament should travel more in order to learn more of the great country in which we are privileged to live. I think that we should, that a great number of us do not appreciate or realize the potentialities and

vastness of the country in which we live. I want to say to. the house today that Canada is a great country, and it seems to me that, instead of the bickerings and lamentations we hear from time to time from members of the opposition, we should slip down on our knees more frequently and thank God for the privilege of living in Canada.
It is not a glamorous country like the United States of America. Neither is it a glorious country like Great Britain with all its history and traditions, but to each and every one of us today I think Canada is an exciting and fascinating country. To those of us with Scottish blood in our veins, may I say, I like to think of that song we sing on St. Andrew's day or on the birthday of Robert Burns, namely:
Oh ye'll take the high road,
And I'll take the low road.
And I'll be in Scotland afore ye. . . .
It seems to me that is typical of the role of Canada today, neither the high road nor the low road but somewhere in between, fabulously right. Today as I speak of Canada I am reminded of the words of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prud-ham) when he said to us some time ago that Canada's real strength is not in its size, great and all as it is, and neither is its strength to be found in its resources, great and all as they are, but rather the solid enduring strength of Canada comes from the character of our people. In other words, the sinews of production are not dollars but rather our effort and the spirit to achieve. That spirit has animated our nation throughout its history, and I predict that spirit will carry our country through every hard test the future may bring.
I submit that the history of Canada has been one of meeting the challenge of difficulty. That is why I say that this year's budget is substantially sound. It is not, as was stated by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), a false budget. Neither is it an Alice in Wonderland budget or a phantom budget. To the sound thinking people of Canada it is like the ones that have preceded it that have been brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It is a stability budget. By whatever waters of Babylon our tents may be pitched, or whatever political differences we may have, none of us can deny that as a result of this year's budget Canada's credit abroad is being strengthened, inflation is being controlled, capital for investment is being attracted, and today our dollar is at a premium in the market places of the world. I should like to repeat the heading quoted from the Financial Post of April 12 by the parliamentary assistant

to the Minister of Finance which reads: "It Hurts But It Is Sound". I should like to read one of the sentences in that article. It is as follows:
There are people in other countries who only wish that their own governments would or could follow our example.
As was emphasized by the minister, our major difficulties are international in their origin. I say again today that freedom is not free. It was bought with a price and we are going to have to pay the price of retaining it. I feel that the Minister of Finance, in the light of the exigencies of the times through which we are passing, has budgeted in the interests of Canada as a whole. I am sure he must have had those lines of Longfellow constantly before him when he was compiling this year's budget:
Build today, then, strong and sure,
With a firm and ample base;
And ascending and secure Shall tomorrow find its place.
The Minister of Finance has set before us a fiscal policy that has made our nation the envy of the world. He has held true to those precepts that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and others with Scottish blood in their veins learned at their mother's knees, namely, to save for a rainy day. In that regard I have here a copy of the Toronto Star of March 24, 1952. It contains an article with the heading, "Saving For Rainy Day Good Idea Frost Says But Doesn't Follow it." The article reads in part as follows:
Almost two centuries ago a noted English author and moralist, Abraham Tucker, wisely admonished people to save for a rainy day. "It behooves us," he wrote, "to provide against a rainy day while the sun still shines." This was sound advice when these lines were penned and it is equally sound advice today . . . Premier Frost himself raised this point in his budget speech. "Credit," he said, "should be soundly used. It is a real asset which should always be conserved. Times come in the life of a province when, because of recession or other conditions, it is necessary to increase the net debt. But in times of buoyancy it is the way of prudence to pay as much of our capital costs as we can from current revenues."
It would appear that the federal government has done this, and that it has reduced our debt in the past five years by almost $2 billion. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the minister must have been reading some of the old axioms before preparing this year's budget. I am reminded in particular of one that is attributed to Confucius. You know, we made Confucius say some silly things but he had his more serious moments; and in one of those serious moments he said this:
It is the duty of us in our day and generation to plant the trees so that those who follow after may enjoy the shade.
I think the minister was following that axiom in this year's budget. He is budgeting
The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray not only for a solvent Canada today but also for a solvent Canada tomorrow. He has indicated that if we are energetic and resolute, and if we work, there is a good prospect of achieving in the not too distant future perhaps not genuine peace throughout the world but at least a position of reasonable confidence and security that can be maintained at a more reasonable cost than we are now compelled to pay.
I agree with the minister that work is the greatest morale building force in the world today, the one thing that gives dignity and self-respect to man. If we will work, by the grace of God we can save ourselves. If on the other hand we become a nation of parasites, as some in this house would want us to be, then I fear that only deterioration and decay can set in. I think of my grandparents coming to this country. Why did they come here? Because they saw in this land opportunity and work for their brood of children. Ofttimes today I fear that opportunity may be beginning to disappear, when in certain quarters you hear it said to men, "Don't work so hard. Get as much as you can." I say that when a seed bursts in the blackness of the soil and reaches to the sunny heavens it is performing a natural instinct; and we are thwarting that kind of effort in Canada if today men are told, "Don't work so hard. Get as much as you can."
So I think the minister is to be congratulated on the stability budget he has brought down this year. We all realize that his role is very difficult; nor has it been lightened by the times through which we are passing. If I were to make one or two suggestions-and certainly it would only be by way of suggestion at this time, not by way of criticism-the first would be that further consideration be given to the medical deduction over and above the 4 per cent allowable at the present time. In that regard I think the minister might very well recognize the principle he established last year in exempting certain drugs such as cortisone, liver extract, and so on. I think that principle might be further extended as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) suggested to include drugs such as di-alpha tocopherol, as well as some of the antibiotics such as aureomycin, terramycin, Chloromycetin and some of those expensive drugs that are on the market today. I say to the minister that hundreds of these new drugs are coming onto the market, and the horizon is equally challenging and tremendous. I think it would help a good many people if consideration could be given to extending the list of drugs to include those I have suggested.

The Budget-Mr. A. C. Murray
Then I am interested and concerned, as I know the minister is, with the present tax structure with regard to corporations. I think a perusal of reports coming from industry for the first quarter will indicate that while business is good and sales are good, money that could be used for further expansion is being siphoned off in taxes. I know the minister will bear in mind that we want to do our best to help the further expansion of these industries that have done so much to build up our country.
Then I would want to say a word at this time on behalf of the dairy industry of my county and particularly the cheese industry, which at this time is in a rather precarious condition. Already hon. members on both the opposition and the government sides have emphasized the position in which the cheese industry finds itself, which is further aggravated by the presence of surplus milk in the country due to the foot-and-mouth disease. I hope the federal government will adopt a very sympathetic attitude toward that industry, which through no fault of its own finds itself in such a position.
Then, sir, I would want to join in the remarks of the hon. member for Kent, Ontario (Mr. Huffman) and the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Robertson) in asking that further consideration be given our rural mail carriers. It seems to me that this is a subject to which every hon. member would like further consideration given; but at this time I only want to join with the others who have spoken in asking that the government give the most careful consideration in order that something better might be done on behalf of these men who give years of service in carrying the mails of our country.
It is not my intention to speak longer in this debate, but in the light of Canada's progress I am sure we must all feel that we are advancing steadily toward full nationhood. This country of 14 million people is playing a far more significant part in international affairs than did the 5 million people who came to our shores from less prosperous lands and I feel that the fruition of the plan of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to build the St. Lawrence seaway, either alone or in co-operation with the United States, will mean one of our greatest adventures in development. We must admit, I think, that while we have been vigilant for our own prosperity we have gone forward steadily and in freedom toward a decent level of life. We have carefully re-examined the way of human

welfare; and as a result of the old age security program of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) thousands of citizens of Canada can now live in dignity and self-respect.
I suggest, sir, that there is a strong tide flowing in the affairs of men. Social injustices are being swept aside and human progress is at the flood. Some may ask what of the future. I suggest, sir, that this is not the time for us to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, as one hears the phrase. This is not the time to be merely on the defensive as to those things that are just and true and of good report. Now is the time for all of us in this great nation to be active thinkers and doers, in furthering and in sharing with others the verities and the abundance of this great nation in which we are privileged to live.
I started my speech this afternoon by saying that it was a privilege to take part in the budget debate this year. I am reminded that privilege and responsibility are veritable Siamese twins in the world of abstraction. You never meet them alone. I say to this house: whether we serve as members of the House of Commons or whether we act as citizens of Canada, each and every one of us in turn has a like responsibility not only to build our defences strong, not only to budget for a pay-as-you-go policy, not only to maintain a sound economy for our nation, but also somehow, in some way, to build the attributes of decency among the peoples of the world and to work for that day when peace shall come and wars shall be no more.
If we do that-if we go our way improving the standards of living of our people; if we help our neighbours where'er in the world they may be-then it seems to me that we can face the future undaunted and with the surety that it will be of our own shaping.
I do not know of any finer way in which I can, with any greater propriety, interpret that closing thought than to give you the thoughts presented by Mr. Cameron Ralston when he visited our nation some months ago. Speaking particularly to those of us with Scottish blood in our veins, he said this: As you know, we in Scotland have a patron saint called Saint Andrew but long ago many of us have substituted a great Scottish son in his place, namely Robert Burns-one who wrote of simple things; one who said that a simple man was the greatest work of God; one whose heart was touched by the affliction of a mouse or a daisy in the field; one who wrote that great and majestic poem: "A Man's

a Man for a' That." If my memory holds, I should like to give the closing verse of that great poem:
Then let us pray that come it may,
(As come it will for a' that,)
That Sense and Worth, o'er a' the earth.
Shall bear the gree, and a' that.
For a' that, an' a' that,
It's coming yet for a' that,
That man to man, the world o'er,
Shall brothers be for a' that.
I therefore say to you in closing this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, that likewise we in Canada have a great responsibility. We have a responsibility not merely to act as a bridge between Great Britain and the commonwealth, and not merely to act as a stopgap between Great Britain and the United States. We have our own torch to bear; to carry and to maintain the highest forms of decency and the soundest forms of fiscal policy that it is possible for the nation of Canada to achieve. That the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has endeavoured to do his part has been exemplified, I submit, by this year's budget. He has endeavoured to plant the trees, in his time and generation, so that those who follow after may enjoy the shade.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the last speaker but one for the stand he took this afternoon when he spoke in this budget debate on the subject of housing. I was very glad to hear him join with us in criticizing the lending institutions for their failure to make mortgage money available for the socially desirable objective of housing for our people. I thought his words were well chosen when he suggested that private enterprise, as represented in this case by the lending institutions, should recognize its social responsibility and should be more concerned about the housing of our people than it is for making a profit out of investments of the kind to which he referred. I was also glad to hear him join with us in prodding the government and in urging that if mortgage money is not being made available by the private lending institutions for housing, the time has come for the government to go into this field itself.
That view of course has been expressed from this corner of the house a number of times; it was expressed only the other day by my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), and I hope that in
The Budget-Mr. Knowles due course between us we shall be able to persuade the government that it has no option but to implement the suggestions made again this afternoon.
I was also glad to hear the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) suggest that improvements will have to be made in the terms of section 35 of the National Housing Act. He spoke, as he always does, in glowing terms of this section, the section which makes possible joint federal-provincial low-rental housing projects; but nevertheless in the course of his speech I thought he made it clear that one of the greatest lacks of our time is still the lack of low-rental housing.
I suggest that one of the reasons there is not as much building of homes for ownership as both the hon. member for Spadina and I would like to see is that many of the people for whom he expressed concern this afternoon simply cannot afford the ownership of homes even on the terms possible under the National Housing Act, and that what is necessary for great numbers of people is low-rental housing.
The hon. member for Spadina, although he praised section 35 of the act, admitted its shortcomings when he pointed out that not enough housing is being built, and when he suggested that probably the proportion to be guaranteed by the federal government under section 35 should be increased from its present figure of 75 per cent up to 80 per cent or 85 per cent or perhaps even higher. I fully agree with him as to the desirability of as much home ownership on the part of our people as possible, but the fact of the matter is that for great numbers of our Canadian citizens the only solution to the housing problem in the immediate future at any rate lies in extending the principle of public low-rental housing. This is a matter of extreme urgency, and I hope that, even as the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) ought to pay attention to our plea that government money be made available for the building of homes where private mortgage money is not being supplied, he will also pay attention to our plea for the improving of section 35 so that it may be used more widely for the actual building of low-rental housing.
I might add further that I was glad to note the statements of the hon. member for Spadina in respect of a number of other matters, particularly when he suggested that there are various fields where social responsibility requires that, private enterprise having failed to deliver the goods, the government, in the name of the people, should step in.

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
There are one or two matters, Mr. Speaker, that were the particular reason for my getting into this debate again at this stage, but before I come to them there are one or two general comments with respect to the budget that I should like to make. I agree with those who have said that one of the faults of the present budget is the manner in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) presented it, particularly in his failure, when he gave us his tables showing the new rates of income tax, to include a column showing what the rates were as actually paid in the year 1951. In most budgets it has been the practice to indicate the amount of tax paid at various income levels for the last year and for the current year. In this instance the minister chose to omit the column showing the actual amounts paid in 1951. He chose rather to compare the rates to be paid in 1952 with what would have been the case if there had been no budget at all. The result is that the minister found it possible by his method of reasoning to suggest that there was a decrease in income tax; whereas in point of fact in the actual amounts to be paid by the citizens of Canada there will be an increase in 1952 over what was actually paid in 1951. I think it is unfortunate that the minister chose to present it in that way, but at any rate it is now painfully clear to the people of Canada that this year's budget does involve an actual increase over what was paid last year in the rates of income taxes.
It is also clear that that increase is felt by our people before the social security tax is added. In that connection I should like to point out that the Minister of Finance seemed to enjoy referring to old age security and its cost as many times as he could during the course of his budget speech on April 8. I am reminded by the minister, the parliamentary assistant and others who refer so often to the cost of social security, of the line followed in this respect by the Winnipeg Free Press which is published ini my own city. That newspaper is most anxious that people realize something that they already know, namely that we do have to pay for social security, and indeed for everything that we provide for ourselves through the medium of our governments. But the Free Press even goes so far as to suggest that the deductions at the source paid by the average worker when he gets his pay envelope should be itemized for him, and that he should be told every time he gets his pay envelope just how much has been deducted from his pay for social security.
I have no objection to that being done, provided at the same time something else is

done-and I hope the Winnipeg Free Press will join me in this suggestion, to be implemented along with their own. I suggest that at the same time on the wage earner's envelope there should be indicated the amount he has contributed, during that period for which he is receiving his pay, to the profits of the corporation for which he is working. After all, that is where the wealth of this country comes from-from the toil of our farmers on the farms, our workers in the cities, our miners, our fishermen-it comes from all those who work to produce the great wealth of this country. It is precisely because the profits of great corporations, defence costs, social security items and everything else, are paid for by the work of our people, that we contend that our people are entitled-not as a matter of charity, not as a handout, but as a matter of right-to social security, not only to the extent we have achieved it thus far, but in an expanded form such as we of this party shall continue to advocate.
One of the reasons I wanted to speak again at this stage of the debate was to discuss briefly with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) what I consider to be a continuing piece of discrimination as between lawyers and trade unionists. I wish to say that I take those two groups for the purpose of putting this matter in a simplified form. There are others who are with the lawyers, and there are others, likewise, who are with the trade unionists.
The Minister of Finance will recall that for a few years leading up to just before his budget speech of last year I had a good deal to say concerning the deductibility of trade union dues, teachers' fees and other like amounts for income tax purposes. I pointed out to him that in practice a line was drawn which, despite the way in which the minister defined that line, for the most part became a line between people like lawyers and doctors on the one hand and people like trade unionists and school teachers on the other. The line that was established was drawn, technically speaking, in terms of whether one's income was gross or net. If one's income was gross, in terms of fees he received out of which he paid expenses -hiring help of one kind or another-he was permitted to deduct fees, such as those of law societies. But if one's income was net, such as wages or salary, he was denied that right.
I believe there is complete agreement between the minister and me as to the facts. Strictly speaking, that was the way in which that line was drawn. Nevertheless, in actual practice, since most lawyers were in the one group and most trade unionists were

in the other, it worked out so that lawyers were getting the right to deduct their fees to the law society, while trade unionists were not getting the same right in respect of their trade union dues.
Part of this is now old history, but it will take only a few moments to review it. I am going through it because it leads up to a continuing discrimination which I hope the minister will even yet bring to an end. He knows that during the years 1945, 1946 and 1947 the law was worded in such a way that in due course the Exchequer Court of Canada decided that it did entitle trade unionists to deduct their trade union dues during those years. That decision was made by Mr. Justice Angers in June of 1949. However, that decision was made because a trade unionist, Mr. Joseph A. Cooper of Winnipeg, a moving picture projectionist, had appealed against the decision of the Minister of National Revenue. Mr. Cooper had sought to deduct his trade union dues. The Department of National Revenue had denied him that right. He went through the usual machinery and, in due course, in April of 1948, appealed the decision to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
Interestingly enough, it was in May of 1948, only a few weeks after Mr. Cooper filed his papers with the Exchequer Court of Canada, that the government brought in notice of a resolution to change the Income War Tax Act so as to make it clear that trade unionists would not have that right. It is my belief that the government took that step so soon after this case was taken to the Exchequer Court of Canada because they had reason to believe that the Exchequer Court might rule in favour of Mr. Cooper, in view of a decision the Exchequer Court had made on November 1, 1946, in the Bond and Rutherford case.
The case of Bond and Rutherford involved two lawyers from the city of Winnipeg who had appealed against a decision of the income tax authorities denying them their right to deduct their bar society fees on the ground that they were on salary-one of them was employed by the city of Winnipeg and the other by the province of Manitoba-and therefore that they were not in the same class as the average lawyer who makes his income by collecting fees and paying out expenses in connection with the making of his income.
Mr. Justice Thorson on November 1, 1946, had ruled that, in view of the way the act then read, Mr. Bond and Mr. Rutherford were just as entitled to deduct their fees to the law society as were other lawyers, even though Mr. Bond and Mr. Rutherford were on salary. I think it followed that, Mr. The Budget-Mr. Knowles Justice Thorson having made that decision in the Bond and Rutherford case, it was almost inevitable that the Exchequer Court would make a parallel decision in the Cooper case.
I draw the government's attention to the fact that nothing was done immediately following the decision in the Bond and Rutherford case, which was made by Mr. Justice Thorson on November 1, 1946. That decision was accepted; the law was not changed. But immediately after Mr. Cooper took his case to the Exchequer Court of Canada in April 1948, in the very next month, the month of May, a resolution was brought in to change the Income War Tax Act and to alter its wording so as to make it clear that the right to deduct trade union dues would be prohibited.
The decision of Mr. Justice Angers was not made until June 1949, and by this time the law had been changed respecting the income taxation years of 1948 and 1949.
The rest of the story is known, of course, to hon. members. The matter was debated in the house three or four times, and was voted down on at least two occasions. But finally, on April 10, 1951, in the minister's budget for that year, he announced that legislation would be introduced to make trade union dues deductible.
Naturally I was very pleased to have this decision made by the government. It was good to know that that battle had been won, and I think all hon. members recognized that it was only a matter of fairness that the legislation be so worded that groups such as trade unionists and teachers would be in precisely the same position as groups such as doctors and lawyers.
So far so good. But it was only a few months after that change respecting dues to trade unions, teachers' associations, bar societies, medical societies and so on was made that there appeared in the newspapers an item *t. the effect that a ruling had been given that lawyers were permitted to deduct for income tax purposes expenses incurred in connection with attendance at conventions of the Canadian Bar Association. I was surprised. I felt, "Well, here we go again; this is where I came in. We have just succeeded in getting one discrimination ended and now another one turns up." I did not know at that time that for some considerable period apparently lawyers had1 been deducting expenses incurred in connection with attendance at bar association conventions provided they were on gross rather than on salary, but it now transpires that that had been the case.
It also transpires that the decision referred to in the press last fall was one given on

The Budget-Mr. Knowles August 30, 1951, by Mr. W. S. Fisher, Q.C., a member of the income tax appeal board. As hon. members know, when the Income War Tax Act was replaced by the Income Tax Act one of the changes made was to provide that appeals which had formerly gone to the Exchequer Court of Canada would now go to the income tax appeal board. Therefore the decision of Mr. W. S. Fisher, Q.C., has in fact the status of the decisions by Mr. Justice Thorson and by Mr. Justice / gers, to which I referred a few minutes ago.
The decision of Mr. W. S. Fisher, Q.C., on August 30, 1951, related to an appeal by Mr. H. F. Parkinson, a lawyer who had claimed a deduction from personal income in connection with expenses incurred personally by him in attending a convention of the Canadian Bar Association, The facts in connection with this decision are to be found on page 1458 of Hansard of April 21, 1952, where answers are given to questions I had asked about this case. It appears that the reason the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue disallowed Mr. Parkinson's claim for this deduction was that Mr. Parkinson was apparently a member of a partnership and was on salary. The department took the view that if these expenses had been claimed by the partnership it would have been a different story, but since they were claimed by Mr. Parkinson as a deduction from his personal income that put him on the wrong side of the line and therefore he could not be allowed that deduction.
As 1 say, Mr. Parkinson was not satisfied with the decision of the taxation division and he appealed to the income tax appeal board. It was held by Mr. W. S. Fisher of the income tax appeal board1 that there was no reason to differentiate between the procedure of deduction adopted by the appellant and the procedure of deduction that would be adopted in the case of the partnership.
I submit that we are right back where we were at the time of the Bond and Rutherford case. We now have a case of an individual lawyer claiming deduction of convention expenses from his personal income. He was denied that by the taxation division but was allowed it by the income tax appeal board which, as I say, is the present counterpart of the Exchequer Court of Canada at the time when the other decisions were made.
My request in connection with this matter is that fairness be established. I am prepared to admit that it is more difficult to make a case for the deductibility of convention expenses than it was to make a case, as we did with eventual success, for the deductibility of dues either to a trade union, to a teachers'


society or to other similar bodies. But I submit that it should be one way or the other, either both lawyers and trade unionists should be allowed their convention expenses as deductible for income tax purpose, or neither should be allowed this right. When I ask that the same treatment be accorded to trade unionists as is accorded to lawyers I have in mind other groups as well, such as farm conventions of one kind and another, church conventions, women's institutes, the Canadian Legion and all the rest. I submit that if lawyers attending conventions of the Canadian Bar Association are permitted to deduct their convention expenses regardless of a line that has been drawn in the act, indeed if that right is given to them, even when they are on salary, by a decision of the income tax appeal board, then the law should be so worded as to grant that right to trade unionists and other groups as well. All I ask is that the law be fair.
I have questioned the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) about this once or twice, notably on October 15, 1951, when I drew his attention to this particular case and asked if steps would be taken to extend the same privileges to trade unionists attending their conventions and to other comparable groups. On that day the minister said that since I had not given him notice, perhaps my question could stand until a later date. I reminded him of it on Friday, October 19, 1951, as reported on page 195 of Hansard for that day, at which time the minister said:
I had forgotten to answer the hon. member's question. Of course it is one of law. I have not examined the decision of the income tax appeal board; but I assume the board must have decided that the lawyer in question incurred these expenses as necessary expenses in earning his income. If a member of a trade union is in the same position in deducting expenses, and if he can say that his attendance at a trade union convention was necessary, incidental to the earning of his income, then I assume that as a matter of law the court would hold the same thing. However, it is purely a question of law.
Those were the words of the Minister of Finance. In passing, may I point out that a trade unionist on salary is not in the same position in the matter of deduction as is a lawyer on gross income, so that that similarity vanishes. But the point that bothers me most about this is the minister's insistence that this is purely a point of law. In view of that insistence I asked the minister this supplementary question:
Does not the minister feel that the law should be changed so as to make sure that all these different groups are treated alike?
This was the minister's reply:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I think it Is strictly a question for the courts.
My point is that when the courts, the Exchequer Court of Canada in that case,

decided that the law as it was worded in 1945, 1946 and 1947 gave Mr. Cooper and other trade unionists the right to deduct their trade union dues, the government took the view that that was not what they had intended. Since the court had drawn their attention to the fact that the law was at variance with their intention they took immediate steps to change the law. In fact they acted in advance; they acted as soon as they realized there would be a decision favourable to trade unionists.
When I spoke about this during the course of one of the debates on the question of trade union dues the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) expressed the view that I should not have chided the government for doing this, that I should rather have complimented the government for bringing the law into line with what had been the government's intention in the first place. The point I am making is surely obvious. If the government jumps in fast to change the law when the court's ruling is such as to give advantage to trade unionists, why is it when a similar ruling gives an advantage to lawyers the Minister of Finance simply says that it is strictly a question for the courts?
I submit it is a question of fairness. It is a question of the wording of the law, and the government should deal with the matter one way or the other. Either it should amend the law so as to make it clear that lawyers cannot claim their convention expenses-and heaven knows what convention expenses might include-or it should change the law to see to it that the same right is accorded to trade unionists, farmers, church people, legionnaires, indeed all those who have conventions that they must attend either in connection with the earning of their living or in pursuit of interests relating to the welfare of this country.
I submit it is a matter of simple justice and fairness. One cannot put the blame for it on the courts. What the courts do is to interpret the law as it stands at any given time. The courts have made an interpretation in the Parkinson case. Inasmuch as the government acted immediately to change the law following the decision in the Cooper case, I suggest they should act immediately following the decision in the Parkinson case and change it either one way or the other.
I would remind the minister that this matter has been taken up with the government by a number of people. I have in my hand, for example, copies of letters that have been exchanged between the Victoria and district trades and labour council and
The Budget-Mr. Knowles the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). My time is passing so perhaps I had better not read all the correspondence. However, I would simply indicate that the Minister of National Revenue replied on January 11 of this year to the secretary of the Victoria and district trades and labour council to the effect that expenses of trade unionists in attending conventions could not be allowed as a deduction from income in their case. He went on to say:
I would draw to your attention that members of the legal and medical professions who derive their incomes from an office or employment are not allowed any deduction from such income for convention expenses.
That is true, Mr. Speaker, but there is a catch in it, for most lawyers and doctors are not in that category while most trade unionists are. That is exactly the position we were in when we were debating union dues versus law society dues. Drawing a line like that is drawing a fictitious and unreal line. The fact of the matter is that in actual practice most lawyers now have the right, if they attend a convention of the Canadian Bar Association, to deduct their convention expenses, but practically all trade unionists-indeed all of them-are cut off from that right because of the nature of their income.
We have had other lines of this kind drawn in the income tax laws throughout the years. I can think of one that used to be there that drew a false distinction between sleeping car conductors and train conductors in respect of a matter having to do with income tax. For years it was held by Mr. Ilsley that nothing could be done about it but in due course the line was changed and a more sensible position was taken. I urge that this matter be looked at on the basis of fairness and that the law be changed so that it will be equal in its application to all our people. Surely that is the basis on which laws should be enacted, and I urge this most strongly upon the Minister of Finance.
There are a number of other matters I wish to speak about but I will use what time I have left to say a few words on the other side of the medal. The Minister of Finance is aware of the fact that I have had a good deal to say in budget debates throughout the years about deductions that I think should be allowed to people, and I think he will give me credit for the fact that the appeals I made have been like the one I have just put forward, on a basis of what I regard as essential fairness. But he may say to me: Yes, but you never suggest ways and means by which more revenue might come into the treasury. I should like

The Budget-Mr. Knowles to make one or two suggestions along that line right now. I have in my hand a clipping from Business Week of April 21, 1951. I admit at the outset that it is about a year old and also that the figures contained in the article relate to the United States and may refer to an earlier year, but I suggest that they are symptomatic and that attention should be paid to them.
The article and the table with it tell us what percentages of various kinds of income are reported to the tax collector in the United States and taxed accordingly. For example, we are told that the picture in the United States is that 99 per cent of trust fund income is reported and accordingly taxed, and that 95 per cent of wages and salaries is reported and taxed. However, only 76 per cent of dividends is reported, only 71 per cent of entrepreneurial income is reported, only 45 per cent of rental income is reported and only 37 per cent of income from interest is reported. Let me make it perfectly clear that these are figures for the United States, and they may be for a few years back because the clipping is dated April 21, 1951, but I suggest that a real effort should be made by the Canadian income tax authorities to make sure that other classes of income are put in the same position as wages and salaries.
So far as the income tax authorities are concerned, the man on a wage, the man on a salary, has had it. His income is spelled out clearly on the T-4 slip he gets at the end of the year. The wheat farmer of the west is in much the same position because he sells his wheat to the wheat board. But there are the other groups which Business Week suggests manage in one way or another to report less than their total income. I submit that, if the figures for Canada are in any sense comparable to the figures I have given, there is a substantial sum of income in this country escaping taxation because it is not got at as readily and easily as wages and salaries.
On the other side of that picture I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the deductions allowed in the corporation tax and the deductions allowed to business people, entrepreneurial people and so on should be tightened up. To my way of thinking there is too wide a discrepancy between the limited deductions allowed to the average taxpayer on wage or salary and the wide variety of deductions allowed to those whose income is gross from which they make their various deductions. We have heard these matters discussed in the house from time to time, trips by businessmen and all sorts of expenses that somehow or other are allowed

if you are on gross income. I suggest there is a real field there for tightening up and for increasing tremendously the amount of income on which government taxation might be levied.
To use the language I used a moment ago, I say again that the wage earner in particular has had it. He gets his income in the form of wages that are paid to him by his employer. In the first place most of his income tax is deducted at the source. At the end of the year he gets a T-4 slip showing the amount he has earned. There is no getting out of that, and the kinds of deductions that he can make on his income tax form are so few that it only takes him half an hour to make out his income tax return. There is nothing he can do about it. But the type of person who is on gross income and who is permitted a whole host of deductions can stay up all night, or two or three nights, thinking up ways and means by which to cut down the amount upon which he pays taxes. I submit that in view of the figures I quoted from Business Week there is a wide measure of income the government could tax to far more than offset what it would cost the treasury to implement these proposals for fairness as amongst other groups to which I have referred. Indeed I am satisfied that what would be lost to the treasury by removing the 4 per cent floor under medical expenses, for which the house voted on March 26 and concerning which I have spoken a number of times, would be more than offset if the minister would pay some attention to the type of suggestions I am now making.
I am just about through, Mr. Speaker, but in this connection I have in my hand a clipping from the New York Times of September 23, 1951, headed "Expense accounts held tax source". The dispatch is by a writer named Clayton Knowles-a namesake, although I do not know him. It is datelined at Washington, September 23 last, and reads:
In a move to increase the tax yield, Senator Paul H. Douglas, Democrat of Illinois, proposed today to limit tax deductions for business entertainment and travel, to reduce opportunity for "high living at public expense."
The article goes on to say that Senator Douglas proposed to strike out deductions for liquor and for entertainment, and to limit allowable travelling expenses to $12 a day. This was commented upon in an issue of The Nation which appeared shortly after Senator Douglas introduced his bill, in these words:
The suggestion of Senator Douglas that congress limit the deduction of entertainment and travel

expenses from taxable corporate income will probably strike more fear into the heart of the average businessman than all the talk of higher corporate rates.
That is why I suggest that if this policy were pursued the minister might pick up quite a good sum of money, more than enough to offset the cost of some of the things we have been asking for. The dislike of business for a suggestion of this kind shows there is real money to be found in this way. This editorial in The Nation goes on to say:
It is no secret that high corporate rates, especially the excess profits tax, have increased the temptation to pad the expense account in order to reduce the tax bill. The "swindle sheet" today takes more money from Uncle Sam than from the employer. So while applauding Senator Douglas' suggestion, we wonder why it singles out liquor and travel.
Time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I hear hon. members calling "time", and for once I agree with them; I see that my time is gone. I commend the rest of the editorial from which I have been quoting, for it makes other valuable suggestions. I hope the minister will pay some attention to the proposals I have made in the latter part of my speech, as to ways in which he might pick up more money; and at the same time I urge him to pay attention to my plea for fairness, which I made earlier in my remarks tonight.

Mr. Speaker, some time ago the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave me very good advice. He said, "Listen carefully for a while, and then make a speech on a subject close to your heart." Tonight I would like to speak on housing, a subject that is close to my heart.
Historically housing accommodation was supplied by fathers to their sons when they got married and set up their own establishments. This was taken as a matter of course and proceeded from generation to generation. Masters provided housing for servants, and it seemed a very workable and very satisfactory system.
Times have changed a lot.

Just as my hon. friend
interjects, times have changed. Whether we liked it or not we had the great industrial revolution, which produced results both good and evil. Unfortunately we have to take the evil with the good. However desirable the old system may seem in retrospect, it is impossible to return to it. So we might as well be realistic and accept the situation as it now exists, and do the best we can with it.
I know all hon. members are as interested in this subject as I am. The situation in the
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer city from which I come and part of which I represent is not good, and certainly is deserving of a great deal of study and research. In Toronto a married couple without children can find accommodation in a single room for a fairly modest amount, and can get along quite well. But as soon as they start raising a family they immediately project themselves into the position of having to seek accommodation which will cost double or treble that which was required of them without children. It is owing to this unfortunate social handicap and to the fact that recently the proportion of house building in respect to total construction has been in serious decline that I feel further study must be given to the problem of increasing the supply.
I suppose the next logical point is, whose responsibility is it? Constitutionally, according to the judicial interpretation of the British North America Act, it is a provincial responsibility. However, I feel that because the constitution is a product of human beings, it should not be allowed to interfere with the welfare of the people. Actually the problem breaks down very nicely and naturally into aspects. The first, the federal aspect, is the financial responsibility. The federal government has been charged with the responsibility over money and banking. Owing to the tremendous capital investment required it is beyond the ability of any other level of government to take care of the problem. It is quite natural, then, that the financial responsibility should be looked after where that can be done adequately, and that is in this federal parliament.
Then there is the provincial aspect. Under our constitution property and civil rights fall within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. Therefore it is quite reasonable and logical that the provinces should undertake the responsibility of providing the land and services necessary for these housing developments. In addition, there is a very definite private responsibility on the part of the industry, and I think the industry will do its part to accept that responsibility.
I will discuss these points in the order in which I have outlined them. The first is the federal aspect. As you all know, through the agency of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the federal government makes joint loans to prospective home owners and also to builders for speculation. These joint loans are made with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation putting up 25 per cent of the money, and the lending institution, ordinarily an insurance company or trust company, the remaining 75 per cent. In effect this means that the availability of mortgage

The Budget-Mr. Hellyer financing is directly tied to the selling of insurance. This raises a very logical question. What possible connection has the selling of insurance with the need for residential housing? In addition, as my hon. friend and colleague from Spadina (Mr. Croll) outlined this afternoon, at the moment we are faced with the problem that the net return to financial institutions on N.H.A. loans, after charges for administration, is approximately 4J per cent.
These companies now find other equally or more attractive investments in the commercial field. This substantiates mere balance sheet decisions against National Housing Act loans. But I personally think that the insurance companies have a great moral responsibility not only to their policy holders but to the public at large; they have a trust to ensure and to preserve our way of life and to keep it worth fighting for.
There seems to be a widespread impression that mortgage financing is in the field of risk capital. I personally do not subscribe to this theory because I feel that in a stable economy investment in good, sound housing is not of a risk nature; it is not of a great risk nature, anyway. If we have another depression which is nearly comparable to the one experienced in the 1930's I believe we would have either a change of government or revolution; and probably in either case th# paper that the mortgage companies and the insurance companies held would not be worth much.
In a stable economy it would seem that the interest rate on residential mortgages is too high. Mr. Speaker, we fight wars with 3 per cent money and we fight the causes of wars with 51 per cent money. Is that a sensible thing to do?
No. It is nonsense.
This is the most sensible speech I have heard from the opposite side of the house.

Next is the provincial aspect. Generally the provinces must co-operate fully with the municipalities in supplying serviced land and educational facilities. In many areas these fields have been left on the doorstep of the builders. I cannot see why the builders should have to shoulder the entire responsibilities of the municipalities and the provinces put together.
If I may mention my own province, may I say that in it there is a great field for educational aid. The cost of education to municipalities makes almost prohibitive the allowing of new subdivisions. Consequently the municipalities are doing everything in their power to restrict and to obstruct new


subdivisions for residential housing. They admit this fact quite openly. In the paper last week there was an article written of and subscribed to by the reeves of various municipalities in the greater Toronto area, stating that circumstances make it almost impossible for them to supply educational facilities for new residential subdivisions.
As a representative of a Toronto constituency I know hon. members will excuse me if I just touch on our own problem briefly in the course of my remarks.
It is a typical problem.

I have here a clipping from the Toronto Daily Star, dated Saturday, March 8, 1952. It is an article as a result of a speech made by a Conservative member of the provincial legislature. The member who was speaking was Mr. Harold Fishleigh, Progressive Conservative member for Woodbine, Toronto. He has this advice for our provincial government:
Appoint an official with authority to:
Acquire land immediately for 30,000 homes. Survey, prepare plans and register same. Let sewer and water contracts; build water works and pumping stations, plus primary schools.
Sell the land to builders at a fair profit and business frontage for as high a figure as can be obtained.
This would give 30,000 homes per year within two years at no loss to the province and give the outside municipalities a chance to obtain more industries on their land and get their affairs in order so they could revert back to installing the services and putting them on the tax rate.
I can offer to the premier of Ontario no better advice than that given by his own supporter. I think it is sound and factual. This procedure would, as Mr. Fishleigh has stated, increase the supply of housing, owing to the favourable conditions; and also-he did not mention this but I think it is almost beyond dispute-it would mean, if that land were sold at even a modest profit to the province, a saving of from $300 to $500 for each and every housing unit built on it. This saving would be passed on directly to the individual purchaser. The entire operation would be self-liquidating and would not cost the taxpayers a cent.
There is also the responsibility of the industry itself. In this connection there is vast room for improvement. I think the industry recognizes this fact and is doing everything that it can to co-operate in overcoming the problems.
First, there is the problem of building products. I have here a clipping from another Toronto newspaper of probably some authority, namely the Globe and Mail, of Monday, February 6, 1950, and which is headed "Sees Obsolete Methods Behind Housing Lack".
The hon. member said the date was 1950.

That is what it says here. I do not know whether or not it is a typographical error. The article reads in part:
Antiquated building methods, lack of organization in the building industry, obsolete ways of manufacturing bricks and restrictive labour practices were cited as among the hitches in housing by two authorities last night.
One of the authorities was P. A. Deacon, Ontario chairman of the Community Planning Association of Canada, and the other was J. Louis Shannon, one of the Toronto controllers. These gentlemen are quite accurate in some of their observations. Even the bricks we use are not standardized. There are many different sizes and such a simple device as a storey rod so that all houses come out at the same level at the first storey is practically impossible because one type of brick runs you an inch higher and another type of brick runs you an inch lower, and standardization is impossible.
Builders in the United States are attempting to inaugurate and implement a system of modular construction; and I understand they are finding it quite successful in cutting the cost of production. I think we would be wise if we could follow their example in that respect. The whole industry needs streamlining. It needs a great deal more engineering. It is of course difficult for this to be done unless it can be provided with some sort of continuity. It is necessary to have a sufficient supply of mortgages to keep building operations more or less continuous. Otherwise the advantages derived from planning and engineering are lost in the muddle of jumping around and waiting for new mortgage finances. It also makes it difficult to maintain an adequate and competent staff. Trained people just do not like jobs in which you need them for a while and then do not need them for a while, where you do not need them for a few weeks, and vice versa, and back and forth. If the flow of mortgage financing was more or less continuous it would enable the industry to enlarge consistently for a few years and provide more capital, it would enable them to buy more and better equipment, to cut costs all the way along the line, and to take advantage of some of the elementary and basic principles of savings that are involved when one plans and co-ordinates production as is done in all manufacturing industries-as a matter of fact, in most industries outside of the house building industry.
The house building industry is probably one of the most inefficient remaining in our country today. One of the greatest single problems is the supposedly uncontrollable
The Budget-Mr. Hellyer factor of the weather. Winter building probably does more to disrupt continuity than anything else except the mortgages. It is a problem that I do not think is completely hopeless, but it does require very extensive research, and also a great deal of capital and very expensive equipment. I have some ideas on the subject which, from an engineering standpoint, I think are quite sound, but it would require a tremendous amount of capital to implement them, and the building industry, owing to the fact that it has had only a few good years, is still slowly emerging from the infant stage and is not yet financially capable of expensive capital outlay. It will take a while to reach the size where it can produce units efficiently the way other industries produce their product. However, there is hope in this field, and every effort should be made to continue the research and to take advantage of any constructive ideas.
Another problem in the house building industry is labour. The productivity of labour in the house building industry is very low. This is not entirely the fault of the workers. As a matter of fact it is probably not even largely their fault. I think that a great deal can be done in this regard, and especially through the medium of continuous building, and if possible year-round building. At the moment the building trades in the Toronto area are seeking very substantial wage increases. Perhaps they are being misled, not intentionally, but inadvertently. Much has been said in the last year about diminishing returns. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) found it only too true with his tobacco taxes. I think that the people engaged in the building trades will find it true this year if they are successful in obtaining the increases that are asked for.
They are going to proceed to price the industry out of the market even further, and it is almost priced out of the market now. It will be impossible to ask the mortgage companies to absorb the entire increase in costs in the mortgages, and it is reasonable to assume that the entire cost of increased wages will be reflected in the down payment, and this will tend to restrict even further the effective demand for housing, with the logical consequence that fewer houses will be built, fewer months will be worked, and on a yearly basis less income will be derived by the people engaged in the industry. It is possible that a few people working in the general construction side of the construction industry may benefit, those who have guaranteed year-round employment; but generally speaking, especially in the house building trades, where employment is of a seasonal nature, they may find that they

The Budget-Mr. Hellyer will have a smaller yearly return with the higher wage than they have at the present time, working more months of the year. This is a very old problem, the matter of short working periods among the building trades, an age-old problem, and it is one of the very difficult and seemingly insurmountable obstacles in the way of streamlining the industry.
It is not fair to take so much of the time of the house talking about housing without making some concrete suggestions. I have a few recommendations to make which fall largely into two classes: First of all, the short term, and second, the long term. In the short-term field I feel that the federal government should immediately increase its proportion of the joint loans from 25 per cent to 33J per cent. I am sure the Minister of Resources and Development will concur in that.
If he were listening.
He is.

And also at the same time reduce the interest rate on the total loan by one half of one per cent, to four and a half per cent. I suppose an aside should not be brought into a discussion on housing, but the Minister of Finance is present tonight, and since this is an address on the budget I might just state very briefly my views on tampering with interest rates as a tool of combating inflation. I personally do not believe that raising interest rates on long-term mortgage contracts is a legitimate method of combating inflation. It is the only method that this government has used in their battle against inflationary pressures that I cannot support wholeheartedly and without any reservation. I think generally speaking they have done a magnificent job, second to none in the world. They have shown that inflation can be curbed by monetary and fiscal policies, but they have also proved to those who are interested in the subject that depressions also can be cured by applying the tools in reverse, and it rather refutes the arguments of some of our friends to the left that in order to have a consistently productive and acceptable economy we must have either a war or a rumour of war. I think that idea in future will be completely disintegrated, and it will become accepted that in a diversified economy it is possible so to control matters that the hills and valleys are levelled out pretty well to a reasonable plateau.
In this respect, I think the government is to be complimented. It has done a remarkably good job on its fiscal and monetary policy, but I think changing the interest rates is a little bit like correcting a school child

by slapping his ears to such an extent that he loses the use of his hearing. It is a longterm corrective. How do we know that ten years from now we will want thousands of contracts with a high interest rate? At the moment it may be expedient to have very high interest rates on mortgages, but what will it be like five years from now or ten years from now when these contracts are still in operation?
This is a subject which cannot adequately be dealt with as an aside in a discussion on housing, and consequently I will not elaborate on it, but I would love to sometime. I cannot agree with the raising of interest rates on long-term contracts, and consequently I propose that in addition to increasing the Central Mortgage proportion of the joint loan, the interest rate be reduced to what it was last year.
Second, I think the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should increase the differential of guarantee on long-term amortization to make it more attractive for the lending institutions to increase the amortization period. At the moment some difficulty, in fact substantial difficulty is being encountered in effective demand, owing to the fact that the people are not making enough money to carry the loans on new houses. If the amortization period could be increased to 25 years it would increase the number of prospective customers substantially, and I think would be very helpful. However, I can understand insurance companies being reluctant to do this unless there is an even greater differential in the guarantee.
Then, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could increase the differential of guarantee for outlying districts, such as North Bay. This would be helpful to the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), who was so concerned about this problem

and rightly so.
Then, fourth, in cases where applications are turned down by lending institutions, and especially in outlying areas, I think Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should again make direct loans available to prospective purchasers.
Turning to long-term requirements: I think the greatest single hope of the building industry is the hope of becoming a greater industry so far as physical volume is concerned, an industry which would turn out more units per year, the year round, and consequently could take advantage of the efficiency to be achieved in that way. This would be real progress, and would be a real gain in wealth which could be passed on not only to the customers but also to the workers in the industry.

Secondly, I think a national conference should be held, or at least that it would be helpful, to discuss building codes and the standardization of materials. Building codes are antiquated. They vary from municipality to municipality, thus making it very difficult for a builder to carry on operations in four or five places at one time owing to the fact that in one place he is permitted to do one thing but is not permitted to do it in another, and vice versa. This makes uniformity and standardization most difficult. Any step taken in the direction of uniformity of standards in building codes, on a national level, would be most welcome. The same would apply to any discussion respecting the standardization of building materials, at the same level.
Such a conference might not accomplish a great deal; its progress might be slow.
