Those of us who are young, in particular, have to learn that progress is slow, and sometimes only piecemeal; but progress is sure if one keeps plugging at it. We must realize that building codes are not going to be made uniform- or standardized- overnight. Building materials cannot be standardized overnight. But progress can and should be made in that direction, so that the next generation will be able to reap the benefits from these tedious but consistent improvements.
In closing my remarks may I point out that in my view housing is a serious domestic problem, especially in the urban centres of our great country. Perhaps the only other comparable one is the necessity of retaining the purchasing power of our currency. If these suggestions are implemented they will aid in the development of a new generation of sturdy, self-reliant and responsible citizens who will take their place, as was said so eloquently this afternoon by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Murray), as our greatest national asset.

Mr. Speaker, my warmest congratulations are extended to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Hellyer) on his most objective approach to a very serious problem, namely that of national housing.
This afternoon the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) made an excellent contribution *to the debate, and this evening the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) dealt with the same subject. From time to time others have laid emphasis upon the urgent necessity for an overhaul of the National Housing Act.
Speaking in the house on Thursday, May 1, my colleague, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), devoted considerable
The Budget-Mr. Shaw time to a discussion of this subject. He concluded his speech with this observation:
It seems to me that this government should introduce some legislation that would afford some protection of the money which the home builder has invested, and which would ensure that the money was properly spent.
It is our conviction that the minister has now heard sufficient hon. members within the house, and also he must have read sufficient criticism as it has appeared in the newspapers emanating from many parts of Canada, to cause him to take immediate action to see to it that appropriate amendments to the National Housing Act are brought before the house.
It is not my intention to devote much time to a discussion of this subject, more than to say that those of us in some of the smaller centres, because of the withdrawal of the lending institutions from so many of the smaller communities within Canada, have been greatly inconvenienced. In this way there have been taken away from the people of those communities benefits which would have accrued to them as a result of the National Housing Act.
May I emphasize that the time has long since passed when, through the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), the government should take appropriate and effective action to solve this mighty and serious problem.
The amendment offered by the Progressive Conservative party is in these words:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"the proposals of the Minister of Finance are unsatisfactory because they would continue to levy excessive and unjust taxation instead of assuring substantial tax reductions.
This house condemns the government for taxing far beyond actual requirements and for its waste and extravagance.
And this house regrets the failure of the government to assure efficient administration in all departments of the public service.
We of the Social Credit group agree with that amendment. It is true that in his budget address to the house the Minister of Finance indicated that there would be certain tax reductions. First of all, there was the tax reduction upon automobiles. The minister was told when that tax was increased-as it was increased some months ago-that there would be substantial hardship imposed upon many persons who found it absolutely essential to have automobiles in pursuing their normal activities of life. He has since learned; but I am wondering if he did not know a year ago, or if this action has not been the result of a lot of costly publicity in which the automotive dealers had to indulge in order

The Budget-Mr. Shaw to secure at least a measure of justice, or to remove a large measure of injustice.
It is also highly significant that only this day has the Minister of Finance deemed it advisable to remove credit restrictions upon purchases. I wonder, too, if it is not significant that that action was taken just at this time, instead of several months ago. I suggest it is highly significant that it is taken at this time, only four weeks away from the election date in a province from which the greatest objection came with respect to these unfair restrictions. I am speaking of the province of British Columbia.
It was also noted that the minister saw fit to reduce taxes on cigarettes. Was he not told a year ago exactly what would happen? Was he not warned that the law of diminishing returns would assert itself? Did he not realize the extent to which smuggling would be undertaken? Could he not have envisioned the tremendous cost, quite apart from the loss in revenue, which would accrue as a consequence of having to have our customs officers and our R.C.M.P. running back and forth across the country trying to apprehend smugglers when there was much more important work for them to do? Surely he must have realized that a year ago. We are not unmindful of the arguments which he advanced in connection with the previous budget and we realize now just how weak they were. I trust the Canadian people do also.
There is a reduction in the taxation upon electrical appliances. I believe it was the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) who laid emphasis upon how unfair it had been to young people who had attempted to set up homes during the past year and who had suffered this heavy penalty as a consequence of paying this tax during the operation of one year. Talk about discrimination, there is an example par excellence.
I have been impressed by certain observations made by hon. members of this house during the course of the budget debate. I was struck by one observation made by the hon. member for Greenwood, I believe on the same evening the budget was brought down. He said that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had made the Canadian people tax conscious-he certainly has done that- tax puzzled-it is not a day dream-and tax angry-which is a reality. All one has to do is to be in closer contact with the Canadian taxpayer than the Minister of Finance seems to be to realize just how true that observation is.
It has been emphasized by some hon. members during this debate that once more there has been discrimination against the


Canadian taxpayer who suffers from an extremely low income. We have again placed him in a position where tax reductions which he receives are on a percentage basis much less than the benefits extended to those in the higher income brackets.
My leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), referred to the disastrous effect which the government's tax policy is having upon farm and other types of production within this country. It has imposed upon the minds of our Canadian producers the fear that something disastrous may result as a consequence of producing to the optimum level. And this in the face of the fact that everywhere in Europe we find that persons are so much in need of the commodities which we are capable of producing. To me all this is not a bit surprising. It simply represents a continuation of unimaginative Liberal financial policy.
The other day I made a rough computation-actually it is not so rough-to ascertain if possible the net effect of the federal government budget upon the taxpayers of the provinces. It was quite natural and normal for me to think of the province of Alberta because that is the province whence I come. Figures were available only for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1951, and I find that during that fiscal year the federal government took out of my province the following amounts:
General income tax	 $40,780,457.98
Corporation tax	 22,587,274.85
Non-resident tax	 809,109.71
Gift tax	 110,028.30
Deferred tax	 4,837.60
Private companies tax	 4,697,480.43
Excess profits tax	 583,338.88
Succession duties	 1,839,098.54

That was a total for one year as far as those taxes were concerned. But let us consider the excise and customs duties. An estimate which has been computed as carefully as it is possible to compute it, and which I believe is on the conservative side, indicates that during the year there was taken from the taxpayers from my province through excise taxes and customs duties imposed by the federal government, a total of $105,285,714, making a grand total up to that point of $176,697,340.29.
Is that all? Certainly not. Through the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, which has resulted as a consequence of federal government fiscal policy, and based on the cost of living index for 1951 of 184-5, the people of my province lost through that devaluation a total of $391,500,000.
Straight confiscation.

Outright and downright confiscation. I have mentioned the losses accruing as a result of the freight rates differential. My province is at the apex of the Canadian freight rates structure. The goods which we export, including our raw materials, must be quoted f.o.b. Halifax, Fort William, Toronto, Vancouver or some other place and then we must pay more for the manufactured goods imported into the province. All this as a consequence of the freight rates structure. Just to show how ridiculous that can be, let me tell you that certain goods manufactured in central Canada are shipped through to Vancouver, placed in warehouses and then shipped back to Calgary and Edmonton by local freight which is more costly than the transcontinental rate. That can be done more cheaply than to unload them at Calgary or Edmonton on their way west. What that costs us, heaven only knows, but it runs into hundreds of millions of dollars every year.
What have we lost as a consequence of the settlement of the British wheat agreement? That must run into tens of millions. Western Canadian farmers as a whole lost $376 million but a substantial part of that was borne by the farmers of my province.
I happen to represent a part of Alberta where a lot of feed grain is grown. The farmers of that area find it profitable to procure feeder livestock and feed the homegrown products. Last year the farmers in my district through two feeder associations bought $500,000 worth of feeder livestock at anywhere from thirty to thirty-four cents a pound. Then what happened? After feeding that livestock all winter the price was pegged at a figure which will gross them about twenty-two cents per pound. Those farmers have lost tens of thousands of dollars as a consequence of that action.
I have always maintained that that was something which could have been avoided had the government taken proper steps. The thing to do was to have called a conference of the provinces so that no such thing as a vicious embargo would be established by one province to keep out goods from a neighbouring province.
Sometimes we are told that we provinces- I am speaking now as though I were a province-should be most grateful for the subsidies and grants which the federal authority makes available to us. But in the case of my own province these subsidies, grants and payments for such things as irrigation and public buildings do not equal more than approximately 50 per cent of the taxes which were extracted from the people of that province by the federal authorities in
The Budget-Mr. Shaw the year 1951. That is without taking into account all these other losses which in some cases it was quite impossible to calculate. I sometimes wonder whether some of these federal grants are made to the provinces with the idea of helping them or is it with the idea of being able to try to claim credit for everything that is done by a province? I well recall that in 1949, after the federal government had undertaken to make grants for hospital construction under certain very specific and rigid conditions, and grants incidentally which in themselves would not build one hospital anywhere in Canada, the government came along at election time and said: Yes, you have lovely hospitals but we put up the money to make their construction possible.
As I say, I wonder sometimes whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was actually concerned about health and welfare or was he more concerned about getting his toe in so that somebody else could claim credit for all that was done? We are grateful for these grants, certainly we are, but at the same time it seems to me that there should be a little reasonableness, a little more good sense, and some people ought to have their feet a little more solidly fixed on the floor before they make some of their utterances.
You have got yours in the clouds.
No more of that.

I do not mind interjections if they are made in such a tone of voice that it is possible to understand them. I am going to move on to something that I think is of practical concern to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson). We happen to come from a province where gas and oil have been found.
Gas especially.
I notice that you are clamouring for it though.
Not this kind.

Developments in the field of gas and oil have been tremendous and have been advantageous not only to -the province but to all Canada. Certainly at a time like this, with warnings coming from outside the country of threats hanging over us, nothing can give us more comfort than the knowledge that our oil -and gas development has been so phenomenal. What does annoy me, however, is what appears to me to be a deliberate effort on the part of some to injure the industry through deliberate misrepresentation. I am going to accuse the Liberals. I dare say there is not a Liberal member from

The Budget-Mr. Shaw British Columbia who would not support the export of gas from Alberta to British Columbia.
You have had our lumber.
That is quite all right. I appreciate that. I am merely asserting there is not a Liberal in this house who would not welcome the export of gas from Alberta to British Columbia.
Hear, hear.

All right. Then I say some of the Liberals from British Columbia should come into Alberta and try to convert their own Liberal leader in that province, a man who is doing more to prevent gas and oil export than any other single person I know. This house was told that the other evening by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle), who certainly knows what he is talking about. It is a strange situation. The Liberal leader in Alberta, not being able to find a sensible election issue, is undertaking to concoct something relative to the oil and gas industry. As far as I am able to ascertain, federal Liberals outside of Alberta certainly do not agree with him. Take a paper like the Lethbridge Herald, a Liberal paper which supports the Liberal party in Alberta. It believes in the export of gas from Alberta. Let us take the Calgary Albertan. I do not think I should call it a Liberal paper although it has said that in the federal field at least it will support the Liberals. It takes strong issue with the Liberal leader in Alberta because of the damage he is doing to gas export from the province.
_ The attack first started last fall. At that time the accusation was that Albertans were being bled of their wealth by money powers outside of the province, and that the people of Alberta were not procuring a fair share of that asset. When that did not work the Liberal leader in that province swung to the other side of the pendulum and started attacking the export question. I know why he is doing it. It is because the leaders of farm organizations in Alberta have taken a position in opposition to the export of gas from that province, and therefore such an attitude appears to be politically popular. Conceivably some of the municipal councils have taken the same position, and there is the possibility that political support may be acquired from those quarters. I have an edi-:orial before me certain parts of which I am joing to read. They relate to the attacks which started last fall with respect to the >hare of gas and oil production which accrues :o the people of the province. I wish to refer o the Calgary Albertan of October 11, 1951. have quoted the first paragraph once before

but it consists of only four lines and I think it is an excellent paragraph with which to commence an editorial of this character. It reads:
It may not be our duty to keep cleaning up in the trail of Mr. Harper Prowse, but somebody's got to do it. The misinformation he spreads, the twisted ideas he leaves, cannot be left to clutter up public thinking indefinitely.
Is he the Liberal leader out there? You would almost think he was from Ottawa.

I sometimes think the Liberals out there wish he were not their leader. The editorial continues:
Once more, this time to a Lethbridge audience, the provincial Liberal leader has repeated the myth that the big foreign oil companies are fleecing Alberta of its rich resources with the connivance of the Alberta government. He says that countries like Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela get up to 70 per cent of the oil wealth extracted by foreign companies, while the Alberta government is content with retaining on behalf of the people a measly 14 per cent. The figure for the other countries is up to 50 per cent, not 70, according to our information.
Mr. Prowse did not explain-or at least it was not mentioned in the report of his speech-that 50 per cent is paid on net profits and in Alberta it is 14 per cent of gross production. In other countries the government takes up to half of what is left after all expenses are paid, while Alberta takes one-seventh of everything and leaves the companies to pay all expenses out of the other six-sevenths.
The rest of the editorial is extremely enlightening, but I have read that part to show that in the light of the facts the charge that was made last fall, which it was thought would make an election issue, petered out. Now it is the question of export, and once again the Albertan comes along with a very effective editorial in their issue of April 30, 1952. Dealing with this matter it has this to say:
The Liberal party will concentrate on the gas export issue in the coming provincial election because it believes the voters can be stirred by it. It will stand unalterably opposed to export, now or ever. Most other issues will fade into the shadows of that one. The Lethbridge Herald supports the Liberal party on general principle. Yet it is also strongly in favour of gas export. We are looking forward to seeing how it can rationalize the contradictions. In its latest gas export editorial it tries to blame the government for public confusion and misinformation. It says the government should have come out frankly two or three years ago and explained why export would be good for the province. But instead of giving that leadership it has been "scared by the political angle," says the Herald.
It is true that the government should have been more forthright, and that the politics of it was frightening. But it must also be admitted that all along the government has been somewhat in advance of public opinion-
I feel I can classify this as a Liberal newspaper; and it goes on:
-and that no government could afford to become too far separated from what the public is thinking.
What the Herald glaringly omits to say is that Mr. Prowse and the Liberal party have been

responsible for circulating most of the misinformation. They have deliberately aroused public prejudice and fanned and fed it. They have created public alarm where none existed. They have misrepresented the issue obviously for none but political purposes and it must be admitted that they have had some success.
A tempest in a teapot.
Right.

That's partly true. But let's not forget that the Leader of the Opposition plays a key part in public affairs, and to the extent that he perverts his responsibilities the business of government suffers. Let's put the blame where it really lies.

It it takes a position in opposition to the export policy of the government of Alberta it is also taking a position in opposition to one of its own Calgary members, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle), who in the course of his speech the other night indicated that he supported the policy of the Alberta government as far as the export of gas was concerned. As far as industry coming to the province is concerned, I would say that quite apart from gas we have not done too badly there. The cost of industrial plants completed or commenced last year in Alberta totalled approximately $65 million, while construction already approved for 1952 is in excess
The Budget-Mr. Shaw of $42 million. We have been getting industry out there, and we will continue to get it. Even though we make surplus gas available to other parts of Canada we will also obtain additional industry in western Canada -industry associated with the extraction of by-products from the gas that comes out of the ground in the several extremely important fields of Alberta.

-when the government did not need it for the purpose of meeting the expenditures of this country. Taxes are far heavier than the people are able to bear. The people are groaning under the weight of taxation which the minister has put on them with such enthusiasm.

I now want to refer to another subject; it is one in which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is interested. I want to refer to railway matters in Newfoundland. In that tenth province we have a main railway line which extends about 545 miles in a semicircle from Port aux Basques to St. John's. It is a narrow-gauge railway and it now has to face the colossal task of handling the increased trade with Canada that has developed since the act of union in 1949. By that union between Canada and Newfoundland, most of the import trade which we had with the United Kingdom and with the United States has been diverted, and most of the imports of Newfoundland are now coming from Canada. The railway is groaning under the task, and is not able to carry the load; it is not able to keep up with the traffic. A piece of goods-for instance, a refrigerator or a boiler or something like that-shipped from Ottawa takes six to eight weeks to get to St. John's. Is the government being fair to Newfoundland if it is not going to give any better service than that? Even an express package takes from seven to ten days to reach St. John's from Ottawa. A person travelling on the railways can generally get there in four days. Seven to ten days is not the right time for an express package to take to get there. Freight has to wait for seven weeks, and I think that is far too long. In fact, I wonder if the railway will ever be able to bear the traffic as it is today. Will it be able to do so?
The minister knows that there is a bottleneck at Sydney. I know that great works are being undertaken to improve the facilities at the two terminals, namely at North Sydney and at Port aux Basques. Please God that in another three or four years we shall have in service across the straits a ferry which will be able to handle the passenger traffic at its peak, and also able to carry most of the freight and to accommodate tourists with their cars in the summertime. But it is going to be at least three years before that ferry will be in operation. Construction has been delayed. It has only just started now, and the people cannot expect much relief in that direction until that time at least.
So bad is the situation that I wonder if it would not be a good idea for the government to give consideration to the question of building a wide-gauge railway across Newfoundland. It is the only part of the main line of the Canadian National Railways in the country which now is left with this narrow gauge. The government had to build a wide-gauge railway in Prince Edward Island in order to accommodate the traffic. Why should it not do so in Newfoundland? Further than
1898	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne that, I have heard the suggestion made that it might perhaps be feasible to convert part of the railway line into a highroad and use diesel-operated trucks to carry the freight. In any event, the responsibility is on the minister and he must find some way of solving this problem of improving the means for the transit of goods to Newfoundland, especially to St. John's.
A copy of the Fundy Fisherman was sent to me the other day. I am not quite sure who owns it or who is interested in it, but I suspect it is either a Liberal senator or a Liberal member of the House of Commons. In it there is an article dealing with Newfoundland, and in which reference is made to the expectations which the people of Newfoundland had when they came into union with Canada in 1949. The writer of the article in that paper says that the people have reason to complain, that they have a just grievance, in that they are not being treated as they should have been treated. The writer thinks that Newfoundland's public facilities, especially with regard to telephone communication, should be brought on a par with those in other parts of Canada. He points out-as have both my colleague the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) and I in this house-that Newfoundland had a small debt in 1949. It was insignificant when compared with the public debt that was being carried by the people of Canada. It was only about one-seventh of the public debt borne by the people of Canada. This article goes on to say that Newfoundland therefore should have its public facilities improved to a great extent in order to compensate for the increased debt which they have been compelled to bear.
It is quite obvious that the public facilities which we must have down there are better wharves, breakwaters, and various other things to facilitate trade and the natural industries of the country.
I must compliment the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) on the fine speech he made in favour of improving the port facilities in the harbour of Saint John, New Brunswick. This spring the board of trade of Saint John, New Brunswick, circularized those members who had visited Saint John last year, and pointed out that the port facilities, although it is a national harbour, were not able to accommodate the steamers coming in there-that they had to wait outside the port for a chance to get a berth at the docks. It is a national harbour, and if the facilities are not good enough it seems to me the government should do something about it.


The Daily News of St. John's points out in its editorial of April 24 that the facilities in St. John's, Newfoundland, ought to be improved similarly; that it ought to become a national harbour. Most of the trade is carried on through St. John's; it is the capital of the province; it is a city of nearly 70,000 people. The principal imports have to go through there, and the exports have to pass through there on the way out. The government ought to give consideration to making it a national harbour. In addition, the article goes on to show that it is important from a strategic point of view. During the second world war many naval ships, British, United States, Free French, Canadian and other allied shipping, were constantly using the port, and yet the facilities are not what they should be, although they received great improvement during the war.
I now wish to pass on to another subject, sir, namely that of housing. I want to compliment the minister responsible for the valuable work he did in connection with slum clearing in the city of St. John's and the 140 units which were constructed there during the past couple of years. It is undoubtedly a great improvement, and I am sure that the people who have benefited by that construction appreciate it very much. I am glad to see that a contract has now been let for about 140 more units to be constructed in the city of St. John's.
Under a Liberal government.
In spite of it.

I want to draw the attention of the house to another serious matter-I think I have done so before. I do not know how much it concerns people living in other provinces, but it seems to me regrettable and something that must be repaired, that in the small settlements throughout Newfoundland none of these housing loans or any part of the housing policy reaches them. A man living in a place like Portugal Cove South, near Cape Race, is in this position. I was in his house this past summer and I asked him how he liked living in a place like Portugal Cove South, which is about 90 miles from the city of St. John's. In the winter the roads are usually blocked. There is no communication by road or by steamer with the city, and they are there for the winter. He said: "Well, I am a fisherman; I have lived here all my life and I would like to stay here, but my wife, she's not so keen on it". They had a fine new house, but all the houses in this settlement are a good distance apart. Usually a man has his house built with a garden in front, and then he has his bam and fields for hay and that

sort of thing, and pasture behind, and a hundred feet away there is another house and so on. But they are not laid out under any regulations. Houses of that type are the most numerous ones in Newfoundland. None of them has received one cent of all the moneys that have been poured out or guaranteed by the federal government.
The minister may be interested to know that the provincial government has just introduced a bill to create community councils in settlements that have no town council. They are not big enough for a town council, but they are going to form community councils. I have been one who has criticized the provincial government very frequently when I disagreed with them. Here is something for which I must compliment them. If they are responsible for introducing that piece of legislation then I tell them they are doing one of the best things that they have ever done.
As the minister must be aware, I am sure, one of the first and fundamental things contained in the report of Lord Durham a hundred years ago when he investigated conditions in Canada was that people were going into parliament with not even the experience of having served on town councils, because no such things as town councils then existed. He recommended as the first step in the development of responsible government the creation of a system of councils. Unfortunately we have never been able to develop them sufficiently in Newfoundland. I remember years ago when I had the honour of being in the government, in 1932 or 1933, drafting a bill to form town councils but the commission of government which came in a year or so afterwards did not implement it as it should have done. But a number of small towns were incorporated, and this new bill is going to create a corporate responsibility in a large number of settlements. I hope that when these community councils are set up the minister will give consideration to granting them assistance for the improvement of housing in the small settlements. It is a matter of great concern. I am sure it must have existed in many places in Canada, and still exists, that these houses are often without a regular water supply. They depend upon wells, and they have no sewerage facilities and no form of central heating system. It seems to me that these three things are vital and ought to be introduced and ought to be in the possession of every family throughout Canada. We cannot say that sound housing is possible until these facilities are available.
I remember the late President Roosevelt of the United States taking great credit for 55704-120J
The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne the rural electrification of the state of Ohio and of other states through his electrification schemes. Well, it seems to me too that in Newfoundland, where we have such a large water supply, electricity could be a great help in that respect. I think loans should be made available to those fishermen who work so hard, deserve such consideration, and get very little. Very few of them can benefit from this wise and prudent policy of the government.
We have just heard an address by an hon. member who represents a Toronto constituency. But I am speaking tonight on behalf of those who do not live in cities and who cannot easily get accommodation when they are looking for a loan to improve their homes. Therefore they must wait even for years before they can get married, because every nail and every piece of timber or every improvement that goes into the home must be paid for in advance. A friend of mine who lives down there has been two or three years building his home. He is waiting to get the home built before he can get married. He is an industrious man. I do not think it is fair to him. The loans are available to people who live in cities. He is a good citizen, an industrious man and he has to pay for everything in cash. He has not the benefit of that accommodation. Therefore I hope that the minister will give consideration to these points I have raised.
I want to refer to another subject that has always been dear to my heart in regard to Newfoundland. I refer to the question of agriculture. This year in Newfoundland potatoes are reaching the highest price in the history of the island. I think they are reaching the highest price in the history of Canada. Anyway, they cost about 50 cents a gallon in the city of St. John's today. I think that is too much for potatoes. Our people cannot afford to pay that. There is something wrong with our Department of Agriculture, which neglected last year to see the general over-all picture when not enough potatoes were planted. The year before I remember the late member for Victoria-Carleton talking about a floor price for potatoes. Now in Newfoundland they have to put a ceiling on to keep them from going too high in price. What sort of an industry is it when it fluctuates like that? Is that the best type of fiscal policy, or agricultural policy, that we can have-a policy where, in one year, an industry is depressed right down to the bottom, while in the next year no one grows potatoes, with the result that people have to pay enormous prices for them?
I do not hear people in this city of Ottawa talking about the price of potatoes. But in
1900	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. W.J. Browne Newfoundland potatoes are a staple diet. Someone told me yesterday that the government is considering importing potatoes from the United Kingdom. I certainly hope they do, if they can be obtained cheaper, and offered at a cheaper price to the people than the price at which the small supply of potatoes now available is being offered.
The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) points out to me that potatoes are coming in from the state of Maine. They have always come from Maine, because it is just across the river from New Brunswick. There has been a constant sale of potatoes right here in Ottawa, from the state of Maine.
I remember that in 1932 we bought potatoes in the United Kingdom, some very fine strains indeed. There were the Aran Banner, the Aran Victory and Kerr's Pinks, which the people still grow in Newfoundland. Those potatoes were rot-free and canker-free, and they gave splendid results. In those dreadful years during the depression, the government, of which I was then a member, imported 30,000 or 40,000 barrels of potatoes and gave them to the people to plant. And it was a good thing we did, because by so doing we provided them with a substantial stock of potatoes to carry them through the winter, and to provide them with seed. These strains have been carried on ever since, with the result that in a year when the blight struck most potatoes, those particular ones were free from blight, and therefore were a great help to the bulk of the people who were depending upon them.
I notice that in the report for 1951 there is reference to the setting up of an agricultural experimental station. I went to see that station in St. John's, and I have nothing but the highest praise for the work being done there. But that is not enough; we want more than one experimental station in Newfoundland. I believe there are more than 120 in Canada; but I do not think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is taking his responsibilities in regard to Newfoundland seriously enough. On an earlier occasion I asked him to give consideration to the setting up of more experimental stations in Newfoundland so as to demonstrate to the people in the different parts of Newfoundland the type of vegetables that can be grown to the greatest advantage. They could be grown in greater quantities, and in this way increase the amount of produce the people could obtain from their own area.
There is a great amount of trade going on. Wealthy manufacturers are producing large quantities of iron ore from Bell island


and from Buchans. We have the greatest pulp and paper industry in the world at Corner Brook and at Grand Falls. We are sending out large amounts of exports of this kind and bringing in a lot of money. But when that money comes in, what do the people have to do? They have to send up to Canada for anything they need. I do not think that is a good condition, when so much they 'need could be produced in Newfoundland. I do not think any hon. members, including those in the government, would want to see us bringing everything over that narrow-gauge railway, which is about seven weeks behind time in the delivery of goods.
The Minister of Agriculture should give consideration to the setting-up of more experimental stations, and he should consider more carefully the situation of agriculture in Newfoundland. I know the minister is deeply concerned with affairs in his own province at the present time, due to the foot-and-mouth disease, over which he had no control. I know he is very much concerned with that. But, apart from that he has not given the proper consideration he should have given to the development of agriculture in Newfoundland. I must appeal to him again, as I have appealed to him before, to get his men busy setting up more experimental stations down there, with a view to improving the condition. Newfoundland has great possibilities. _ I know it can produce all the potatoes it needs, because I have studied the matter for years, and have compared imports with the amount required by the people. I know that in some years the total imports have amounted to no more than 50,000 bushels, which is only about 16,000 barrels; and I know that the total production of the country was nearly three quarters of a million barrels. Potatoes are a vital product, so far as the people of Newfoundland are concerned.
Finally, I wish to make reference to the fisheries in Newfoundland. As we all know, fishing is an important industry today in Canada. Through the acquisition of Newfoundland, Canada can now claim to be the greatest fishing country in the world. I know the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) has expressed great interest in the matter. I read an article recently in the Fundy Fisherman, taken from the Liberal Advocate. It was written by the minister, who makes reference to various aspects of the fisheries. This spring when I asked him if a date had been set for the killing of seals, he admitted that he should have known but said that he did not know. I suggest there are certain features in connection with the sealing industry he ought to look into. I am glad

to know that a date was agreed upon between the Norwegian interests and the interests in our country in regard to the date of killing seals. This is a very important factor in the sealing industry.
Last year the situation was disastrous because there had been no convention, with the result that the seals were killed when they were very young and had not reached a prime condition. Therefore although a ship might bring in 100,000 seals, or 40,000 seals, they would weigh only a few pounds each. On the other hand if they had waited several days, in the light of the fact that a seal increases its weight at the rate of two pounds a day, the seals would have been much heavier in weight and the results would have been more profitable to all concerned.
This year I spoke to the captain of the first arrival, The Arctic Sealer-Captain Hill- who is a very experienced sealing captain, and he asked me to draw the attention of the minister to the desirability of protection for certain kinds of seals. There is a seal which is a breeder seal, and which should not be killed. It should be protected for a certain number of years so that the future of the herds may also be protected. I believe it is the Bedlamer seal to which he was referring. Perhaps the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Bradley) would confirm what I say in this respect.
I suggest the Minister of Fisheries should give consideration to this point. In the article in the Fundy Fisherman the minister pointed out that the government was always giving consideration to the matter of protecting the fisheries. Through an error in the article- and I am sure it must be an error-there is a statement that these fisheries are inexhaustible. I think it should have said that these fisheries are not inexhaustible, and that therefore they must have protection, and that if they are not properly protected they will become exhausted. Certainly if they are not protected they will become seriously depleted, and the industry would suffer.
We know that salmon fishing is a very profitable industry in British Columbia. It is important also in Newfoundland. Fishermen catch salmon and sell it fresh. They also put it in tierces and sell it in a pickled condition. In addition to that, salmon fishing is a great attraction to the tourist. Many Americans come down there in the summer months and fish our rivers for salmon. I have been a rod and fly salmon fisherman for many years and I regret that our rivers are becoming very bad. During the last twenty-five or thirty years I have seen a tremendous difference in our rivers. Too much wood has been cut along the banks and when we have rain or snow there are not sufficient trees to hold
The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne back the moisture so that it can flow gradually into the river. The result is that the water runs off quickly and we have floods which wash away the spawning beds. And then quite often a drought will follow and the river becomes low and the fishing is no good. The salmon have trouble getting up and those that do get up die off.
I know that the minister is talking of facts when he speaks of the assistance which has been given in connection with the development of salmon hatcheries and the building of fish ladders and that sort of thing in British Columbia, but he has not done very much in that respect in Newfoundland. I must ask him that he do something about this because it is a pity that our salmon rivers are becoming depleted and are less attractive at a time when we were hoping to profit so much from them.
I am glad to note that we are getting more plants in Newfoundland to preserve codfish in the fresh state and that our United States markets still continue to be profitable. That market is capable of further exploitation. A good deal of fish is sent to different parts of Canada. I am glad to note that at Fermeuse in my own constituency a new plant will go into operation within three or four weeks. The manager of that plant has written to me complaining that he must send forty or fifty miles to get a customs officer in order to enter and clear vessels as that port is not yet a port of entry. I am sure the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will give consideration to a reasonable request that a customs post be established in that settlement.
In order that the earnings of the fisherman may be constant he needs a constant supply of bait. Nothing is more important to our fisheries than the provision of bait depots. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) seems to be a rather timid person and not as generous in supplying bait depots as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) in the building of breakwaters and wharves. I am very glad to note that in the constituency of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert two large breakwaters are to be constructed, one at Chance Harbour and one at Lorneville in the constituency. I noted an article in the Fundy Fisherman referring to a meeting attended by the hon. member at which they passed a vote of thanks for his attendance. I think he deserved it for getting two breakwaters, one costing $200,000 and the other costing $280,000.
I am sure that both those places are important and that the breakwaters will be most useful, but that total of nearly half a million dollars would construct about eight bait depots. When I write to the Minister of
1902	HOUSE OF
The Budget

Mr. W. J. Browne Fisheries about bait depots he always replies that there is not as much fish caught this year as was caught last year and that there was not as much caught last year as was caught the year before, and so on. He comes back with figures and I must admit that perhaps he is right. There was not as much fish caught this year and there will not be as much caught next year because the people are leaving these settlements. They cannot catch fish unless there is a regular supply of bait.
There is a method of catching codfish known as trawling. This consists of a long line with hooks placed every five or ten feet, the hooks themselves being suspended on lines about four feet long. A trawl might be half a mile long or a long line may be four, five or ten miles long. As every hook is baited you can imagine the amount of bait necessary to bait all the hooks on a line ten miles long when you have a hook every four or five feet. They must have a regular supply of bait. It is most important that the fishermen of Newfoundland should have more bait depots, or if that cannot be done there should be holding depots, places where a supply of bait is readily available to them to prosecute their fishing.
Although the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) has many arduous duties to perform he has riot lost interest in the fishermen. Recently he made a broadcast which brought forth a blast of withering scorn from the minister of fisheries of Newfoundland. I do not propose to intervene in this interesting argument between the Secretary of State and the provincial minister of fisheries, but the Evening Telegram of recent date took up the cudgels on behalf of the Secretary of State.
In an editorial they quoted with approval what appeared to me to be extracts from that radio address by the minister. I am not sure how far I can go quoting these, but reference is made to profits of around $10,000. I was interested in finding out the results of the experiments advocated by the Secretary of State and on March 19 I asked certain questions in this connection which were answered by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacNaught). The Northern Construction Company employs 2,000 Canadian workmen, and seven United States citizens. These seven United States citizens consist of one project manager, three superintendents, one tunnel walker, and two civil engineers.
The Mannix Company Limited have ten United States citizens and 1,130 Canadian employees. Of the ten United States citizens there are one project manager, two superintendents, one assistant superintendent, three foremen, two construction machine operators, and one general office manager.
The Morrison Knudsen Company have 3,100 Canadian employees and 99 American personnel. Then there follows a long list of this personnel.
In general the policy is to admit skilled foremen, and the like, who are permanent employees of these construction companies. I am informed by the companies that they have some difficulty inducing these people to come to Canada to supervise the work because they say that wages are higher in the United States than they can obtain in Canada. Nevertheless we do grant temporary entry to those who, it would appear, could be used to advantage in construction work and thus give employment to Canadians engaged in that work. The personnel representatives of the companies have been in touch with this department and with the Department of

subtopic: PAYMENT TO ESTATES OF FULL AMOUNT OF POLICY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lapointe for the second reading of Bill No. 183, to amend the Veterans Insurance Act.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO ESTATES OF FULL AMOUNT OF POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at eleven o'clock last night I had intimated that I had a few words to say on this bill to amend the Veterans Insurance Act. The bill is a short one, and it is not my intention to delay the house very long in discussing it. As I understand it, this amendment was made necessary by an oversight last year when the bill was being considered by the veterans affairs committee and the house.
I feel that, generally speaking, the Veterans Insurance Act is a good act, and I believe that is the feeling of most veterans and members of this house. It was discussed thoroughly last year in the veterans affairs committee. But there is one section of the act which is considered by many veterans to be unfair and as incorporating a wrong principle so far as veterans insurance is concerned. I refer to section 10. When the committee met last year, Mr. T. D. Anderson, general secretary of the Canadian Legion, brought this matter to the attention of the committee. This section as it now stands reads:
Subject to subsections two, three and four of this section, where on the death of the insured a pension becomes payable under the Pension Act or any pension law of the United Kingdom or any of His Majesty's dominions, to any person mentioned in

subsections one or two of section six or in subsection one of section seven of this act, there shall be deducted from the amount of insurance the aggregate present value of the pension or pensions so payable computed on such basis as the governor in council may prescribe.
Under that section, when a person who has been insured dies and his widow or beneficiary is entitled to a pension, a deduction is made from the amount of insurance paid. It was felt by members of the committee last year, by the Canadian Legion and other veterans bodies that this was an unfair principle and that some change should be made.
It is suggested that the cost of insurance under the Veterans Insurance Act is comparable to the cost of insurance sold by private companies, and no such company makes a deduction such as is provided for here. It is felt that these deductions should not be made.
There are certain classes of persons who are not insurable under the Veterans Insurance Act. In some ways this act is more strict than contracts with private insurance companies. I think it is only fair that when an insured person dies his widow or dependent should be able to expect that the full amount of insurance will be paid.
This constitutes a great weakness in the Veterans Insurance Act. It is most unfair to make these deductions. When the Veterans Insurance Act was being amended at this session I had hoped that consideration would be given to deleting this particular section. The recommendation made by the Canadian Legion to the committee last year was not considered because it was ruled that the terms of reference were not wide enough. That recommendation was as follows:
The Legion would accordingly recommend that section ten either be deleted or so amended as to provide that no reduction in the amount of insurance payable under the act be made because of any pension paid under the Pension Act or other legislation referred to in section ten.
As I say, that recommendation was not dealt with by the committee last year, and I had hoped that it would be dealt with this year.

speechtext:
Before the minister replies, may I say that it is not in order to discuss an act generally when it is before the house for amendment. Only the principle of the amendment should be discussed. I did not interrupt the hon. member, but as there are other similar bills coming up later this day I thought I should bring the rule to the attention of the house.
If the minister speaks now, he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: PAYMENT TO ESTATES OF FULL AMOUNT OF POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the remarks made 'by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). I am aware of course that this matter has been studied previously. I believe that to get a true picture of veterans insurance one must go back to the legislation dealing with world war I veterans, the Returned Soldiers Insurance Act. It will be found that section 10 of that act has the effect of providing that if a pension under the Pension Act is awarded on the insured's death, the proceeds of the policy will not be paid as insurance but will be limited to the return of the premiums with compound interest. Of course there is the $500 exemption, of which hon. members are aware.
This section was included in the Returned Soldiers Insurance Act because of the very low medical standards required under the act, and to provide against the payment of insurance in the event of early claims together with the payment of a pension for the same beneficiary. I also understand that the original intention of that act was to provide insurance for returned soldiers who could not be insured elsewhere and whose widows might not be pensionable in the event of the death of their husbands. Under those circumstances it was reasonable to include such a safeguard.
When the Veterans Insurance Act was considered in 1944, somewhat the same principle was applied, for the same reason. The medical standards set by schedule B of the Veterans Insurance Act were such that very few applications were declined. In fact I am informed that since the enactment of the legislation not more than sixty applications have been declined. However, the amount payable under the Veterans Insurance Act is calculated in a different way. Generally speaking there is again the $500 exemption, but on the balance of the insurance the amount paid is the reduced paid-up insurance value available at the date of death. What that actually means is that the amount payable is in proportion to the part of the premium term that has elapsed. In other words, every policy that is fully paid up is paid in full; but let us take the case of a 20-payment life policy that has not been paid up in full; if the policyholder dies after twelve years, the amount payable would be approximately the $500 which is exempt, plus twelve-twentieths of the balance of the policy.
I can quite understand that this matter is of great interest to all those concerned with the welfare of veterans, and if the committee should see fit to do so I would certainly have
Pension Act
no objection to its calling before it the actuaries of the department, who are familiar with the actual workings of this insurance scheme, in order that they may secure from them all information respecting the actual basis on which this insurance plan works.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OP CLOTHING ALLOWANCE IN CERTAIN AMPUTATION CASES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is one point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The bill is really like all Gaul; it is divided into three parts. The purpose of the first is to make more adequate provision with respect to the allowance for excessive wear and tear of a pensioner's clothing when he wears a prosthesis. The purpose of the second part is to make more adequate provision when there are two dependent parents of a deceased veteran, and the third part is to provide what are described in the explanatory note as a few administrative changes.
We heartily agree with the proposed changes to benefit those veterans who have had amputations, and also with the increase in the benefits for dependent parents. There

Pension Act
will of course be an opportunity in the committee to consider the adequacy or inadequacy of these increases.
The administrative changes are contained in sections 3 and 4 of the bill. The purpose of section 4 is merely to correct an error in the present Pension Act, but it seems to me that the other so-called administrative change is a pretty drastic one. I suggest to the minister that he should have his officials give it further consideration. This change takes away the right of a veteran or a veteran's dependents to sue the crown where a pension is either paid or may be paid under the Pension Act. The explanation given for taking away that right of action reads as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to ensure that an applicant whose claim is based on accidental injury or death due to negligence of a servant of the crown, shall not be placed in any better position than an applicant whose claim is based on disability or death due to enemy action.
On the face of it that looks like a reasonable explanation. I presume the difficulty has arisen because it has now been made so much easier to sue the crown, and also because there are many more men and women in uniform now than at any other time when Canada has been at peace. However, I would point out the comparison with a veteran who is disabled in war is hardly a fair one. I think a better comparison would be with the widow of a civilian who is killed.
Take for example an automobile accident on the Pembroke road in which a truck belonging to a crown company, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, which, as the minister knows, operates the atomic energy plant at Chalk River, collides with an army truck and a veteran is killed. This section will deprive that veteran's family of the right to take legal action following his death, because the widow and children would be pensionable under the Pension Act. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is practically certain to have insurance on its trucks. If it does not have such insurance I would say there is gross negligence. But whether or not it has insurance, surely the widow of that veteran should have the right to sue the crown company if she so wishes and recover damages, which might run to $25,000 or $50,000, depending upon the number and age of the children, the income of her husband, and so on.
I cannot see why that right should be taken away. I grant that if the widow does sue a crown company and gets a judgment which would amount to more than the pension commission would pay, certainly no pension should be paid by the government. There is similar protection now in the Pension Act.

I think sections 18, 18(a) and 18(b) contain the provisions applying to similar cases. But I am afraid it is going much too far simply to put a section in the Pension Act which entirely takes away the right of the veteran or his widow and children to claim damages, merely because they might have a pension or might be able to qualify for a pension. In any event I would ask the minister to have his department give this section very careful scrutiny. I can see no reason why that right should be taken away as is provided by this section.

He said: Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned the other day when introducing the resolution, the bill which hon. members now have in hand is a complete revision and consolidation of the existing legislation with the changes which are being brought forward by the government this year. Naturally the most important amendments are the increases in rates and the introduction of a new procedure in determining the basis on which veterans allowances will be paid.
The other day I explained briefly that it was proposed that recipients of war veterans allowance would be permitted to take what might be termed casual or seasonal employment without having the income derived from such employment taken into consideration in the computation of the amount the recipient is to receive under the War Veterans Allowance Act. In other words, the allowance will be paid on a monthly basis rather than a yearly basis.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that one section of the bill, namely section 3, sets out those who may qualify as recipients of war veterans allowances. It is mentioned that, subject to the general clauses of the act, any veteran who has attained the age of 65 may qualify. When the bill was drafted it was felt that all veterans who applied for war veterans allowance at the age of 60 would be dealt with under the new section 4 which introduces the new principle I just mentioned. I understand, however, after discussing it informally with the various groups, that this might be interpreted as raising the age at which a veteran may qualify for war veterans allowance. Since it is not intended by this legislation either to take away or to restrict any of the privileges of veterans but rather to make this legislation a more flexible instrument for the veterans welfare, I have no objection to the 65 which appears in the bill being changed to 60.
As I stated, my understanding of the operations of the act would lead me to believe that a veteran of 60 would benefit under this bill as it stands, but if there is likely to be any misinterpretation I have no objection to a


change. I would ask the chairman of the committee to entertain any amendment, when the bill is before the committee, which would recommend that the words "60 years" be substituted for the words "65 years" appearing in the bill. That is all I wish to say at the moment.

As a matter of fact, I felt myself that 65 was a mistake.
As the minister said, this is a complete revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act. As far as that is concerned I think we are all in agreement with the revision and the consolidation. It is quite a difficult matter to have to go through a number of acts to find what you require. If we have all the different amendments in one consolidation, then I say it is all to the good.
As the minister has intimated, there are more changes, and I shall discuss them later. For a few minutes I should like to go over the background, Mr. Speaker, if I may, of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Now that we have a new consolidation I do not think it is out of place that I should do so.
In the last few months all hon. members have had a splendid opportunity of acquainting themselves with the background of the War Veterans Allowance Act, as it has been published in the Legionary, the official magazine of the Canadian Legion. In three past issues they have given us a very clear picture of the War Veterans Allowance Act, and the different steps which led up to the legislation which we have at the present time.
It is very interesting to note that it was in 1930 that the first act was passed. It is also interesting to note that the basic principles, as we understand them at that time, are practically the same as the basic principles of the War Veterans Allowance Act today; that is, that men were prematurely aged and were more or less unemployable. Medical authorities stated that a man who had served in France, with all the suffering, privation, and so on, may be said to have his life expectancy lessened by from five, six, seven to ten years. I was interested to read the basic reasons, from the medical standpoint, as given by Dr. White of the city of Saint John in 1928 when the provincial command of the Canadian Legion met in that city. I may say that Dr. White was the mayor of the city of

Saint John at the time, and also one of the leading surgeons and physicians in Canada. He also had considerable experience in the veterans hospital at Saint John. Dr. White stated at that time regarding this subject:
The war and Its effects, the stress and the strain, the privations, the wants and the diseases and all that he may have suffered while he was away have lessened his efficiency, have drained his vitality which came about in three, four, five, six, yes, perhaps, ten years, and we find that a man-a robust man-with all his ambitions before him which have been largely set aside on account of his patriotism, unable now to carry on as he would have been had he remained at home. He begins to feel the infirmity of advancing years much sooner than he otherwise would have done or much sooner than in the case of other men, and yet he has no way in which officially he may receive treatment when he presents himself at one of the hospitals in the country, nor has he any remuneration whatever or any official protection. What is going to be done with the man whose life is threatened, whose health is injured, whose efficiency as a breadwinner is impaired and yet who has not upon his discharge papers a single bit of evidence that will entitle him to treatment in the hospitals, to say nothing of pay and allowances?
As I say, that statement was made by Dr. White to the command of the Legion in Saint John at that time. The War Veterans Allowance Act has been the answer to that statement.
There are men whom I should like to mention this afternoon-I cannot mention them all-who have been greatly responsible for the present act. The first man I would mention is the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who attended this meeting in Saint John at that time, and who on that occasion said that he agreed with Dr. White, and that his committee and he himself were trying to work out a scheme. There are other men whose names I am sure come to all veterans: Sir Arthur Currie, Brigadier Ross, General LaFleche, General Price, Alex Walker, Brigadier Foster, the present president of the Canadian Legion. These men have all striven, and I think the act we have today is the result of the hard work of these men and many others.
I might also say, Mr. Speaker, that I know the War Veterans Allowance Act has been a godsend to many of our returned men, who would have been in a distressing position in this country today if we did not have it. Not only were these men aged prematurely, but they had another claim. Those of us who were in the first war and those who were in the second war know that the rate of pay the men received was very low. The man who spent five or six years in the army at $1.10 a day and came back found that the man who had stayed at home had received very high wages and had been able to establish himself in a far different position economically from the man who had served
War Veterans Allowance Act overseas. Therefore on two counts, both physically and economically, the man who had served overseas was in a very different position from the civilian.
The amendments in the new bill provide for certain increases. A single man has been receiving $40 a month under the present act. This is to be increased to $50. A married couple have been receiving $70. This is to be increased to $90 a month. The question which naturally arises in the mind of every veteran is: Is this enough; considering the cost of living as it is today, considering the situation as it exists today, is this increase sufficient? The Legion have made a very careful study of the war veterans allowance situation in Canada, and as a result of that study they set out in the Legionary of April of this year the situation regarding the recipients of war veterans allowances.
I am not going to take the time of the house this afternoon to quote the different exhibits of the Canadian Legion. The first one they have is veteran A. Here is a veteran who served in the first war, in the battle of Amiens and Cambrai. He was gassed during the battle of Canal du Nord. However, after he came back he was able to carry on until he was 64 years of age, and when he became unable to work he was receiving $160 a month. He was placed on war veterans allowance, the only income that he had. His wife was ill. His income for the month of February, as stated in the Legionary, was $56.46. I may say that he had received unemployment insurance, had been overpaid, and that amount paid was particularly small, owing to the fact that some unemployment insurance payments were being deducted. The monthly expenditures for this man and his wife were $95.76. This amount did not include clothing. In this case the Legion pointed out, very properly and conclusively, that the amount these people were receiving at that time was not sufficient. Even the amount of $90 a month now suggested would not have met the expenditures in this case, leaving aside those amounts spent for clothing.
Then, they referred to veteran B, a man 66 years of age who received $180 a month while employed. He became unemployable, with no means other than his war veterans allowance of $40.41 a month. Out of his total income he paid $373 for food, and $6 a week for room, amounting to $312 a year. At the end of the year this man found that, to live, he had to borrow money.
This is just one more case indicating the impossibility of those who are unemployable living on the amount of war veterans allowance formerly paid, or on the amount proposed in the new legislation.

War Veterans Allowance Act I could go on and give other examples mentioned in the information I have before me, but I feel it is not necessary to do so. All these cases were given careful study by the Legion, and they came to the conclusion that if these people were to be permitted even to exist, a certain amount would have to be paid to them. After making careful analyses and investigations'the recommendations of the Legion were as follows:
1.	That the basic principles upon which war veterans allowance is allowed and paid be unchanged.
I think that principle is being retained.
2.	That war veterans allowance be increased from $40 single and $70 married to $60 single and $120 married.
I would point out that these amounts were set after very careful consideration and study of the cases I have mentioned. There is no member of the house who could not multiply the cases I have mentioned, or who could not describe such cases by the hundreds all across this country. I believe all hon. members will agree that not only the Legion but the National Council of Veterans and other veterans organizations have never been exorbitant in their demands upon the government. They have always kept in mind, first, the requirements of the veterans and, second, the burden upon the taxpayers. If I might make a comparison, they have never tried to obtain large sums of money from the government or from the people as have the legionnaires in the United States. I suggest therefore that the Legion's recommendation of $60 a month for a single person and $120 for married is not unreasonable. I am surprised that at this time, when the act is being consolidated, the government is recommending the payment of $50 to a single veteran and $90 to one who is married.
To continue with the recommendations of the Legion:
3.	That the total ceiling be raised to $1,200 single and $2,000 married.
What do we find in the new legislation? We see that the ceiling is to be $720 for a single man and $1,200 for one who is married, allowing a spread of only $120. Under the old act it was $125 for a single man, and $250 if married. In the present instance, however, we have a spread of only $120 in each case. I am sure this is not going to be satisfactory to the Legion, and I feel certain it will be equally unsatisfactory to the members of the veterans affairs committee. Then, to continue:
4.	That Canadians who served in England only in the first war be entitled to war veterans allowance.


I do not like repetition. I mentioned this matter the other day, and it has been discussed in the house on many occasions. It has been debated in the veterans committee. I have always felt that England should be included as a theatre of war, so far as the payment of war veterans allowance is concerned, and that these men should come under the act. It is not necessary at this time to repeat the reasons. We know there was considerable hardship and suffering on the part of men in the first contingent who went overseas. I see the minister smiling, but I suggest there can be no question that there was suffering, because the men who were stationed in the south of England for purposes of training were exposed to serious hardships. They were away from their families and receiving $1.10 a day while the people at home were receiving high pay, and had the opportunity to re-establish themselves during a time of war. However, those men in England did not have that opportunity.
There are many other reasons I could give. There can be no doubt that the Legion is making a fair request when it asks that Canadians who served in England during the first war should be entitled to war veterans allowance. To continue with the recommendations:
5.	That widows of imperial or allied services with twenty years residence in Canada be entitled to war veterans allowance regardless of the date of death of their husbands.
I have no doubt other hon. members will make reference to this suggestion. The argument has been before the committee on many occasions.
6.	That home exemption be raised to $9,000.
I see that in the act it is raised to $6,000, and I shall reserve my comment as to whether $6,000 is a satisfactory amount. That, however, is one of the minor provisions in the bill.
I am sure the measure before us will not be considered satisfactory by the committee now set up, and that it will not be favourably received by members of the House of Commons. More particularly I am sure that it will not be satisfactory to the Canadian veterans across the country. This legislation reminds me of that which was brought before the committee in 1948. The government suggested at that time an increase of ten per cent in the pension, and it will be recalled that that percentage was scorned by members of the committee, with the result that it was increased to twenty-five per cent. I believe that when the veterans committee

now set up considers the matter it will conclude that the government has not suggested the proper amount.

As I was saying when the minister interjected, as to war veterans who are 60 years of age and who have passed the medical test and are totally unemployable in the regular labour market, if the ceiling on permissible income was removed and these men were permitted to go out and earn something during four, five or six months of the year if they could find suitable employment, I think you would find many of them taking employment if they knew that their assured income of $25, $30, $40 or $50 a month was not going to be interfered with. They would thus not only increase their own standards but would contribute to the pool of wealth of the country at the same time. I know that war veterans are much concerned about that point.
The minister has already stated that we can amend the section raising the age to 65.
I would also suggest that the provision for permissible income, which has been cut down from $250 for a married man and $120 for a single man, should be restored. That is another amendment that should be made. I am never very much concerned about the amount of money. There are other things that are just as important.
I think the minister's advisers made a mistake. I am sure it was not the fault of the minister. I know he is subject to the treasury board and a whole lot of red tape, that he cannot just say, "I am going to do this." He has his own troubles, and I appreciate that. But I believe he should have included in this bill at this time a provision that would enable payment of this allowance to be made to the widows of imperial war veterans, many of whom were just on the borderline. Their husbands died without having resided in Canada for the full twenty years. They were perhaps a year short, or six months, or maybe two years. But the fact of the matter is that it is not the dead man who is looking for something; he is well taken care of. It is the widow who still has to eat and wear clothes and maintain some kind of shelter. She has met the residence requirements, and I believe the act should have been amended to enable many widows of imperial veterans, who up to now have been ruled out, to receive this allowance.
A second point of discrimination that I think the minister should have given consideration to is the matter of veterans who


served in England during the first war. Previous to the second war the veterans took that situation for granted, and there was not very much agitation about it. I grant that during the second war there was bombing and all that sort of thing; but when the second world war veteran, who spent most of his time in England waiting to get into the war, was qualified for the allowance, it naturally caused resentment among the older veterans who had spent their time in England. It was not their fault. They were kept there, assigned to duty there, and they feel they should be entitled to the allowance as well. I believe wiping out those two points of discrimination and injustice, concerning the widows of imperial veterans and men who served in England during the first war, are just as important as stepping up the allowance. Hundreds of veterans and widows are suffering under that injustice.
I said I was going to be brief, Mr. Speaker, and I am. I feel very strongly about these things, but I am a member of the committee and I am going to reserve any further remarks until we call in the Canadian Legion and hear their representations. I am sure if the minister is as flexible in regard to the rest of the act as he is on the section which provides for a step-up in age, this legislation is going to come back with a lot of amendments. So I will reserve any further remarks until such time as the committee has dealt with the bill, when I hope we will bring it back pretty badly emasculated as compared to its present form.
