speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a good piece of social legislation, for the obvious reason that only three elements are required for the grant of an allowance. If I am wrong about it, I hope the minister will correct me. The first is service. The records of all veterans are kept in the department, and it is easy for those

concerned to decide whether or not an applicant is qualified from the point of view of service. Then there are two other elements, and I am referring to the latter part of clause 3, not speaking of age. Those elements are disability and need, and there shall be no relation between the disability and the service, which makes the difference between this legislation and the Pension Act.
In virtue of this legislation, if a veteran who qualifies as such under paragraph (k) of section 2 is ill and unable to earn his living, he is entitled to the allowance by right; and the legislation does not make the grant of the allowance humiliating for him. This is the way I see this legislation, and naturally the only thing to do is express one's appreciation to the minister who sponsors the bill and to the government, for correcting certain difficult cases in order to make life happier for veterans who were unable to secure high enough pensions, and who were in hardship. I hope the members of the committee will take these remarks into consideration when the bill is before them and will hasten their report to the house, so those who will come under this bill may secure some benefit from it at the earliest possible opportunity.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Temiscouata-I should say my good friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot)-has just said the War Veterans Allowance Act is social legislation. In that he is wrong, because in reality it is a partial payment for gallant services rendered. The vast majority of the recipients of war veterans allowance were front-line troops, Canada's fighting men. In their civilian life they have shown the same courage and the same sense of responsibility they showed on the battlefield; and they have great pride in their service. They do not consider that in getting the war veterans allowance they are accepting any handout. They believe they have more than earned that allowance, and they are correct.
This act was passed in the first place on the basis that because of their front-line service these men were pre-aged to the extent of ten years. That was why the qualification age was made 60 instead of the age of 70 which was set for the old age pension. These men are veterans who have been badly handicapped in civilian life because of their war service, and they have been in great need. Unfortunately when we were doing justice to the war disability pensioners of Canada last year we were unable to help the recipients of war veterans allowance. Many of us regretted that fact and, as Your Honour
War Veterans Allowance Act knows, expressed our opinions on the floor of the house on more than one occasion. However, be that as it may, we now have before us a complete revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Because that is the case we must be certain that the new act is expressed in terms which are fair to these veterans.
There are several provisions in the bill which bother me a great deal, and today I propose to deal with five of them. The first one is the point the minister mentioned when he opened the debate. I was very glad to hear him give an assurance that the committee would be requested to put the main age qualification back from 65 to 60. The raising of that qualification from 60 to 65 was a very unwise move, and I am surprised that the bill, as presented to this house, brought about a change of that kind. The terms of the bill as we now have it do, of course, provide an exception in the case of a veteran who is employable; the age at which he can qualify is now set at 60.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The majority of the war veterans allowance recipients have always qualified on the basis of having reached 60 years of age. There is, of course, a provision in the act for veterans under that age to qualify, but only if they are permanently unemployable. I believe that only a very small number have come under that latter provision. This idea that the veterans have, by their service, been pre-aged to the extent of ten years is basic. It was behind the original act and the raising of that age to 65 would have wiped out any idea of preaging. I say that because civilians are now qualified for old age assistance at age 65. As a matter of fact, to be consistent with the provisions covering old age assistance for civilians from 65 to 69 and old age security paid civilians over 69, this War Veterans Allowance Act should have been changed to reduce the age from 60 to 55 and to make the payments automatic at 60. I am not advocating that today, but I say that to be consistent that is what should have been done rather than to shove the main qualification age up to 65.
The second point about which I am
bothered is this exception which is contained

War Veterans Allowance Act in section 4 of the bill. Let us see how it reads. The sidenote reads "employable veterans", and the headnote above section 4 reads "allowances to employable veterans." Subsection 1 of this section reads:
Subject to this act, an allowance is payable to a veteran who resides in Canada, has attained the age of 60 years, is unable to maintain himself by following his former ordinary occupation but is capable of taking light or intermittent employment and is unemployed.
It would seem that this would put some at least of the recipients of war veterans allowance on a monthly payment basis. I would point out that this section has several effects. In the first place, it introduces entirely new phraseology which is quite different from that in the present War Veterans Allowance Act. Of course, that means there will be difficulty of interpretation. I refer for example to the words, "by following his former ordinary occupation." As hon. members know, that is something entirely new. Another new phrase is "capable of taking light or intermittent employment." I think those phrases will bring a good deal of difficulty into the administration of the act.
Further, this new provision will mean more and bigger investigations. They will have to take place more frequently because the payments will be on a monthly basis. It will mean more snooping by departmental investigators which has been one of the objectionable features of the act right through the years. It will mean also more means testing and a larger staff. Again, the provision is not applicable to widows.
I have no doubt that the intent behind this proposed change was good. I think the minister and his officials are trying to help the veteran, but I suggest that a better way to meet the situation would be to exempt earnings-and I mean earnings as distinct from other income. I would refer the minister and other members to section 6 of this bill. Under the heading of "exempt income" we find listed the various types of income which are not to be taken as income for the purposes of the act. One of those types, contained in paragraph (d), is "any casual earnings of the recipient." Now, I suggest that paragraph should be changed to read "all earnings" instead of "casual earnings". The effect would be to remove from consideration any money that the veteran was able to earn once he had qualified for war veterans allowance. That is what I should like to see, but if the minister will not go that far, he might change the words "casual earnings" to "earnings from light employment", which would give a much broader coverage.

If this suggestion is adopted then once the veteran had qualified for the allowance all his earnings would be exempt. And that would be a tremendous help to the veterans. It would be a great incentive to them to keep active, to try to carry on in some sort of occupation; it would have very little or no effect on the employment situation in Canada, and, Mr. Speaker, it would be directly in line with the principle of our old age security legislation. Those payments are made automatically, and the recipient is encouraged to go out and get some kind of job. If the civilian of 70 is to be encouraged to go out and earn what he wishes, then I submit that the veteran should be encouraged to do the same thing at 60, and that an amendment should be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act to bring about that result.
The third point in this legislation which bothers me is the amount of the increase. I believe it is insufficient. Some earlier speakers in the debate have referred to the amounts, but I should like to point out once more that the single veteran is being raised only $9.95 a month, from $40.41 to $50.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: It is $9.59.

speechtext:
Yes; I have that in my note, but I read the wrong figure. Taken on a yearly basis, he is being raised from $485 a year to $600, which is an increase of $115. The married veteran will be raised from $70.83 a month to $90 a month, which is $19.17; on a yearly basis that means a raise from $850 to $1,080, an increase of $230.
I believe that $50 a month per person is the minimum for a mere existence in Canada today. I do not believe there is one member of this house who would contradict that statement; and yet these men will not be getting that under the amendment. Certainly a man and his wife will not be getting that. It has been recognized in at least some of the provinces that $50 a month per person is a very minimum, because in my own province of British Columbia, and in Alberta and perhaps some other provinces, old age assistance payments and old age security payments have been increased by the provincial government in question by the payment of an additional $10 a month. We should not ask the veteran to switch over to old age assistance or to old age security. We should not ask that, because he is the responsibility of the federal government of Canada and he should be paid, and paid an adequate amount, by the federal government of Canada. Yet if this bill goes through in its present form the married war veterans allowance recipient in British Columbia and in Alberta will be wiser to switch over to the civilian form of assistance.

The fourth point about which I am concerned is the amount of permissive income over the allowance. It has been reduced by this legislation to $120; whether the veteran is single or married, his permissive income over the amount of the allowance is only $120. For many years, I believe from the start of the act in 1930, although I may be wrong in that, certainly for many years, there has been set out in the War Veterans Allowance Act permissive income for the single veteran of $125 a year, and for the married veteran $250. Under the Old Age Assistance Act, passed by this house last year, there is a permissive income of $240 a year. That applies both to the single man and the man who is married; and certainly there should be just as wide a coverage for the veteran.
This question of permissive income is very important for quite a large group of veterans. Clearly those who are also in receipt of a small pension are caught when the permissive income is too low. Hon. members need only be reminded that last year, when we raised the pension, those men who were in receipt of a small pension and who also had their war veterans allowance had that allowance cut by the same amount that the pension was raised, so they derived no benefit whatever from the legislation of last year.
The final point about this bill which gives me great concern is the failure to incorporate in the act, or to place in some other statutory form, provision for what is called war veterans allowance assistance. For three years, I think, there has been an annual vote called the war veterans allowance assistance fund. From that fund payments could be made to a recipient of war veterans allowance who had no other income whatever. He could get a maximum of $10 a month if single or $15 a month if married; but that payment is subject to a second means test, and it is not made necessarily in the form of money. It may be by supplying clothing or furniture; it is just general assistance. At the time that that policy was introduced, some of us complained that it should be in the form of a statute rather than subject to an annual vote which meant that it could be changed each year. I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) will remember that at that time he intimated he wanted to try out the new plan first, but agreed that before long it should be covered in some kind of statute.
Now that we are revising the War Veterans Allowance Act I believe that we should include in it provision for this war veterans allowance assistance fund. Last year the Legion asked that those recipients of war veterans allowance who were unemployable should get $60 a month single and $120 a month if married. I believe that their
War Veterans Allowance Act requests were within reason. The minister told us the other day when the resolution preceding this bill was being debated that he did not intend to make the allowance fund statutory, but rather intended to continue it as an annual vote. I hope that he will give further consideration to that question.
There are several other points which could be raised and which are equally important, such as the inadequacy of the provision for the widows of imperial veterans, and some of the procedure followed in making claims for repayment under the act. However, I shall have a chance to discuss those points in committee. I did wish to place these other points before the minister and the house before the bill is sent to committee.
In conclusion may I repeat a word or two about these veterans. They are splendid citizens; citizens to whom Canada owes a debt which can never be repaid in full, no matter what terms we write into the War Veterans Allowance Act.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that this bill as a whole is to the advantage of the veterans, and we are pleased to see it before the house. However the sore spot in the whole War Veterans Allowance Act is that the means test remains in it. It seems strange that, although the total earnings of recipients are increased, the extra earnings a veteran may get are reduced to the extent of $5 a year. If the government does not see fit to take the means test off, as most of us would like to see, then I cannot see why it did not increase the maximum earning allowance of veterans.
As it is, the veteran is put on the spot. It looks to me very much as though he is being encouraged to take the old age pension and to forget about the war veterans allowance. Outside of that, the point that I thought was so detrimental was that of raising the age limit from 60 to 65. I am glad to hear that the minister is going to consider an amendment to reduce the age to 60, because the age 65 violates the presumption upon which the age limit was established, and that is that veterans pre-aged by ten years as a result of military service. With the old age pension coming on at 70, and with the group from 65 to 69 included under an old age security scheme, it would appear that the veterans were not being pre-aged at all.
However, I am glad the minister is considering making the reduction to 60 years when the matter is discussed in committee. I am pleased to see that the allowance for a single man is increased to $50, which brings it up to the same amount as the old age pension in Alberta. However we do regret

War Veterans Allowance Act that the married allowance is only $90, which in our province gives them $10 less than that received by the old age pensioners.
On many occasions the Legion has suggested $60 for those who are physically handicapped and cannot take any advantage of casual earnings. They should be given at least a pension equivalent to the total earning power of a veteran under the War Veterans Allowance Act. We would like to have seen a much greater increase, brought somewhere in line with the cost of living index. However, those things may come in time-at least we hope they will.
I shall have more to say on these points in committee. I believe section 4 of the bill has some merit, in that it enables the veteran to work for a short period of time without having his allowance cut. However, it looks to me as though this is a sort of top-heavy arrangement, and that it will require a good deal of administration. It may be difficult to keep up with these veterans who are working at odd times. We will need to have a good many inspectors running around to find out whether or not the men are working.
The whole thing would be much simpler if the minister would say, "We will wipe out the means test, and put the war veterans allowance recipient on an equal footing with the old age pensioner over 70 years of age."
I was glad to see an increase in the exemption on homes and premises from $4,000 to $6,000. To my mind that is still pretty low, because today a $6,000 home does not amount to much. Even a modest home is valued at much more than that.
Then, the measure does not take into consideration the widows of imperial veterans whose husbands died before they had their 20-year residence qualification. As I have said before, it seems a pity that these widows are being penalized just because their husbands died. That does not make sense.
No recognition has been given to those world war veterans who served only in England. Many of those men put up with hardships, sickness, cold and misery, and the only reason they were not sent to France was that they were needed in England. Many of them served as instructors, and the like.
I know of one imperial veteran who served in England during world war I, and whose health was impaired as a result of that service. That man gets the grand pension of something like $8 a month. He is almost 70 years of age now, and for several years has been living on that $8, and a railway pension of $25. He could not qualify for a war veterans allowance, even though his health was impaired to the point where he was given a pension for it.


I do not intend to say more at the moment, but I shall have more to say in committee, and perhaps when the bill returns to the house.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what caused the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) to become so excited this afternoon, because, in my parliamentary experience, it has always been the custom for several members of each party to express their views on second reading of any bill concerning veterans affairs.
As a member of the committee on veterans affairs I do not propose to repeat any of the arguments expressed this afternoon. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) expressed my views, and I have nothing further to say at this time.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to the house I have had the opportunity of serving on various committees on veterans affairs, and naturally I have interested myself in the welfare of the returned man.
This year I am not on the committee. I should like to address a few remarks and perhaps offer a few suggestions to the committee, in the hope that they will give cognizance to what I have to say. The minister has intimated that he is prepared to entertain amendments and in fact has suggested one himself.
I should like to stress the importance of striving for simplicity when amending this War Veterans Allowance Act. We are dealing with many ageing men who do not react as quickly as younger men to complicated arrangements and administrative procedures. Anything which can be done to make this act simpler would be of great advantage in enabling these ageing veterans to understand it more easily.
That brings me to section 4 of the bill which introduces the new principle of seasonable employment. It seems to me that this is a most complicated clause; it is another "if and when" the individual will be permitted to draw an allowance. I am not clear from what has been said whether the veterans will receive the other benefits under the act, such as hospitalization, when he is actually in employment. The benefits of hospitalization are one of the outstanding reasons why many men who might otherwise go on old age pensions prefer to remain under war veterans allowances.
At the present time we have in British Columbia a form of hospital insurance which is compulsory. If a veteran is not on war

veterans allowance he must pay the provincial hospital insurance. That is why I stress this point. I want to know whether the veteran will still be protected for full hospitalization when he is in seasonable employment and will not have to pay the provincial hospital insurance during that time.

speechtext:
When I refer to the need for simplicity I cannot help feeling that the same result could have been achieved if the ceiling on permissible earnings had been at least doubled. I believe that would take care of men who get seasonable employment and also the large number of marginal cases who are just able to earn enough, perhaps by some form of permanent employment for a day, a week or something of that sort, or who are drawing small incomes or pensions which now prevent them from obtaining war veterans allowances because their outside income is more than the very strict means test now applied to these allowances. I suggest that it would have been simpler to do it this way and perhaps the committee will entertain as an alternative a considerable raising of the ceiling as opposed to the introduction of this new principle.
There is one other small point I should like to deal with concerning South African veterans or veterans who have served in other countries. With regard to the South African veteran, the amendment deals with the time of the actual landing on the continent of Africa. It just so happens that a Canadian contingent had left Canada and was en route to South Africa at the time peace was signed. Should not this amendment be more in accordance with the principle now adopted in so far as Korea is concerned? Should we not apply the date when the man left Canada in order to go to South Africa rather than the date of landing? If a man volunteered to serve in South Africa and was actually on the high seas en route to that theatre of war when peace was arranged he should receive consideration. I suggest to the minister that he consider changing that wording and instead of having it the date of landing in South Africa it should be the time the individual left Canada. That would be in conformity with the practice now being followed in connection with troops serving in Korea who receive veterans preferences when they leave Canada.
I should like to repeat my plea for the men who served in Great Britain only during the first war. These men are ageing and I should like to see them included in these benefits. If that cannot be done, perhaps some special latitude could be given to the minister to deal
War Veterans Allowance Act with individual cases where great hardship is evident. I happen to know of one case where the minister was able to obtain special permission for the hospitalization of an old veteran. I do not know of anything in the act that gives the minister the ministerial prerogative, shall we say, to act in exceptional cases. I commend the minister for having found a way to deal with this one case, but similar cases are bound to arise and perhaps more flexibility should be introduced into the act to permit these old veterans being looked after.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a member of the committee but I have carried on a considerable correspondence with the department on behalf of veterans in my riding and have received a number of submissions from Legion branches in my riding. Therefore I feel I am justified in making the few comments I want to make regarding this bill. I regret that the government did not see fit to bring in this amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act last fall. While the increases are to be retroactive the fact is that by delaying this amendment for five months or since the pensions were increased a considerable amount of unnecessary suffering has been caused to many thousands of veterans.
I suppose one of the reasons for the necessity for this legislation arose out of the fact that a great many veterans could not receive pensions who were in reality entitled to them, and they were covered by this legislation. Veterans have pointed out to me that if section 63 of the Pension Act, under which a veteran is supposed to be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, were operative, many veterans who now have to receive the veterans allowance would be in receipt of basic pensions. Over the years I have had occasion to take up scores of cases with the department, and I cannot recall a single instance where the veteran was given even the shadow of the benefit of the doubt. In every single case I have taken up with the department, unless the veteran could establish the fact that his present incapacity arose out of or was caused by his service, or unless some medical officer could certify to that effect, there was never the slightest benefit of the doubt given to the veteran.
One of the things that veterans in my riding have been protesting is that while this act is being amended the Pension Act is not being amended at the same time so that the veteran may be given the right which he is supposed to have under section 63 of that act.

I have read the same magazine you have.
Mr. Nose worthy: -to remind him and his officials who administer veterans legislation of the promise Sir Robert Borden made to the men of the services at that time. He said:
I give you this assurance: that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done . . .
This is the point that is interesting.
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire.
The thought expressed there by Sir Robert Borden is that of the government attempting to guide the country, to guide public opinion, the government trying to induce public opinion to support the government in its generosity toward the veteran. Look at that promise in the light of the history of what has happened since 1917. When have we ever found the government trying to convince the public to support them in their efforts on behalf of the veteran?

speechtext:
Year after year it has been the other way around. Representatives of veterans organizations have had to fight just as persistently and with just as much

determination to get what they considered a fair deal from the governments of the two parties that have been in power as they had to fight the enemy to win the war in the first place. That has 'been the history of the veteran's fight with governments through the years since 1917. Instead of the government being out in front trying to induce the public to agree with them that the veteran needed these various benefits, it has been the veterans organizations, the parliamentary committees, members of the House of Commons almost unanimously year after year and people throughout the country pushing the government in order to induce them to deal fairly with the veteran.
From day to day we find in the press considerable criticism of some of the social services that the government is rendering. Certain sections of the press are very critical, but I have yet to see any section of the press throughout Canada that has been critical of the government because the government was too generous with the veterans of world war I and world war II. The country has been pushing the government and not the government trying to induce the country to be more generous to the veteran. The current issue of the Legionary has an editorial on the War Veterans Allowance Act to which it gives the title, "The Long, Long Trail". I think it might be well to look for a few moments at the length of that trail and the nature of the struggle that veterans have had along the trail. It was not until September, 1930, eleven years after world war I, that the War Veterans Allowance Act first became operative. At that time single veterans received $20 a month and were allowed to earn an extra $10, as much as they are allowed now under the new act. Married veterans were paid $40 a month and were permitted to earn an extra $20, twice as much as they are allowed to earn in addition to their allowance under the present act.
The next amendment was made six years later in 1936. That year the age of eligibility was reduced from 60 to 55 years. Two years later economic handicap and not age was made one of the conditions of eligibility; still no improvement in the allowance. In 1941 by order in council special provision was made for an extra $5 per month for single men and $10 for married men by way of a supplementary grant; still no change in the basic rates. In 1943 widows' allowances were provided; a long time after 1919. In 1944 free treatment and domiciliary care were provided. In that year world war II veterans and northwest rebellion veterans were included.
Then we come to 1946, when the basic rate was increased from $20 to $30 for single men

War Veterans Allowance Act
and from $40 to $60 for married men, and the allowance on behalf of children was continued until the age of 21 provided they were still at school. The ceiling on earnings then was $125 for single men and $250 for married men, a little more than twice what is allowed under the present act. In 1948, in line with the cost of living, the rates were stepped up again to $40.41 and $70.83 per month. Then in 1949 a sort of second means test was applied, making available $10 a month for single men and $15 for married veterans from the war veterans allowance fund. Then, after a fight lasting twenty years from the time the act was first introduced, imperial and allied veterans were brought under it. Now we have this amendment under which single veterans are to receive $50 and married veterans $90, with a ceiling of $120 a year on additional earnings whether married or single.
I think these rates should be taken into consideration along with the latest request of the veterans organizations, when they appeared before the cabinet last November. At that time they asked for $50 for single men and $100 for married men, and they wanted outside income permitted up to $250 for single men and $500 for married men. They also asked that those totally unemployable should receive allowances at the rate of $60 and $120 for single and married men respectively.
I submit that those requests are very modest. Certainly they are not out of line with the promise that has been made during the war years to those who served. I think a country that can raise over $2 billion for defence should be able in some way or other to raise the ante for single and married veterans to $60 and $120 per month respectively. I do not believe that would endanger the economic position of the country. I believe it would be a token to the veterans, especially those of world war I, that at last the country is recognizing and attempting to implement the promises that were made over thirty years ago.
There are a number of items pertaining to this bill that have been referred to and about which veterans have written to me. These have been mentioned already. Certainly veterans are going to find it very difficult to understand why the ceiling on additional earned income should be limited to $10 a month. I can see no good purpose to be served by that limitation except perhaps to save the government a few paltry dollars. I suppose it will amount to this, that any veteran who can struggle to work by any means will continue to work as long as he can stand up, rather than have to live on
the meagre allowance provided by this act. And as long as he can do that the government will be relieved of the responsibility of paying him that allowance. That is the only purpose I can see to be served by limiting additional earnings to $10 a month.
Then I notice that the act distinguishes between intermittent and casual earnings. When the minister closes this debate I hope he will point out just what distinction the department draws. I have been asked that question, and I have not been able to give an answer. I suppose that intermittent earnings are those of a man who is able to hold a job intermittently; who is not able to hold a steady job but is able to take intermittent employment. He would be entitled to come under the act. If a man takes casual employment, however, his casual earnings are not considered as income for purposes of the act. If the minister will clear that up it will be appreciated, because veterans are under the impression that if they earn over $10, whether it is casual or intermittent or anything else, and the department finds out about it, that amount will be deducted from their allowance.
There is one other question I want to mention to which I think the government should give consideration in paying the veterans allowance. That is the plight of veterans today in the matter of housing. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) put on record the economic position of a number of veterans as reported in the Legionary, listing them as veteran A, veteran B and so on. I am going to add a little more from that same article:
Veteran A now lives in two makeshift basement rooms seven feet below ground level. They were formerly a basement storage, actually just one room, and the small curtained-off portion now used as a bedroom was a coal bin before they moved in.
That was veteran A. Veteran B:
A small $6 a week room is his home.
Veteran C, a widow, has given up her apartment since her veteran husband died, sold her furniture and gone to live with her niece.
Veteran D, another widow.
She is living in two damp basement rooms and during the winter stays in bed most of the forenoon, partly because of her health and partly to keep warm as she cannot afford an adequate supply of fuel.
That is the treatment which today is being meted out to the men who served in world war I, and to the widows of those men. The prime minister of this country at that time assured these men that the government would take the lead in trying to induce the Canadian people to agree to giving them that to which they were entitled. Does it not seem evident that today the people of
1926	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act Canada have reason to be ashamed of the treatment that we as a -country are meting out to those who served in world war I, and who now can scarcely find enough on which to live?
I think, Mr. Speaker, that when the committee is reviewing this act they may well do so in- the light of the promises which were made to these veterans, and they may well consider giving to these men an allowance of at least $60 single -and $120 married, with -the ceiling on earnings either removed or raised to what the veterans themselves requested, $250 single and $500 married.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I feel that this is an occasion, Mr. Speaker, when the members of this house, particularly those who are not members of the special committee on veterans affairs, should express to that committee their views concerning this bill. I suggest that the Canadian Legion and the other veterans organizations that will appear before the committee should know when they appear what the views of members are. I feel that it is our duty to speak at this time, and I only wish that more members on the government side would speak, so that we can back up the Legion in what some of us believe will be -the requests that they will make to that committee.
I think the first criticism that all of us feel about the bill whic-h has been presented is the inadequacy of -the amounts provided. As members have put on the record repeatedly today, the bill raises the amount provided for single veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act from $40.41 to the sum of $50 per month. It raises the allowance provided a married veteran from $70.83 to $90.
Mr. Speaker, on the desks of a good many members in the house -this afternoon there is a copy of the afternoon edition of the Ottawa Journal. The main heading reads:
Abbott predicts 10 years of good times
To me it is incongruous, whether or not that prophecy is correct, that on a day when we are told that we are in for ten years of good times we should be asked to accept a bill which provides to our burnt-out pensioners only $50 a month in the case of a single veteran and only $90 a month in the case of a married veteran. When we were at the resolution stage preceding this bill I expressed the view that if the government did not measure up to the requests of the Canadian Legion, the members of the house and of the committee would have to do their best to try to persuade the committee to measure up to those requests. Many of us were deeply disappointed when we received


the bill after first reading and learned of the amounts upon which the government had decided. As I say, there is no doubt in my mind, particularly in view of the amounts the Canadian Legion has requested, that this phase of the matter will be discussed at considerable length and in considerable detail by the special committee on veterans affairs.
I want the Canadian Legion and others who are appearing before that committee to know that, in their request for a larger amount, they have the support of a great many members of this house. They have the support of their veteran colleagues, and -they have the support of those of us who are not veterans and can perhaps speak in a special way for the general population of the country. I urge most strongly, Mr. Speaker, that when this bill is before the committee the government pay attention to the request that will be made at that time, and pay attention to the request of members of parliament generally that the amounts be set higher. I want to say again tha-t I wish a few more members on the government side would speak in this debate, even if only briefly, and express their views with regard to these amounts. If they are satisfied with them, let them stand up and say so. But if they are not, as I am sure-at least as I hope-is the case with a good many members on the government side, I think they should join with us in saying that these amounts of $50 and $90 are inadequate, and that the request of the Canadian Legion for not less than $60 single and $120 married should be granted.
I see that it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 2, consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation- Mr. Larson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when
speaking on this bill to incorporate the Boundary Pipeline Corporation last Friday evening for a few minutes I took the opportunity briefly to point out that we in this group are in particular opposed to the granting of charters to companies for the building of pipe lines under private ownership. My time was so short that I had only the opportunity more or less to commence my introduction; therefore I am going to

take the opportunity to elaborate somewhat further on our point of view in this group with respect to the public ownership of pipe lines, and to deal with a few other aspects of this bill which is so important to Canadians generally, and which unfortunately many people in Canada are not greatly concerned about.
We in this group, Mr. Chairman, believe that it would be to the advantage of the Canadian people if pipe lines were nationally or socially owned as common carriers. We believe that national planning on that scale would prevent, as I said the other evening, the duplication of charters for the building of pipe lines across Canada. During the last three or four years we have seen the competition between various companies endeavouring to secure a charter giving them the right to build a pipe line over a designated route. No doubt if three or four charters are granted covering a similar route, then it simply means that some of these companies have a charter which they could sell to the highest bidder without building a route at all. Therefore we believe in public ownership, particularly with respect to national transportation, because a pipe line as a common carrier would be part of our national transportation system. If it were publicly owned it would give an easy opportunity for planning, and an opportunity to prevent duplication as a result of the competition between various companies in the building of these pipe lines.
My second point is that because competition would be eliminated between these various companies and we would not have two pipe lines built where one would suffice, there would necessarily by good management be a lowering of the costs to the consumer. The experience of Canadians with respect to railway freight charges and railway transportation charges would be different today if it had been possible when the railways were built in Canada to have a nationally-owned railroad system and to have avoided some of the expensive duplication that exists today such as the parallel railroads from Kamloops to Vancouver on both sides of the Fraser river and so on. We would have more than lower costs to the consumers. Instead of the profits going to private interests, and in the majority of cases in connection with these pipe lines to nonCanadian interests, these profits would be retained in Canada and would be added to the total revenue of this government for the advancement of social services and things of that kind, which would make it easier for the government to add $10, $15, or $20 to the war veterans allowance that was advocated in the debate this afternoon.
Boundary Pipeline Corporation
Many of us think that the Canadian National Railways is losing a great opportunity by overlooking the possibilities for the national ownership of pipe lines as public carriers in Canada. They have the rights-of-way; they have the grades; they have the bridges built; they have all the facilities to unite a public pipe lines transportation system with their railroad system. It is amazing even today, with regard to the publicity given to the great development of oil and gas in Alberta and to the numerous debates in this house which members on the government side listen to with great interest and enjoyment throughout the years, to find that there is still a great laxity and a great lack of interest and appreciation of what this oil and gas business means to Canada at this time and in the days to come.
To support that argument, Mr. Chairman, I want briefly to quote from the Ottawa Citizen of March 10, 1951, which contained an article entitled: "Gas for Canadian cities"; and also the subtitle: "Lack of interest in pipe lines may result in Americans getting Alberta's fuel." The article reads:
The idea of building a pipe line from Alberta to Winnipeg is too much for the average Winnipegger's imagination, this despite the fact that an oil pipe line now connects the Manitoba and Alberta capitals. Yet even a gas line from Edmonton to Montreal would be a routine construction job compared with some of the lines that have been built elsewhere in the world.
Mr. Chairman, members in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, when we were dealing with this bill, and when the companies' agents were producing their witnesses, emphasized the difficulties of building a trans-Canada pipe line to Montreal. Further on, this article has this to say:
By contrast, the cities of the northern United States are exceedingly aware of the possibilities for growth that would follow the tapping of Alberta's gas resources. The promoters seeking to serve them have shown ten times the activity of those who want to serve Winnipeg. Finally, to complete this catalogue of contradictions, there is no financial problem involved. Money for a gas pipe line, any pipe line headed in any direction, is available in plenty and in fact clamouring for a chance to be spent. If there is one thing that there is plenty of today, it is money for investment in pipe lines. That, more than any other factor, makes this sleepy-headed attitude of Canadian cities utterly baffling.
There is a lot of truth and common sense in that article. While we have American interests competing with one another to build these pipe lines in Canada there is a lack of interest on the part of Canadians themselves to build them. The capital is in Canada, and the government has credit resources with which to build these lines. I am of the opinion that in the days to come

Boundary Pipeline Corporation if we do not change the direction of our policy in this connection we will have cause to regret it.
It is mentioned here that money is available for investment in any quantity. Why? Because in the carrying of gas and oil there is, if one may judge from United States history, an increasing profit. That is why in this group we are continually reiterating our belief that these pipe lines should be nationally owned, that they should be part of the Canadian National Railways system, and that these commodities could be provided at a lower cost, leaving the profit for -the Canadian people.
Last year there came before the house and the committee a bill making provision for the building of a pipe line from western to eastern Canada. The pipe line, to operate as far east as Montreal, was to be operated by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. That bill received considerable discussion in the house and in committee. I should like to remind the house that, as a result of the efforts of half a dozen members in the committee who had tried to make certain again and again that the pipe line bills would be amended so that the main pipe line would be in Canada, an amendment was moved1. The amendment was to make certain that Canadian requirements were served first before Canadian gas and Canadian oil was exported to other countries.
In this application to build the Trans-Canada pipe lines it was proposed to build a gas pipe line from Alberta to Montreal, following an all-Canadian route, paralleling the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. The pipe line would be approximately 2,200 miles long, and would gather in lateral lines of about 900 miles. The main transmission line from Alberta to Toronto would consist of 30-inch pipe and from Toronto to Montreal of 24-inch pipe.
That charter has now been granted and because we believe that Canadian requirements must be served first some of us in the committee, and some in the house, are concerned about the granting of a charter to the company now applying, in case it may jeopardize the building of the pipe line under the charter now granted.
In that respect, and in connection- with the bill known as the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines bill, I want to quote from a paper presented at the annual meeting of the Engineering Institute of Canada -at Montreal on May 9, 1951, by Dr. G. S. Hume. This paper is entitled "Utilization of Natural Gas in Canada". 1 should like to quote from it some references he makes to the granting of

*a charter to the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company Limited. Dr. Hume has this to say in that connection:
Finally, the last export permit for gas from Alberta is being requested by a group of Texas operators representing Delhi Oil Corporation of United States and Canadian Delhi Oil Limited for a project, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, to bring gas from Alberta, starting in the Princess area, eastward to Winnipeg, and thence across the Pre-eambrian shield via Fort William and Port Arthur, via Sudbury to Toronto, and thence to Montreal, with a branch line to Ottawa.
When we know about the intentions of this company, and what the building of a pipe line would mean, from Alberta to Montreal, some of us are rather surprised that more Ontario and Quebec members have not shown some concern in making certain that Canadian gas goes first to Ontario and Quebec rather than first to the United States. Dr. Hume goes on to say:
Various routes across the Precambrian shield from Fort William to the vicinity of Sudbury are being investigated. This pipe line as proposed would- be 30-inch diameter capable, with the requisite number of compression stations, of carrying initially 365 million cubic feet a day increasing to a maximum of about 500 million cubic feet a day. The cost is estimated at about $250 million.
Then farther on Dr. Hume says, in connection with the pipe line:
There are certain features for a pipe line project of this kind which appear to be essential if the pipe line is to operate with the greatest efficiency and hence provide as reasonably priced gas to the consumer as can be obtained. One such is underground storage as in depleted or partially depleted gas fields of Ontario during the off-peak summer months so that the load factor of the pipe line could be kept up as nearly as possible to the maximum. A low load factor on such a pipe line would make it uneconomic. Thus underground storage facilities for gas is a prime consideration from the price standpoint even if the pipe line could operate economically without such storage. In addition to providing a means of taking care of off-peak loads, storage also gives a considerable measure of insurance in the consuming area against interruptions in service due to breaks of the transmission line. Long pipe lines are operated, of course, without underground storage facilities. There are various ways of taking care, at least in part, of the variable load.
Then, after dealing with that technical problem, he goes on to say:
These are what are known as industrial interruptible sales. This is a partial compensation for more nearly uniform sales throughout the year. There is no doubt all these features will be fully dealt with by competent engineers before the proper authorities when and if consideration of the pipe line project reaches the final stages. No specific data have yet been made available, but it is known that studies are now under way.
That company has already received a charter from parliament. It has been before the board of transport commissioners, and at this stage had spent a considerable amount of money-and this paper was written about a year ago. We are wondering if we would

jeopardize the building of that pipe line to Montreal if we were to grant the charter sought in the bill before us. This bill would make provision for a smaller pipe line to Winnipeg, and we are of the opinion that if the charter were granted for the smaller pipe line it would become economically unfeasible to build the pipe line from Alberta to Montreal.
That is our major argument. We are concerned about the granting of this charter, unless we can be assured that gas will flow to Ontario and Quebec as a result of a firm and sound exchange arrangement between Canadian and United States producers.
Further to illustrate the great value of this natural resource, and the great competition there is in the United States for charters, as well as the influence brought to bear, 1 should like to read briefly from an article in the Ottawa Citizen of May 5, 1951, headed "U. S. Pressure in Gas Deal". The article reads:
Export of Alberta gas to Montana demonstrates how demand for Canada's natural resources mixes in U.S. politics.
But using political influence for corporate gain is part of the warp of American democracy. It is done as a matter of course. Persons or groups who find themselves facing obstacles that they cannot surmount, instinctively turn to the government for help. There is a revealing paragraph in the first letter from Mr. C. E. Wilson, president of the office of war mobilization, to Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe. It reads:
"During the past several months, I have had several letters from interested American groups, urging that I ask your intervention and assistance in persuading-'(Alberta)'-to give assent and encouragement to the construction of a pipe line for the sale and delivery of gas to the American northwest."
Mr. Wilson went on to explain that he had refused to intercede for these groups.
I might interject here to say that I think Alberta is following a very sensible policy by moving slowly in connection with these growing demands for the export of Alberta natural gas. I think that is a sound policy when-

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: They are always sound.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
-they are not sure of then-reserves. The article goes on:
The Canadian dilemma at the moment is that, through the exercise of influence at Washington, plus a desire to co-operate to the hilt with the United States in re-arming, we may be pressured out of some of our resources which from a longterm Canadian view it would be better to keep.
Title to most of our oil and gas resources In Alberta have already passed into American ownership. American owners naturally think in terms of their operations as a whole. They do not separate in their minds their foreign assets unless they are forced to do so. When they discover that they can achieve their ends in Canada by nudging Washington, they'll nudge Washington.
Boundary Pipeline Corporation
Then the article concludes:
Alberta with its oil and gas, Quebec with its iron ore, are roughly in the same position today that Venezuela was in two or three decades ago. We welcome foreign capital with open arms. We offer them our resources on terms so generous they rub their eyes in wonder. And because we speak the same language they are not conscious of being in a foreign country. It is like being at home where, if they can't get what they want from a state government they hop a plane for Washington.
I read these quotations to indicate that Canadian writers and people interested in the gas and oil industry in Canada are concerned about the lack of interest across Canada in the development of this great natural resource. We in this group urge public ownership of pipe lines. If that is not possible at the present time, then our second policy is to press, in co-operation with other members of this house and other parties, for the provision of Canadian natural resources to Canadians first before they are exported from this country. We believe that we should use this fuel, this power and this heat in Canada to our own advantage before exporting it because it will mean taxes paid to the national, provincial and municipal governments; it will mean the employment of labour and the development of our own industries. The Ottawa Morning Citizen of February 4, 1951, contained a very interesting article entitled "Exporting Natural Resources" by James H. Gray. He has this to say in conclusion:
If the gas, or the iron ore, or the pulpwood, were processed completely in Canada, a dozen tax sources would be created. The production companies would be taxed on income, the workers employed would be taxed on income. The same would be true of the processing companies and the people with the end product.
Curiously enough, one of Anaconda's main competitors in the copper business in Canada is Consolidated Mining and Smelting. Anaconda is protected by three cents per pound tariff against Canadian copper. Without Canadian gas it would have had to use 1,600,000 barrels of oil, or 500,000 tons of coal annually, at two or three times the price. That would have given a competitive advantage to a Canadian company, if it could have used the gas instead of coal.
I have quoted these articles from various newspapers and other sources to try to prove my argument that we in this country should be careful in granting these charters for gas pipe lines when we are not sure of our own requirements or our developments in the future. During the past ten years industrial development in Canada exceeded the expectations of everyone prior to that time. We do not know what the future will bring and a few years may find us in the position where we find it necessary to use our own total gas resources.
I should like to deal briefly with two aspects of the bill as discussed in the committee. I have found from my experience

Boundary Pipeline Corporation in the committee, as I said before, that a number of members have made every effort to be certain that Canadians shall have the first opportunity to use their own gas and oil. When this bill was before the committee I must say that the company had a most excellent witness in Mr. Herring. I do not think any member of the committee doubted that he was an expert in his field and I am sure that all would say that he was one of the most competent and clear-cut witnesses that have appeared before the committee in -connection with any of these applications for charters.
He was asked a series of questions over a period of three meetings of the committee and I know that other members as well as myself were impressed with his frankness and clear explanations of the technical aspects of the production and marketing of gas. I want to repeat what I said the other evening that we were most fortunate in having the hon. member for Calgary West as a member of the committee because without doubt he has a thorough knowledge of the production and marketing of oil and gas.
The witness gave an excellent description of the economic aspects of the project. He described the purposes of the company and its future intentions. He said that the purpose was to proceed to Winnipeg first, but many of us in the committee noted a change of emphasis after two days of cross-examination. There was considerable emphasis on Winnipeg being the first objective of the company with the possibility of building the line to the United States border if supplies were sufficient.
Later on in the committee proceedings the witness rather played down the possibilities of the company exporting gas to the United States. I think other members of the committee will agree with me in that. He saw that there was consistent opposition to this matter of exporting gas to the United States to the detriment of Ontario and Quebec. I should like to quote from page 97 of the report of the committee in that connection, when I was cross-examining the witness as follows:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the witness a question. I would like to be able to understand the situation. Throughout his evidence it seemed to me that the witness emphasized that the real purpose of building this pipe line-I think that during the whole of the time on the first day this witness was giving his evidence he emphasized the possibility of continuing this pipe line into the states, to cities like Minneapolis and other centres, and the possibilities that that offered for the exchange of gas between Canada and the United States so that Ontario could get it. Now, just a few minutes ago in answer to a question the witness stated


definitely that the success of this venture rests upon moving gas to the Winnipeg market. I would like him to explain to me the reason for the change there.
Mr. Herring then replied as follows:
I see your point. Our recommendation to our people is that we feel that if 75 million cubic feet of gas can be obtained from Alberta that would be adequate. We have recommended- an economic pipe line to Winnipeg for that gas. I did not emphasize any other point except that. I have always stated that at such time as additional reserves were available in Alberta that we would recommend to them at that time the most economic application of such reserves to their system, within limitation. If that gas, as it increases in Alberta, becomes available in sufficient volume-and we spoke of the northern natural market over in Minnesota, and that is what we recommend when we come to that point because at the present time we cannot see the economics of going into Ontario and Quebec across Canada.
That is just the point so far as certain members of this committee are concerned. We are hesitant about giving our support to this bill because we believe that the ultimate objective of the company is the piping of much larger quantities of gas to the northern part of the United States than would be used between Winnipeg and the source of the gas. We are hesitant about supporting the granting of the application of this company until we are assured that the interests of Ontario and Quebec are protected so far as the receiving of natural gas is concerned prior to its export to the United States.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: As a member of this committee I voted for the bill after moving an amendment. There is no more honest or efficient committee than the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and I think this measure was pretty well handled by it. However, I think all hon. members will admit that those who are putting up the money have a good deal of the say as to where the line will go. When a bill of this kind is being discussed there are people who have an axe to grind, and I admit that I am one of them. I have an axe to grind. I object vigorously to any measure providing for a pipe line that will come to Winnipeg but will not come to Fort William and Port Arthur. I supported this bill-

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: It stops at Winnipeg.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
-because the amendment 1 moved was carried. The purpose of my amendment was to eliminate the words "outside Canada" so that it would be an allCanadian route. That may not go far enough but it was as far as we could go at the present time. There are those who think that Fort William and Port Arthur are merely two little spots amidst a lot of bush, rock and great lakes. Fort William and Port Arthur are among the most progressive cities in Canada, and they will need a lot of gas and oil. On

the way to Fort William on the C.P.R. there are towns that will need gas and oil such as Kenora-the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River will support me-Keewatin and Sioux Lookout. At the lakehead there are towns like Nipigon and Schreiber and new places that have sprung up with quite large populations such as Terrace and Marathon. They will need oil. Then there are the mining towns of Geraldton, Beardmore and Longlac. There would be a good deal of encouragement for the building of such a pipe line to the lakehead. I represent those at the lakehead who say that while it would cost a lot to build a pipe line to the lakehead it is only fair that that region should have some consideration when our own natural resources are being sold. I also admit that the dominion government is not investing one dollar in it and is taking no risk. The people who supply the gas and who put up the money are taking all the risk. I am going to support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the hon. member, who is the mover of the motion, speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member closes the debate I would like to say a few words regarding this bill. I congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on his persistence on behalf of this amendment. He covered ground again this year which has become quite familiar.

I am not going to attempt to make the same points I tried to make when the bill came up last year. Amongst other things I said then that I would give close study to the pros and cons of this question, and I have tried to do that. Nothing I have seen has caused me to believe that it is a very bad thing to adopt the voluntary check-off when it has been arranged by agreement between the two parties concerned. I think it has many things to commend it, just as so many other items agreed to by collective bargaining have much to commend them. While the present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is not to everyone's desire, and perhaps would be a sorry document if it were, on the whole it works very well.
Of one thing I have become quite sure, in connection with this effort in encouraging industrial peace in Canada; the spirit of good will and co-operation between the two bargaining parties is of far greater importance than trying to make the act so tight, so rigid and mandatory in the hope that it might be able to cover all contingencies that might come up from time to time. We in the federal Department of Labour have been doing our very best to help create the kind of industrial atmosphere in Canada in which peace and good labour relations might flourish. For the past year and a half I have heard from time to time the most forceful exhortations from those speaking on behalf of wage earners generally. In this house and even more especially outside it I have been told in no uncertain terms in reference to what happened here in September of 1950, in connection with the railway strike, that the principle of compulsion must not-and I repeat must not-be allowed to creep anywhere into our permanent labour legislation.
I take that to mean that if it is possible to avoid it, government legislation should not compel either side to agree to any bargaining item normally coming under collective bargaining. I will admit that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act does have some compulsory provisions. For example, there is the provision that an agreement must not be for less than one year. These compulsory provisions, however, apply to both parties. I am not going to say for a moment that never again should the act be amended so that this principle might be included. It may be that the time may come when this amendment should be included in the act as part of a well balanced over-all review, based on a reasonable period of experience in its present form.
I am fully aware that there are members in all parts of this house who feel that that time may be now, and I have the greatest
Industrial Relations
respect for their views. But I do maintain that we can afford to go slowly as we have done in adding further compulsory items and particularly a compulsion which, for the first time in federal legislation, would impose duties on one party to collective bargaining and not upon the other. I should like to be sure also that the establishment of the principle of parliament determining such questions as are now active in the area of industrial self government does not run against the long term best interests of organized labour itself. I am confirmed in this let-well-enough-alone attitude when I reflect that parliament made it quite clear in section 6 of the original act that there is no restriction whatever on the rights of parties to collective agreement to include such a provision.
I should like to repeat that this government is not opposed to the voluntary checkoff in those industries coming under the federal labour code. But the government feels that, for the present at least, the checkoff should be made effective only through a freely negotiated agreement by means of collective bargaining.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
This is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that I have had the opportunity of expressing my views on the attempt which is being made by this bill to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. During the debate which was opened by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on April 1, members will have noticed that the discussion tended to show the desirability of applying the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off to industries under federal jurisdiction, without placing too much emphasis on the method which is being advocated to attain that aim. We all agree on the soundness of this principle of the voluntary revocable check-off as the least possible measure of union security to which the trade unions of this country are entitled.
I am afraid, though, that a member who has been listening to the debates which have gone on in the past years, and again this year under this bill, has been misled in some way since the whole discussion has been on the principle of the check-off, the development of check-off provisions in the country, and so on. Figures have been given showing what the situation is in the manufacturing industry, for instance. Tonight I should like to discuss the effect that the passage of this bill would have on the act which it proposes to amend, the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. The bill is directed at inserting in this act a subsection 3 to section 6, which is one of the sections under
1936	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act the heading of "Unfair labour practices", and which would operate upon the request of any certified trade union to compel the employer to comply with the procedure of the voluntary revocable check-off. My point is this. Even if all the members in this house were to agree on the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off, and wished to see it applied in all plants in this country where the workers are properly organized, the method advocated in this bill to achieve that end within the field of federal jurisdiction is wrong and objectionable.
I have taken the same stand in past debates on the same subject, and it is the stand I am taking today against this bill. I was unavoidably absent when the bill came up for discussion for the first time on April 1 of this year. I have read in Hansard the address which my colleague, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Dickey), delivered on that occasion. He has taken the right approach in examining the bill from the angle which I have just mentioned. He made a very fine address and I wish to compliment him sincerely.
As it is now nine o'clock and I should like to proceed further, I move the adjournment of this debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lapointe for the second reading of Bill No. 181, respecting allowances for veterans and their dependents.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION-INCREASE OF ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock we were discussing the motion for the second reading of the new War Veterans Allowance Act. I had just indicated, as had other members who had preceded me, my feeling of disappointment that the government is asking the house to raise the amount paid under the War Veterans Allowance Act to only $50 a month for a single veteran and to only $90 a month for a married veteran. I had just pointed out that I felt it was particularly incongruous that on this day we should be reading headlines in the papers to the effect that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is predicting prosperity and good times for the next ten years, and at the same time we are asked to agree to such small amounts for our burnt-out pensioners, to whom all of us feel we owe so much. I earnestly hope that those who appear before the special committee on 

veterans affairs, when they request that committee to increase these amounts, will know that they have allies in a good many of us in the house. We earnestly hope that their pleas for amounts such as $60 a month single and $120 a month married will be accepted and recommended back to this house by the special committee on veterans affairs.
I feel too, Mr. Speaker, it is most disappointing that the government at this time, when it has chosen to rewrite the War Veterans Allowance Act, has retained the means test to the extent that it is retained in this new version of the act. Under the act as it stood before this bill was brought in, a single veteran was permitted to have $10.42 a month other income and still draw the full amount of the burnt-out pension. A married man was permitted to have $20.83 a month other income, and still draw the full amount of the war veterans allowance. Actually, those margins between the amount of the allowance and the total income that a burnt-out pensioner could have, have been reduced. They have been reduced in both cases to the sum of $10 a month.
In passing I want to say at this point that I still think it is unfortunate that we had by accident back in 1949, in connection with the Old Age Pensions Act, the introduction of the idea of the other income being made the same both for a married couple and for a single person. As I have said, it was an accident; it was done for reasons I need not go into, but I registered my objection very strongly at the time. Now that idea has been carried forward in the present Old Age Assistance Act and here we have it introduced for the first time into the War Veterans Allowance Act. Previously this legislation always provided that the amount of other income permitted to a burnt-out pensioner was twice as much in the case of a married veteran as in the case of a single veteran. Now it has been made the same in both cases, and that margin, as it were, has actually been reduced from the former figures down to $10 a month. I realize that the minister can reply-but I suggest to him that it is only a debating point so far as this margin is concerned-that the ceiling has been raised, but the fact of the matter is that the ceiling has not been raised to the extent that the amount of the allowance itself has been raised, and that is what accounts for this lessening of the margin to which I have referred.
In view of the feeling of a great many Canadians that there should not be any means test at all with respect to the war veterans allowance, it does seem unfortunate that this measure now before us provides

not only for the retention of the means test, but for the lessening of the margin that is permitted to a burnt-out pensioner. I hope that this point will come in for considerable discussion in the special committee on veterans affairs. I say again to the representatives of the Canadian Legion, and to the others who will appear before that committee, that in their request that the income ceilings be raised to $1,200 single, and $2,000 married, they have allies and supporters here on the floor of the House of Commons. I know that members of the committee will listen closely to what the representatives of the Legion have to say, and I hope that not only the private members of the committee, but the government representatives on the committee will pay attention to the Legion's request for considerably increasing the ceilings.
It is obvious now that the government is not going to agree to the removal of the means test from the War Veterans Allowance Act. In that circumstance it means that we will have to concentrate on the effort to secure the raising of these income ceilings.
I believe that consideration should be given to the point that was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) when he suggested that the objective sought by the portions of the act that are designed to permit burnt-out pensioners to engage in employment on a monthly basis without losing all their burnt-out pension in other months could be achieved just as well by raising the permissible income ceilings to the figures suggested by the Canadian Legion, and in so doing some of the other difficulties would be taken care of as well.
I think again of the ill-feeling that has developed in a good many quarters over the way in which burnt-out pensioners, on receiving the old age security pension, have had their burnt-out pension reduced. We understand it in this house at any rate that there is no means test in the Old Age Security Act itself. Everyone 70 years of age who meets the other qualification, namely, that of sufficient residence in Canada, qualifies for the $40 pension under that act regardless of his means. Most people in Canada who qualify for the pension under the Old Age Security Act do not suffer any loss in their other income by virtue of the fact that they are in receipt of that other pension; but in the case of war veterans allowance recipients, when they receive the old age security pension, it is taken into consideration by the war veterans allowance board in computing the burnt-out pension under the means test. In other words, they are still under a means test.
War Veterans Allowance Act
I remind the house and the government that it would have been possible, if the government had seen fit to do it that way, to put income received under the Old Age Security Act in the same class as income under the Family Allowances Act. Income under the latter is referred to in the War Veterans Allowance Act, and is not counted as income for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act. In other words, technically speaking, legally speaking, it could have been done. If the government prefers not to do it that way, that is another of the problems that could have been solved if the suggestion of the hon. member for Nanaimo were taken, and the permissible income ceilings were raised substantially rather than following this other method of providing for part-time employment.
As I say, and as he said, if you raise the permissible income ceilings to figures such as have been suggested by the Canadian Legion, a burnt-out pensioner over 70 who is on the old age security pension would not suffer any loss in his war veterans allowance and at the same time you would take care of the burnt-out pensioner who would be able to take part-time employment. They would both be protected by legislation of that kind.
