I am sorry there is no change in the new bill with regard to the definition of "theatre of war" for those who participated in world war I. It does seem to me that the case we have been making across the years for an ever-dwindling number of men in this category is one which should not continue to fall on deaf ears. There is not only the


plight of the veterans themselves who, through no fault of their own, were not able to get beyond England during the first world war, but there is the plight of the widows of those veterans who, though they qualify in every other respect, are denied the allowance provided under the act. Similarly I support those who have urged once again that the widows of imperial veterans be granted the allowance, if they have had the required residence in Canada, and that they should not be denied it merely because their husbands happened to live in Canada prior to death something less than the full 20 years.
There are other aspects of the matter upon which I might comment. However I do not believe it is necessary to do so at this time. I confess I have spoken with respect to this legislation on a good many occasions. I have done so because this legislation is extremely important to the needy older veterans of this country. There are many who, though they have served their country well, do not qualify as some of us feel they should qualify under the Pension Act. They must fall back on this legislation, and I feel we should take every possible step to make this the kind of legislation which shows for our burnt-out veterans a high degree of respect, and I think it should really show our appreciation of what they have done for us.
I earnestly hope that these important aspects of the matter, the amount of the allowance, the means test, the relation between war veterans allowance and old age security, as well as other aspects, will be fully considered in committee, and that the committee will be the kind of committee we have had in some years in the past. They have not all been the same. There have been committees in which there was a certain amount of wrangling, as indeed there is in most committees of the house. On the other hand there have been committees when it has seemed to us that the veterans have got together and, on a co-operative basis, recommended what was best for their comrades as a whole.
I hope that will happen this time, and that when the members of the committee have so recommended the government will accept the recommendations they make for real improvement in this very important piece of legislation.

But it is only fair to indicate at this stage that the legislation does not come up to our expectations.
As the debate progressed I was just thinking that this is a clear indication of the tremendous impact of war on society. Thirty-four years have gone by since the close of the first great war, and we are still attempting to settle some of the problems that affected those who served, and their dependents.
The War Veterans Allowance Act affects people who served in the South African war, which was brought to a conclusion fifty years ago this month. Then, there are a few survivors from the northwest field force whose active campaigning in western Canada occurred about sixty-seven years ago. But this does serve to indicate the shocking impact of war.
In 1979, thirty-four years from the close of the second great war, I suppose the survivors of that war will be arguing about the matter of assistance for veterans. I would hope that we could have the matter solved before too long.
Another point I would mention is that the number of people involved under this legislation is very small. According to the figures available at March 31, 1950, the survivors of the northwest field force who were benefiting under this act numbered only 60, while there were 336 from the South African war and about 24,700 from the first great war. Incidentally I hope that the veterans of the second great war will take a keen interest in the veterans of the first great war, just as the veterans of the first great war felt indebted to the South Africa veterans. It is sometimes overlooked that the South Africa veterans played a great part in the organization and training of the armies who fought in the first great war. Because of their experience, the contribution they made was considerable. As the veterans of the second great war mature a bit they may perhaps acknowledge that the veterans of the first world war made a similar contribution toward their activities.
The number is small compared to the total population of this country. In 1930 there were 51,000 in round figures drawing benefits 55704-1231
War Veterans Allowance Act under this particular legislation, and I am referring only to veterans and not to widows and others. That number has since dropped to 25,000.

That shows that in 1930 the number drawing allowances under the War Veterans Allowance Act was 51,000, which number has now dropped to 25,000. I maintain that it is a decreasing obligation so far as the veterans of the first world war are concerned and I think we can afford to be reasonably generous with these men. In order to qualify they must be sixty years of age or over and must prove that they served in a theatre of war. I remember the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) giving in the house what I considered to be the finest exposition of the service rendered by the men in this category.
These men were not wounded during the war but they suffered the hardships of campaigning. It has become quite obvious that men who underwent the campaigns in northwest Europe from 1914 to 1918 have in many instances suffered as a result.
I recall one sergeant, subsequently a sergeant-major, who came from the maritimes. He had served in France, first in an infantry regiment and later in a machine gun battalion, from the spring of 1915 up to the end of the war and then through the occupation in

War Veterans Allowance Act Germany. He was never wounded and to my knowledge had not missed an action except when he was away on annual leave. That is only one instance and I know of others whose service was lengthy. While they were not wounded they have now reached the age of sixty or over and are beginning to show signs of their exposure to the elements during the campaigning they endured. It was to aid these people that this legislation was enacted.
I think that they are as deserving of generous treatment as any of those who come under our veterans legislation. Consequently I think the Legion is well advised to suggest that the allowances should be increased. I would be happy to support their suggestion. It has been pointed out to the minister before that the Legion and other veterans organizations which deal with these matters are responsible bodies. The Legion has not put forward any extravagant claims at any time. They give close attention to matters of this sort and have not wished to be a burden on the country. Their representations have been carefully investigated and have received close attention indeed.
I regret that the means test has not been removed. This ceiling on the earnings of those coming under war veterans allowance is most annoying. I can give the minister instances where the burden falls largely upon the wife of the veteran. Take where a war veteran is burnt-out and unable to work. He finds that he cannot support himself and his wife on the allowance and the wife must go out to work. We must remember that the wives of those on war veterans allowance are not young women. They have reached the time when they should be retired but in many instances, in order to maintain the home and provide food and clothing, they have to go out to work. At that point the ceiling comes into effect.
I know of one instance of a war veteran suffering from arthritis who is unable to do any work. His wife, who is not a young woman, goes out to work every evening cleaning and sweeping up in a business block. The combined earnings exceeded the ceiling permitted and then the means test was applied and the war veteran was threatened with a reduction in his allowance. When the wife discussed this with the officials they drew attention to the possibility of casual earnings. This is a difficult matter for some people to understand, but it amounts to giving up a steady job and just going around to work a few days here, a few days there and a few days somewhere else and keeping your earnings down to a point where they do not exceed the ceiling.


I think one of the worst features of this legislation is the means test and the establishment of the ceiling, and I should like to lodge my protest. These people, few in number, an ageing group, should be given every encouragement. Where you have dependents who are doing their level best to assist, that should be recognized and these people should be given the benefit of the extra work they do. I hope that during the course of the meetings of the committee all these matters will be discussed in detail and that more generous treatment will be afforded these people on war veterans allowance.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak for a moment on this matter. As one who has been associated with the Legion for many years, in fact from the very first time to which Your Honour referred a few moments ago when the first payments of war veterans allowance were made, and having been here when the matter was dealt with at that time, I have some special interest in this legislation. Unfortunately I am one of the veterans who cannot be on that committee, and it is for that reason that I transgress on the time of the house for three or four minutes. I think the point made by the hon. member who preceded me is an important one. The group affected by this legislation is small in number and must inevitably become smaller as time goes on. As he says, there will be no replacements for those who took part in the first world war, and it is going to be many years before the veterans of the second world war can be affected by this legislation. We do not know under what circumstances, financial or otherwise, the country and the government will be operating by that time.
In the meantime we have a direct responsibility to these pitifully few veterans from earlier battles and wars. There are only a relatively small number from the first war. Having studied the legislation, and without committing oneself as to any definite figure as to the payments which should be made, there should be substantial increases. We have the recommendations which will be presented, as we know, by the Legion to the committee. I am sure the minister will agree that all Canadians can be proud of the attitude that has been taken by the veterans organizations in Canada in the past, and particularly the Legion. Their attitude has

been different from that which may have been taken by similar organizations in other countries. They have shown a degree of responsibility towards such matters which has inspired confidence on the part of the country.
One reason why the demands of the veterans as expressed by the Legion have general support throughout the country is that throughout all these years the Legion has always taken a sane and rational approach to the different problems. A great many members of the Legion give of their own time at inconvenience and expense to themselves to service and look after their comrades who have suffered disability or are burnt-out as are the ones we are dealing with today. When such an organization appears, as it will, before the committee in the very near future I suggest that its representations should be received with the greatest of respect. I trust that the committee, as I am sure it does, appreciates the fact that not only the returned men who are members of the house but practically all members of the House of Commons welcome their views and are inclined to endorse them.
As I said, the number of men concerned is diminishing, and surely in these times, when we have a degree of development such as we have never known before and when we are looking forward to further thresholds, returned men who suffer from no particular disability except the fact that they were burnt out in the interests of their country should be properly looked after. I suggest it is not right that there should be a ceiling with respect to them such as is imposed by this legislation. There should not be control of casual earnings, whatever they may be, in the way that is proposed by the legislation. I hope that these matters-and I know they will-will be considered by the committee.
While the members on the other side of the house who are returned men perhaps feel for various reasons that they do not want to take part in the debate at this time, nevertheless we know that they are interested. They have exercised influence before in committees and on the government. There have been times when they have exercised very substantial influence in connection with these matters. I simply speak as one who will not be a member of the committee. I think I am expressing the views of everyone. I know I am expressing the views of all who sit around me, and I believe of members generally and of the people of the country. The country expects the committee to deal with this legislation in a most constructive way and to report it back to the house on a scale considerably modified from that in which it is sent to it.

Mr. Speaker, I merely want to add my voice to the protests respecting the regulations concerning supplementary earnings that have been voiced by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and other members of the official opposition. I do so because I consider that it is an economic error. There are veterans of the first world war with considerable technical skills and who from time to time over short periods can command considerable earnings. I have in mind a veteran who appealed to me. He is a radio technician capable of doing special work on electronics. He could earn $1.50 to $2 an hour doing his specialized work but he was informed that if he accepted a job with one of the firms in that line of work he would lose his war veterans allowance.
On the face of it probably that is just. However, this man suffered an eye injury during the first world war, and his age was such that a company employing him could not in any way guarantee him permanent employment. Nevertheless from time to time he was capable of doing extremely valuable highly skilled work but because of his eye injury he could only do so on a temporary basis. No employer could possibly employ him on a permanent basis when his disability prevented him from working steadily. I feel that a man with such skill should be encouraged in every way to do as much useful work as he possibly can. I feel that the regulations limiting extra earnings not only destroy his morale and his ability to do useful work, which is in itself an extraordinarily bad thing, but also prevent a great deal of useful work being done throughout the country, which is also a bad thing.
Third, this man with special skill had to make a decision whether he would undertake the work-and in this case the job sought the man-and thereby lose his war veterans allowance, with the knowledge that should there be a recurrence of the eye injury, which was expected, that would prevent him from continuing with this work, he would become unemployed and would have to reapply for the war veterans allowance.
I mention this case, Mr. Speaker, because in my opinion one thing we should do from an economic point of view is encourage all the useful work that can be done in Canada. Anyone with special skill, anyone who can do work even of a temporary nature, should be encouraged to do it. If a man suffers a recurring disability which from time to time prevents him doing regular work, nevertheless he should be encouraged to work whenever it is possible for him to do so. It

War Veterans Allowance Act is good for the morale of the man. It is good for the morale of the country, and it is good for our economy.
I feel that these regulations are negative. Believe me, a lot of these old soldiers are extremely proud. More than anything else they want to be usefully employed, but these regulations virtually prevent their employment in many cases. This has come up on several occasions through people who have appealed to me. While they have received sympathetic consideration, nevertheless they have had to come to a decision-and it is a dreadful decision for anyone of any age to have to make-as to whether they would do useful work or attempt to live on the allowance the government granted them. It seems to me nothing would be more calculated to destroy the morale of those in receipt of war veterans allowance, those veterans of the first world war, than to so limit their extra earnings as is proposed under this legislation.

speechtext:
I am not going to detain the house very long; but like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), since I am not a member of this committee I would like to place before the house the consensus of opinion of the veterans in my riding, who number several thousand. Tonight we are dealing with a bill which will affect a large number of people in my constituency, many of whom have come there to enjoy the better, drier climate we have in that part of the country. Their number is gradually diminishing. I am afraid that unless something is done quickly the benefits we are hoping to render the burnt-out veterans will be wasted. They will not be there; they will have completely burned away.
To me this is a form of adjustment of a debt of honour, a keeping of faith with those who passed on fighting for these very things: higher standards of life, greater security for their fellow men. If we do not carry out what we fought for in the first and second world wars we will be breaking faith with those who have gone before, particularly if we cannot take better care of their dependents.
The disabled veterans are satisfied with the generous treatment they were accorded last session. I certainly hope the same generosity will be shown in dealing with this group of veterans. In the case of the disabled veterans the brief presented to the committee by the Canadian Legion became practically the blueprint of the final legislation. I feel that was because of the careful thought and study put into that brief by the officers and members of the Legion. It represented the carefully collected and studied


opinions of all the branches throughout the dominion. The same careful canvass has been carried on again with regard to the veterans allowance. I may say I know the work of the Legion very well; I have been a past president and am now a life member. I joined the Legion within the first few months after it was formed, so I know the thoroughness with which the brief will be prepared before being presented to the committee.
From information that has come to me I have some knowledge of one or two points I know will be dealt with in that brief, and on behalf of the people I represent I ask the minister to do something about those matters. In the first place they ask that the principle of the war veterans allowance be not changed, but they ask that it be increased from $40 for a single man and $70 for a married man to $60 for a single man and $120 for a married man. I think that is a reasonable request. I do not believe they are asking for too much in view of the high cost of living today. With the dollar only worth fifty cents, they are practically asking for half those amounts. So while the bill does not contain any figures, since the minister has already changed his mind about one matter I hope he will change it about this as well.
Another point is that the total ceiling should be raised to $1,200 for single men and $2,000 for married men; and to carry that out I suggest that the minister go further and entirely remove the means test. I believe we should encourage these burnt-out men to take any work they can do in order to keep up their morale and give them something to live for. Even though they may earn a little more than the minister believes they should, we must not forget that they can still render useful service to society. I have in mind my own district, where for two or three months each year we have a scarcity of labour to pick fruit. It is true that these veterans cannot do any hard work, but they are ideal for this type of labour. They can work for two or three months picking fruit and sometimes it pays very well, because of the rush nature of the work. So I feel the minister should consider allowing money so earned to be added to their allowance without penalty. Otherwise the fruit industry would have to do without the help now given by these men.
Then the widows of imperial and allied veterans with twenty years of residence in Canada should be entitled to the war veterans allowance regardless of the date of death of their husbands. I believe this is absolutely

War Veterans Allowance Act
correct. I am speaking on behalf of the veterans of my riding, and they are 100 per cent behind that thought.
I well remember Canadians serving in England who would have liked to have gone to France but could not. They had to stay behind in a training camp or work in hospitals or in charge of supplies. During the last war, in many cases, these men ran risks equal to those run by men who were in the front-line trenches. I remember that during the first war the men had to work pretty hard at the base looking after the supplies, whether the base was in England or in France. They were pleased when they were ordered to the front, because they went to the trenches for a rest. Therefore the veteran who served only in England may well have rendered, in that time spent in England, service equal to if not greater than that rendered by one who went to France, who perhaps even then did not see the trenches.
I feel that the implementation of this policy to increase the allowance is long overdue. I could name dozens of cases in which there was hardship that have come to my particular notice. On their behalf I urge the minister to reconsider the bill, especially after discussion with the members of the Canadian Legion. I do not believe the cost would be very high, but that can be considered after the numbers have been arrived at, the ages and the amount to be paid. I feel that the implementation of such an act would round out the program of care that we have developed for our ex-service personnel. It would give us a complete program of care. At present we have looked after the disabled, and we have looked after other small groups. This would complete the program, and Canada could be proud of the service rendered to returned men because it would be the equal of any country in the commonwealth of nations. I hope that the minister, who has already shown a tendency to modify his views and change what is already incorporated in the bill, will continue to do so until the needs of these men have been taken care of.

The purpose of the debate is to obtain the views of the members concerning the legislation before it is sent to the committee. I do feel however that, in fairness to myself and to the government which is bringing forward this legislation, there are some comments which I should make.
At the opening of the debate I stated that I would ask the chairman of the committee to see that an amendment was introduced to a section of the bill in order to change the
1944	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act qualifying age from 65 to 60. I tried to explain then, but quite possibly I did not succeed, that my understanding, and that of my advisers who have had considerable experience in the interpretation of veterans legislation, is that the insertion of the words 65 years in this particular section would not change anything as compared to the present application of the law. I understand, however, that it might be interpreted as raising the age at which veterans could qualify for veterans allowances. Since I do not want any such interpretation to be given to this legislation, which is an endeavour to make it a more flexible instrument for veterans welfare, I had no objection at all to the changing of the age from 65 to 60. Some hon. members have seen fit to argue the bill as though this change were not to be made. They have not taken my remarks into consideration, or possibly I did not express myself clearly; otherwise, I should think that they would not have spoken as they did.
Much of the discussion which has taken place today has been on the question of ceilings on casual or intermittent earnings by the recipients of war veterans allowance. Many of the speeches this afternoon were on that particular subject. I feel that some hon. members have not fully understood the purpose and effect of the new section 4. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) -I am sorry he is not here-said that the veterans felt that the putting into effect of the ceilings of $720 or $1,200, as they are now, is not only doing a disservice to the veteran but is causing a loss of production which would benefit the country. He went on to ask: How does the government benefit by making mandatory in the legislation that if a veteran is in receipt of the maximum amount of the war veterans allowance he must stay at home and do nothing because otherwise he will interfere with his allowance? This shows a complete misunderstanding of section 4, Mr. Speaker, as I tried to point out to him during the course of the debate. The whole purpose of that section is to permit a recipient of war veterans allowances to take employment, employment of the nature which was described by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) tonight. In fact, I think the best argument in favour of section 4 was the speech made by the hon. member for York West tonight when he described to us the situation of certain veterans who are skilled workmen. Because of ill health certain veterans are not capable of holding full-time employment; but in a period of full employment they are capable of taking a job for three or four months. Under the legislation as it stands today they 

would not take that employment because they would lose their war veterans allowance. That is the case at the present time. But when this new section is in the act any such veteran who is receiving war veterans allowance may take this employment and may receive this salary, whatever it may be. It may vary from a very low salary for unskilled labour to a relatively high salary for skilled labour. And when he ceases to work at this particular employment he will immediately be qualified to return to war veterans allowance and start to draw his war veterans allowance. In other words, as I mentioned when I introduced the resolution preceding this bill, the general effect of section 4 of the present bill is to take away the ceilings on earned income. I do not believe that ever before has any of our legislation gone so far forward. I know that the necessity for such legislation has been urged for some time.
Suggestions have been made that the same result would be achieved through other means in amending the act. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) suggested that this was new phraseology, new wording introduced in the legislation, and that it might bring about difficulties. I sometimes find that certain people would rather be wrong than be recent. I do not believe the fact that new wording or new phraseology is introduced into the act means that the principle which it carries is by any means wrong, and I do not think that my hon. friend would pretend that either. He may fear administrative difficulties. I think he mentioned that. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have the responsibility of administering this legislation as I have the responsibility of administering the department; I believe that generally speaking hon. members will agree that the officers of the Department of Veterans Affairs are competent. Most of them have been devoting many years to the cause of veterans. They have followed this legislation; they have taken part in the evolution of the legislation, and I believe they are in a position to foresee any difficulties that may arise out of the administration of the new principle.

That it is expedient to present a bill conferring authority upon the governor in council to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct a line of railway from Terrace to Kitimat, in the province of British Columbia, a distance of approximately 46 miles at an estimated expenditure of $10 million and an average expenditure of $217,391.30 per mile. subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM TERRACE TO KITIMAT, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution seeks to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct a branch line of railway between Terrace and Kitimat, in the province of British Columbia, a distance of some 46 miles. The resolution may be divided into three parts: First, that part which confers upon the Canadian National Railways the right to construct the line at a cost of $10 million; next, that part which authorizes the Canadian National Railways to issue securities guaranteed by the government in respect of the cost of construction of the line; and last, that which provides for the making of temporary loans out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purpose of meeting the cost of the line as it is being constructed.
The Aluminum Company of Canada is engaged at the moment in the development of a large-scale aluminum industry at the head of Kitimat Arm in British Columbia. The construction of the railway from Terrace to Kitimat Arm will be the means of enabling the Aluminum Company to proceed with a series of plans it has in that area. These plans I shall discuss in greater detail as I proceed.
The present plans call for initial production at the rate of 91,000 short tons of aluminum annually, and while it is impossible to forecast at the moment what production will be, the assurance is that the ultimate capacity will be in the neighbourhood of
550,000	short tons annually. The production of this aluminum, as the house knows, is dependent upon electrical energy.
The Aluminum Company has, over and above the establishment of the plant, also in mind the production of electrical energy to the extent of 1,600,000 horsepower.
The construction of the proposed branch line from Terrace to Kitimat will not only enable the company, as I said earlier, to proceed with the development of the electrical energy; it would also make possible the development of substantial timber resources

Canadian National Railways in this area. In addition, the opening up of another seaport at Kitimat will have economic significance in not only developing a seaborne trade out of Kitimat, but also in developing trade in the area. Much more tonnage will arrive by water at Kitimat than will depart from there at the outset. But as the plan which the company has in mind progresses it will, I believe, become easier to develop export trade than will exist at the outset.
The full development of the company's plans aims, first of all, at the establishment of a hydroelectric plant at the nearby coastal point of Kemano on the Gardner canal. This plant will utilize a head of 2,600 feet of water which will be diverted by a system of lakes at the head of Nechako river, which will develop the 1,600,000 horsepower referred to earlier.
Also there will be constructed a transmission line which will transmit the electrical energy from the area of the tunnel to Terrace, a distance of 55 miles. There will also be established under this plan a deep-water dock for the handling of waterborne material, equipment and supplies for the outward movement of a proportion of the finished product. And, finally, there will be set up a new townsite in conjunction with the plant, and industrial works, with schools, recreation and other facilities which should accommodate, ab initio, some 8,000 people.
The estimated cost of constructing a line as set out in the resolution is $10 million. This relatively high cost of construction is due to the difficult terrain over which the line will have to traverse. I have before me, and there will be available in the committee- to which I take it the bill based upon this resolution will be referred-a report prepared by the Canadian National Railways, research and development section, which will give not only a detailed analysis of the traffic which is likely to accrue out of the construction of the line, but also the financial return which should come from it.
That report will indicate that there should be an annual freight traffic accruing to the Canadian National Railways of 113,535 tons during the first five years of operation of the line, and 168,685 tons during the second five-year period. The principal sources of rail traffic, other than those derived from the Aluminum Company, would be forest products; and a minor but probably increasingly important resource would be that of fisheries.
There has also been prepared by the research section of the Canadian National Railways a statement indicating the traffic,

from the point of view of revenue, that is likely to accrue during the first five years of operation of the line, and during the second five years.
During the first five years of operation it is expected that there should be a net betterment to the Canadian National Railways operations of $1,100. That is arrived at by total revenues of $1,854,800 and total expenses of $1,503,700, plus interest on the cost of construction, which would leave the $1,100 net operating result for the first five years.
The position is better for the second five years to the extent that it is expected there will be a net operating revenue of $323,000. I need not go into detail, because that can be done at a later stage.
Then, following the practice it always follows-in my experience at least-in connection with the construction of branch lines of this kind, the Canadian National Railways seek to reach agreement with the company in question. In this instance they have entered into an agreement with the Aluminum Company which guarantees a minimum volume of traffic during the first ten years of operation and provides for the allocation of a substantial amount of electrical power for general industrial purposes, and the industrial development of the area.
Under the terms of the agreement the Aluminum Company undertakes to secure to the Canadian National Railways gross system earnings in freight, passenger and express traffic during the first ten years of operation of the proposed branch line equal to the capital cost of the line, but not exceeding $10 million.
The proposed bill would authorize the Canadian National Railways to expend on the construction of this line the sum of $10 million, and would be similar to bills of this nature which have been passed previously by the house. It would provide for the granting of temporary loans to the railways and a government guarantee of securities issued by the railways for the amount of $10 million necessary for the construction. The Kitimat project of the Aluminum Company is of great importance to the economy of Canada. I need hardly say to the house that it is of great importance from the point of view of the production of more aluminium which is required urgently at this time.
I believe that it is fitting that the Canadian National Railways should be the agency to enter into an agreement with the Aluminum Company for the construction of the line. It is fitting also that the Canadian National Railways should have taken such a prominent part in the development of this natural

resource as it did in the development of the nickel deposits in the Sherridon-Lynn Lake area and as it did in the development of the timber resources in the Kiask Falls-Barraute area on the national transcontinental. This measure to authorize the building of the proposed branch line is one which I am sure will commend itself to the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM TERRACE TO KITIMAT, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the official opposition strongly favour the construction of this branch line. The minister has given the house most of the details, but I would like to point out that although the line will run about 400 miles north of Vancouver it will be south of the Canadian National Railways line which runs from Jasper to Prince Rupert. Incidentally that line was the main transcontinental line through British Columbia of the old Grand Trunk Pacific. Half of the province of British Columbia lies north of that line and practically all of that half, with the exception of the Peace river belt in British Columbia, is undeveloped. Therefore this railroad holds great possibilities for the west coast province.
Terrace is an incorporated village on this line from Jasper to Prince Rupert and is about 100 miles inland. It is situated on the Skeena river in the midst of good farming country.
I take it that the proposed line is to run in a southwesterly direction from Terrace to Kitimat, which is a small Indian settlement on tidewater where there will be built an allyear port; navigation will be possible in and out of Kitimat throughout the winter months.
This line is needed because of the huge undertaking by the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited in that area. If their whole plan materializes there will be situated at Kitimat the largest aluminum smelter in the world. That may seem odd to hon. members as I must admit it did to me when I first heard of the plan. Here was this great company going into unsettled territory and proposing to establish this huge plant. However, the main reason for that is the tremendous power potential. The production of aluminum requires vast quantities of power. Materials can now be taken in by ship and when this branch line is constructed it will be possible also to bring them in by rail and of course the products of the smelter can then be transported either by ship or rail.
The project is really an amazing one. The company is building a large dam on the Nechako river about 140 miles inland from the Pacific coast. This river now drains to the east into the Fraser river which flows into the Pacific below New Westminster. They are damming that river and its tributaries and changing the whole drainage system from the -east to the west; at the western end of this
Canadian National Railways system they are boring a tunnel through a mountain to the Pacific coast for a distance of ten miles; this tunnel will have a diameter of 25 feet and, as the minister has said, will have a drop of about 2,600 feet.
The power plant is not to be located out in the open, but is to be inside this mountain in the Kemano district in an excavated cavern 1,400 feet underground; the power plant site will be 1,000 feet long, 80 feet wide and 100 feet high. Those are the dimensions of the cavern which is to be tunnelled out of the mountain and in which this power plant will be installed. That of course will protect the plant against atomic bombs and landslides and apparently will help in the production of the power.
From that power plant transmission lines will run, not to Terrace as the minister said, but about 50 miles over the mountains to Kitimat which is to be the site of the smelter and the terminus of this branch line. That transmission line goes over territory so rough that in spots the materials needed to be taken in by helicopter.
As I say, the smelter is to be located at Kitimat. The first stage of this development at Kitimat is to be completed in the spring of 1954 and it is hoped to produce at that time 83,000 metric tons of aluminum annually. According to the literature of the Alcan people there will be a town there then of from 6,000 to 7,000 people, of whom about 1,100 will be production workers. The cost of that first stage will be about $160 million and I believe the horsepower to be produced is roughly 420,000. Incidentally they are not going to bring bauxite, the raw material for aluminum, to Kitimat; I understand the plan is to process the bauxite partially in the Caribbean and bring to Kitimat a product known as alumina.
World markets for aluminum are steadily expanding and it is hoped by the company that because of those expanding markets and the establishment of other industries at Kitimat it will be possible shortly to go ahead with the whole plan. If that is done there will be eventually a production of over
500,000	metric tons of aluminum annually and the population of Kitimat will be about 50,000. It is expected the total cost will be over $500 million, or half a billion dollars, and the power developed will total 1,600,000 horsepower. That means doubling the Canadian production of aluminum. As I said before, it means the largest aluminum smelter in the world; half as large again as the aluminum smelter at Arvida in the province of Quebec where, incidentally, I believe only 1,200,000 horsepower are produced.
1948	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways
For British Columbia and Canada this is a most promising development. It will mean a great deal for Terrace and the vicinity. Farmers there will have a market for their crops. There is also good farming land to the east along the main line in the north of Canadian National Railways. It will mean jobs for the people who are already in that central portion of British Columbia. It will mean a great increase in population in all the centres along the line from Prince George right through to Prince Rupert.
I believe this Alcan plan will develop the whole of central British Columbia and should greatly hasten the construction of a railway outlet from the Peace river to the Pacific. It will also help to open that portion of British Columbia lying north of the line from Jasper to Prince Rupert.
It can very well be compared with the developments that are taking place in other parts of Canada. In Quebec we have a railway line being constructed into the region of the iron ore deposits, a line running over 300 miles from Sept lies right up to the border of Labrador. Last year we approved the construction in Manitoba by the Canadian National Railways of a new line from Sherri-don to Lynn Lake, a distance of about 155 miles. In northern Saskatchewan there is the development of the uranium mines, and the northern part of Alberta of course is a hive of activity. In the Mackenzie district there are also great developments taking place. All these northern developments are significant and I believe they are of the utmost importance. I think the future of Canada depends largely on expansion of her activities northward.
With regard to this proposal, in so far as Canadian National Railways is concerned the minister intimated that the railway is to be asked to pay the whole cost of $10 million That seems to be a different course from that followed last year with respect to the construction of the railway line from Sherridon to Lynn Lake. In that case the Department of Defence Production undertook to pay $4,725,000, practically one-third of the cost. The railway was not charged with that much of the cost. The reason given was that the opening of the line was partially for defence purposes; that it would mean the production of nickel, copper and other metals useful for defence preparation.
Here we have a branch line being constructed which will aid in the production of aluminum, and I do not understand why help should not be extended to this line by the Department of Defence Production in the same way that help was given to the Lynn Lake line. If my suggestion were carried out
(Mr. Green.]

the cost to the railway would be that much less. Canadian National Railways would have that much more opportunity to make the line pay. When the minister closes the debate, or in the discussion of the resolution in committee, I hope that he will explain why a different course is being followed in this case.
In the construction of the Lynn Lake line the mining company concerned, Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited, undertook to pay $5 million which was a little over one-third of the cost, the other $5 million being provided by Canadian National Railways. There is no mention here of the Aluminum Company having to pay any portion of the cost although they will get most of the benefit from the branch line. It is true that in the case of the Lynn Lake line there was a provision for repayment if the tonnage carried on the line' exceeded a certain figure. However, the minister has intimated that the only agreement made in the case of the Terrace-Kitimat branch line is that the company will guarantee a minimum amount of traffic for the next ten years, and will guarantee to supply a certain quantity of electric power to Canadian National Railways. I believe he did not indicate how much power was to be supplied. In the case of the Lynn Lake line the agreement also covered freight rates. There was provision for the freight rates that were to be paid on the line. We would like to know whether there is any similar provision in the case of the Terrace-Kitimat branch line.
I mentioned earlier in my remarks that it was hoped that other industries would be established at Kitimat. We are getting encouraging news in this regard every day. For example, since my return from the coast after the Easter recess press dispatches have indicated that there is reasonable expectation of a great pulp and paper plant being erected there by the Powell River Company, one of our timber companies, which is planning to act in co-operation with the Aluminum Company. There has also been an announcement that the Canadian Liquid Air Company will establish a plant at Kitimat where they will produce some of the products required by the Aluminum Company. We hope these are only the forerunners of many other industries that will come to the Kitimat district because of the immense production of power.
The official opposition agree that, the bill should be sent to a committee. We suggest the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines where it will be possible to hear evidence from the officials of Canadian National Railways and possibly also from the Aluminum Company of Canada

Limited. The committee of course will have charge of the conduct of its own meetings, but we hope it will be possible to get the full story of the branch line and the developments that are to take place in the Kitimat area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the representative in this house of the area where the whole Alcan development project, including the proposed railway line, is located, it would be impossible for me to let this resolution pass without saying a few words on it. Naturally the first words I say in this connection, on my own behalf and on behalf of the people of the Skeena district whom I represent here, should express our appreciation to the management of the Canadian National Railways, to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and to the government for the prompt action they are taking to assure adequate transportation facilities in that area at the earliest possible moment, and as soon as they will be needed by the large development which is taking place.
In that connection I would like to invite the Minister of Transport-and again I am sure I am speaking on behalf of those I represent-to come out to that area and be there when this railway is started. I would suggest also that he return to be there when the line is officially opened. In both cases I am sure his presence would be welcome; and if he wished to make it even more enjoyable for us he might bring along his parliamentary assistant as well.
I do not want to let this occasion pass without expressing one other word of approval and commendation which I feel is due. I would like in this house to express the very great debt of gratitude owed not only by the people of Skeena, not only by the people of British Columbia but by the whole of Canada to Hon. E. T. Kenney, minister of lands and forests of British Columbia, for his many years of effort which have culminated in the introduction of a bill to build a railway from Terrace to Kitimat. This railway line is just a symbol of the tremendous development going on in that area at the present time, a development so great I noticed it was mentioned in the British House of Commons no later than the 21st of last month.
I am one of those, Mr. Speaker, who have been guilty-if "guilty" is the word-from time to time of asking for subsidies and artificial aids to be contributed by governments toward the promotion of some industrial developments. This particular development is based on nothing of that sort. It is a sound
Canadian National Railways business proposition following sound business lines, because the resources of power are there. It will be able to carry itself, and in so doing it will be part of the development of a very large, practically new area of this dominion. It is such a large development that its beneficial effects will be felt far and wide. Our suburbs as far south as and including Vancouver will gain some benefits from this development. It is a fact that in such areas as Vancouver-and Vancouver is not alone; this is also true in cities like Toronto, Montreal and other large places you always find people expressing surprise that there should be a major development somewhere else. I do not think there is any call for any Canadian city to express surprise that major development is taking place in what they very often picturesquely call the hinterland, because it was on the hinterland that all these cities were built.
Turning to the line itself, I understand from the minister it is expected that this railway will be completed in the fall of 1954. It is expected by the Aluminum Company of Canada that their smelter will be in the initial stages of production at the same time. I mention that fact for a reason. I have heard the criticism, not in this house or in these buildings but in other parts of the country, that this line was being built in order to enable the company to take in materials for the construction of their smelter and townsite, and that from then on the line would be a dead issue. I point out that the line will not be completed until at least the first stage of smelter construction has been completed. Therefore the purpose of the line obviously is to serve an operating smelter, not to make it possible to build one.
The development of which this is only a part has its lessons which we have to learn. It has a very definite lesson, I respectfully submit, for the government of the Dominion of Canada. They are not only going to have to provide that area with a railway line, through the agency of the Canadian National Railways; it is going to be absolutely essential that the other services provided by the dominion government be brought up to the same standard of development which the Canadian National is now proposing to introduce. Increased population of course will result from this area of industrial development; but I might mention that a great increase has already taken place in the population of that area. Little communities which 18 months ago could number their population by the dozen, or in some cases by the hundred, are now numbering their population by the hundreds and thousands. When I first saw the town of Terrace some 13 years

Canadian National Railways ago it would have had a hard time to count a total population of 700. Today its population undoubtedly will be over 3,000 and in another 18 months over 5,000. Terrace is just one example. The population which is moving into that area will have to be given all those services for which this government and this parliament assume responsibility.
I think it would be only fair to say that this part of British Columbia is going through a period of expansion which will last about five years. During that period it will make the same gain in population and industrial activity that the extreme southeastern part of British Columbia made in forty years. The development based on the Kimberley mine and the Trail smelter, so well known to the members for Kootenay East and Kootenay West, is roughly the same size and importance as this development will be. 1 know that country. It took it from 1913 to the present time to build up to the extent it has. We are going to go through the same development in a period of five years, and we are certainly going to suffer some growing pains in doing so.
This line will run from Terrace to Kitimat. At Terrace we have a municipality which will shortly be a flourishing city. Eighteen months ago the population of Kitimat was 42, including Indians. Within the foreseeable future, say within three to five years, we will have a city comparable to Arvida. The development which will take place at Kitimat is primarily, as we all know, in connection with an aluminum smelter. But this railway line we are now asking the Canadian National Railways to build is not a one industry affair. It is not being built to serve only one company. According to its own figures the company proposes to eventually develop over
1,500,000	horsepower. It proposes to develop immediately 450,000 horsepower, and to use immediately 300,000 horsepower. So 150,000 horsepower of electrical energy will be immediately available. As their electrical production increases it is to be expected that further surplus electricity will be available for sale to other industries. We know of several who are now planning to go in there. So I would not like the impression to get out that this railway is being built solely for one company.
There are those in the country-I am not referring to anyone in this house-who take every possible opportunity to criticize anything in the nature of improvement or expansion of Canadian industry. They will raise the claim that Canada is building a railway for one private company, but that is not
the case. I have no intention of talking out a measure in which I have such an interest.
I shall close by saying this. It would be surprising if the member who represented the district in which such a tremendous development was taking place did not take a tremendous pride in what is going on in his own constituency. I should like to say further that I take great pride in the knowledge that this tremendous development, which will be of such great value to Canada, was engendered and brought to fulfilment in an industrial and economic climate fostered by a Liberal government.

speechtext:
So that this resolution will pass, 1 will not keep the house beyond eleven o'clock. I should like to add my voice, however, as another member from British Columbia, to most of what has been said by the member for Skeena (Mr. Apple-whaite). I should like particularly to express the pleasure which all of us from that province feel in the development which is now taking place in an area which suffers so much from climatic and other conditions. These disadvantages are now, to a large extent, going to be compensated by this tremendous industrial development, and thus people will overcome their otherwise natural disinclination to visit that area.
In a serious vein, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of pleasure, particularly to any member from any part of British Columbia, to see the development which is going on in that province, and which has been fostered and is taking place in an atmosphere which is probably unique in the history of this country. One has only to recall the fact that our province has increased in population by fifty per cent or more in the last ten years to realize what is going on out there. It is true that as yet we do not match the pace of the industrial development of Ontario, although in proportion we come very close to it. I think it is correct to say that we match, proportionately, the pace of the development in Quebec.
A list of the projects which are now on the map for British Columbia, starting if you like at the project of Alcan; the project of Kitimat; followed by the prospect of increased and expanded oil refinery capacity; followed by prospects of a tremendous increase in all sorts of natural energy which will flow from the introduction into British Columbia of natural gas from the Peace river district from both Alberta and our own province; accompanied at the same time by tremendous developments in the pulp and paper industry, which both accompany and are assisted by the possibilities of the chemical industry which flow also from the introduction of

natural gas; all those things, Mr. Speaker, indicate that if the twentieth century belongs to Canada, certainly the second half of the twentieth century belongs to British Columbia. There was one thing particularly which the member for Skeena said which impressed me, and which I think will be obvious to all members. It was that these tremendous industrial developments, accompanied as they are by an increase in population, make increased demands upon the services provided by government as well as those provided by private industry.
I regret to say that there are not many minutes left in which to lay before the house some of the ideas with which I wanted to deal in that connection.
